News.title: Family of 13-year-old hit-and-run victim heartbroken as killer set for release after just two years
News.content:
THE family of a 13-year-old boy killed by a hit-and-run drunk are devastated the driver could be freed from prison after just two years.

Kaylan Hippsley died in 2024 when he was hit by Harley Whiteman, 19, who then abused paramedics treating the teen.



He was jailed for six years, increased to nine after Kaylan’s family appealed.

But Whiteman, now in an open prison, has since had his sentence cut to just four years, so is to be freed in October under Labour’s early release scheme.



Kaylan’s family in the Rhondda, South Wales, urged PM Andy Burnham to keep him locked up.

His sister Chloe Williams said: “We as a family are calling on Andy Burnham to review our case and demand immediate action.

“The decision to move Kaylan’s killer to an open prison after barely two years goes against everything the Court of Appeal ruled.

“It feels like justice has been stolen from us.

“We will not accept this. We demand that he serves his full sentence behind closed doors. Kaylan deserves nothing less.”

And cousin Julie Craig said: “It beggar’s belief that after two years he’s allowed back into the community.



“It’s absolutely devastating.

“This just feels like a kick in the teeth.”

News.title: Cops seize three tons of cocaine worth over £200m at British port after drugs concealed in bananas sent from Colombia
News.content:
NEARLY three tons of cocaine with a street value of £232million was discovered in a container of bananas.

Border Force officers with sniffer dogs found the drugs in the consignment from Colombia.



The National Crime Agency was alerted and officers seized the dope at London ­Gateway Port in Essex on Friday.

They then watched as a man in a truck drove the shipment — minus the cocaine — to a warehouse, where a crime gang had “a massive panic” on finding the drugs missing.



The NCA raided the site near Buntingford, Herts, and eight Brits and one Dutchman were arrested.

A source said: “They must have thought they had been turned over by criminals but, worse than that, the NCA went steaming in.



“It’s the biggest seizure of cocaine in the last few years and this will cause serious grief in the criminal underworld.

“There could be massive fall-outs over the loss of the drugs.’’

The nine arrested, most in their 20s, have all been bailed ­pending enquiries.

NCA officers were still searching the warehouse on Monday.



The largest ever seizure of cocaine in the UK came in Southampton in 2024.

A total of 5.7 tons was found hidden in banana containers heading to Europe from Colombia.

News.title: Fuel prices have soared and what has Labour done about it? Sat back and raked in an extra £1BILLION in tax
News.content:
ANDY BURNHAM says he wants to “pull every single lever” to bring down the cost of living.

He’s off on a summer tour of the country, in what No10 calls “listening mode”, asking ordinary people how the Government can make their lives easier.



It’s a nice image — the Prime Minister, freshly back from holiday, rolling up his sleeves and heading out to the regions to hear from the public before he’s even properly unpacked his boxes in Downing Street.

I’d love to believe it. I really would.



But if these last few months have taught us anything, it’s that the political elite still seem completely disconnected from how the real world operates outside the M25 and the M60.

The latest figures from the RAC, released last week, tell their own story.

Petrol has climbed to around 161p a litre.

Diesel has surged to roughly 181p.

Filling a standard 55-litre family diesel car has breached the £100 mark once again.

Since the Iran conflict flared up, UK drivers have been forced to find an extra £5.5billion just to keep their tanks full for work.



Around 70 per cent of that has landed on diesel drivers — the tradespeople, the hauliers, the people who actually keep this country moving.

And what has the Government done about it?

It has sat back and let the Treasury quietly pocket close to £1billion in extra VAT.

As pump prices rise, so does the taxman’s take.

Ministers are, in effect, making money from the very crisis that is squeezing working families and pushing up the cost of everything else.



So while Mr Burnham talks about pulling every lever, the lever he really should be reaching for is the one sitting right in front of him at the pumps.

In his first week in the job, he announced a cut to VAT on household energy bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, both presented as “everyday fixes”.

Fine as far as they go — but they don’t go very far at all for the millions of people whose working lives simply cannot be organised around a bus timetable.

Like so many metropolitan leaders before him, Burnham seems to have a shaky grasp of how towns, villages and rural counties actually function.

For millions of people, driving isn’t a lifestyle choice.



It’s how they earn their living.

A nurse doing a 2am shift at a regional hospital doesn’t benefit from a bus fare freeze.

A care worker doing her rounds between elderly patients can’t plan her day around a patchy rural timetable.

A plumber, an electrician, a carpenter — none of them can lug their tools on to the number 42.

Farmers and hauliers, who keep the supermarket shelves stocked, certainly can’t move Britain’s goods by public transport.



These are the people generating the tax revenue that keeps the country running, and yet they’re the ones being squeezed hardest to pay for it.

Even if you wanted to swap the car for the bus, good luck.

One in five buses fails to run on time.

Average bus speeds in major cities have dropped by 23 per cent since 2010.

In London, the average bus now crawls along at 8.6mph during peak hours — slower than 50 years ago.



In Manchester and Birmingham, congested routes barely outpace a brisk walk.

Meanwhile, 15 per cent of the entire bus network outside London has vanished since the pandemic.

At the same time, Burnham is happy to take credit for a rail fare freeze that his predecessors actually announced, even as a season ticket from Crawley to London Bridge still costs £4,856 a year — around a fifth of a minimum-wage worker’s salary.



Bus caps and rail freezes make for tidy photo opportunities.

They give increasingly image-conscious politicians something shiny to stand next to.

But they mean very little to people whose jobs cannot be squeezed into a timetable dreamt up in a city-centre office.

Those people need help at the pumps, and they need it now.

The existing 5p fuel-duty cut, still in place thanks to The Sun’s Keep It Down campaign, predates this latest crisis and simply isn’t enough on its own.



Cutting VAT on household energy bills is welcome, but it won’t take a single penny off the cost of filling a van.

Other countries have already worked this out. Italy cut diesel taxes by 15p a litre.

Greece targeted reductions of up to 13p for hauliers and professional drivers.

Ireland slashed excise duty by 27p on diesel and 23p on petrol.

Even further afield, Thailand, the UAE, South Korea and Australia have all stepped in with targeted relief.



Britain, by contrast, has simply let the Treasury enjoy the windfall while treating drivers as an easy top-up to the public purse.

So here’s my message to Mr Burnham as he sets off on his listening tour: Actually listen.

Cut VAT from 20 to 15 per cent and you knock 7p off a litre of petrol and 8p off diesel overnight.

Pair that with a genuine duty cut and you’d finally be delivering something that matters to the people who keep this country moving, rather than another photo beside a bus.

Cheaper transport is great for those who can use it.



But Britain’s tradespeople, carers, farmers and hauliers have no alternative but to drive.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They’re not a bottomless cash machine, and they’re certainly not the enemy.

It’s time to stop posing beside buses and start backing the workers who actually keep Britain moving.

News.title: Andy Burnham must find a way to keep PC Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars or face public’s fury
News.content:
Find a way

ANDY Burnham has apparently been told by hand-wringing civil servants that it’s “not possible” to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.

They need to be told to try harder.



There are a few hundred inmates serving time for manslaughter.

Burnham needs to order officials to find a way to bar those serving the longest sentences from being freed.



That would minimise the threat of any legal challenges from lags and ensure remorseless thugs Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole stayed behind bars.

As the petition to keep Bowers and Cole locked up ticks up towards one million, the public’s demand is crystal-clear.

They expect Burnham to meet the hopes HE raised in the first place.

The Prime Minister must realise he has the power to overrule Government officials and lawyers all too often stuck in their comforting bubble of State uselessness and a lack of accountability.

With a massive majority behind him, this issue boils down to a question of sheer will.

Push boat out

HOW much longer must Brits put up with migrants and people-smugglers making a mockery of our open borders?



Yesterday’s raid on UK waters by a mega-dinghy carrying a record 230 illegal asylum-seekers opened up a new front in the small boats crisis.

It’s clear that far from the gangs being smashed, the criminals are running rings around French cops.

Their new tactic of packing as many as possible on a single craft — enough yesterday to fill a Boeing Dreamliner jet plane — could soon make 1,000 arrivals a daily occurrence.

It’s not just the sheer numbers. The cost is becoming astronomical, too.

In 2023, the Home Office estimated each migrant costs taxpayers £106,000 minimum over four years in free housing, healthcare and other benefits.



That means yesterday’s mega dinghy could cost nearly £25MILLION.

That’s a staggeringly high price to pay while Burnham & Co leave Britain without any kind of plan.

Betting slip

FOR a bloke who claims to love sport and champion working-class culture, Andy Burnham seems surprisingly keen to demonise anyone who likes a flutter.

The Prime Minister says he will boost our High Streets by making it harder to open vape shops and . . . bookmakers.

But bookies are not anti-social enterprises. They provide good jobs and help keep sports like racing and rugby league afloat.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In any event, it’s hard not to conclude Burnham’s plan is purely performative.

Thanks to Labour’s tax raids on gambling, what’s actually happening is hundreds of betting shops are closing.

News.title: Brit tourist, 66, dies in horror parasailing accident while on holiday with husband in Benidorm
News.content:
HOLS TRAGEDY Brit tourist, 66, dies in horror parasailing accident while on holiday with husband in Benidorm

A BRITISH tourist has died in a horror parasailing accident in Benidorm while on holiday with her husband.

The 66-year-old crashed onto rocks after a powerful gust of wind caused the line tethering her parachute to the boat to snap.



The woman went into cardiac arrest, but desperate efforts to revive her she was pronounced dead at the scene.

It was not immediately clear whether the unnamed holidaymaker’s husband was injured in the ordeal.



He is believed to have suffered broken ribs and was reportedly “walking wounded” following the horror crash.

The tragedy unfolded in Benidorm’s Rincon de Loix are at around 6pm on Monday after a sudden change in weather conditions.

Prior to the incident, a red flag was raised, warning holidaymakers at the famous Costa Blanca resort.

Witnesses described chaotic scenes as the parasail spiralled out of control.

After the line snapped, the couple hurtled towards jagged rocks as they were left at the mercy of the wind.

One witness said: “It was clear they were going to crash.”



A police investigation has been launched and remains ongoing.

This comes after a 16-year-old British cheerleader was killed in a horror boat accident while holidaying with her family.

Abbie Lainton, from Swindon, died “in a terrible accident” off the coast of a Caribbean island that also left her two siblings injured.

Abbie died after she was badly burnt when a tourist boat carrying around 35 people suddenly ignited and blew up off the coast of the Dominican Republic.

She was rushed to intensive care but died three days later.



Her siblings remain in hospital.

Authorities said 24 people were injured with 11 taken to hospital for treatment for burns.

Gisell Segovia and her husband Navin Torres, 35, were on the boat when it blew up and saw Abbie badly injured after the explosion.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Navin told The Sun how he was with the Brit teen as she fought for her life, calling Abbie “a warrior” who “did not go out without a fight”.

Authorities have not yet revealed the cause of the fire but have launched an investigation.

News.title: PC Andrew Harper’s colleague says Government is ‘spitting in the face of police’ over killers’ early release
News.content:
ONE of the first cops on the scene after PC Andrew Harper was dragged to his death has accused the Government of “spitting in the faces of police officers”.

Retired dog-handler Chris Bushnell spoke out as Downing Street ruled out an exemption that would stop PC Harper’s killers getting early release.



No 10’s rejection means that two of the officer’s three smirking killers, Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, will be free within months — despite one of the biggest-ever public petitions demanding they be kept locked up.

Chris, 59, drove after the cold-blooded burglary gang that dragged 28-year-old newlywed Andrew to his death in August 2019.



He told the Old Bailey how the gang tried to ram his car with their Seat Toledo before fleeing the scene to their homes on traveller sites.

Chris spoke of the pain he still endures over his colleague’s death — and his anger that two of the killers are due to be freed.



He said: “When I first heard they could be let out early, I was shaking. It’s absolutely outrageous.

“I am angry with them, but I’m also angry with the Government. They’re spitting in the face of police officers.”

Chris said the prospect of early release will impact and demoralise many officers traumatised by losing a colleague in such a violent way.

He said: “This belittles them. It makes them feel worthless.”



Chris, who retired from Thames Valley Police in 2022, said he will “never forgive” Andrew’s killers for what they did.

He added: “To think these people could be out within weeks is appalling. The Government has to understand that this was the death of a police officer.

“Andy did his duty that night. The least they can do is show respect.”

Chris was working on a West Berkshire dog unit when Andrew was killed, and recalled having a cup of tea with him earlier in the day.



He said: “He was so friendly and always asked about the dog. He was an animal-lover, a nice lad.”

Late that night Chris was alerted on his police radio about a burglary gang that stole a £10,000 Honda quad bike from a house near Sulhamstead, Berkshire.

Unbeknown to Chris, Andrew had been lassoed round his ankles by a trailing rope from the teenage traveller gang’s car.

Andrew — due to go on honeymoon with wife Lissie after he finished his shift — was dragged more than a mile down a country lane.



Chris was waiting in a lay-by for the suspects’ vehicle when he saw it emerge from the darkness without its lights on.

He later fought back tears as he told the Old Bailey how he initially believed Andrew’s body was a deer carcass — before realising it was human as it accelerated away.

Chris pursued the vehicle and came to a fork in the road, telling jurors when he looked to the right he saw the Seat driving at him.

He said: “Without warning it was coming straight towards me.

“I then reared to the left. I took the view that they had deliberately chosen to drive straight at me.”



Chris gave chase after the vehicle until an inspector instructed him over the radio to stop.

In the meantime, Andrew’s patrol partner radioed: “My crewmate is gone. I don’t know where he is.”

Minutes later Chris received the devastating news that his colleague had been killed.

He said: “I’ve seen people die before. I’ve seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful.”

Chris was left “numb and in disbelief”.



He received counselling and support from the Police Federation, and revisits the scene of Andrew’s death every year.

He said: “I will never get over it.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A petition organised by PC Harper’s Police Federation branch — demanding his killers are kept behind bars — was set to hit 900,000 signatures on Monday evening.

Aileen O’Connor, chair of the branch, said: “The public are speaking loudly and clearly. The silence from the Government is deafening. What they’re doing is indefensible.”

News.title: Special Concorde flights, 500k flocking to Cornwall & biggest ever power surge… How UK stopped for 1999 total eclipse
News.content:
CROWDED on to rooftops, ships, hillsides and bridges, millions of us were awestruck as we witnessed 1999’s total solar eclipse.

The date was August 11, and it was the first time this country had experienced the celestial spectacle for 72 years.



No one wanted to miss it. Like the audience at a 3D movie, they wore special glasses to protect their eyes so they could gaze to the heavens as the moon covered the sun.

Factories closed, roads were clogged by traffic jams and trials at the Old Bailey in London were even briefly paused so that judges, lawyers, and jurors could watch day turn to night in the first full eclipse visible in the UK since June 29, 1927.



Tomorrow, the nation will once again have the chance to witness this incredible phenomenon when 90 to 95 per cent of the sun is hidden from view in a dramatic partial eclipse.

These cosmic coincidences happen because the sun is about 400 times larger than the moon, and about 400 times further away from Earth, making them appear almost the same size in our sky.



This allows us to witness wonders such as a breathtaking total solar eclipse, where the moon can perfectly cover the sun.​

So be sure you do not miss out on tomorrow’s marvel because the next full one is not due until September 23, 2090.

Dr Cyrielle Opitom, a member of the Royal Astronomical Society council, tells The Sun: “If the moon had been just a little bit further away from us there would never be a total eclipse.”

The moon passes just above or below the sun every month.



Normally, when this happens, the moon is not visible because it is obscured by the solar glare.

But during an eclipse, the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun.

In another stroke of random good fortune, Cornwall should again be the best place to view the phenomena.



In 1999, the “path of totality” — meaning the point at which there is a 100 per cent eclipse — passed between Penzance and Falmouth on the peninsula of England.

This time, around 95 per cent of the sun will be blotted out above Cornwall just after 7pm tomorrow.

Edinburgh and London will both see a 91 per cent eclipse, while it will be 93 per cent in Belfast and 92 per cent in Newcastle.

Anyone wishing to enjoy a “totality” tomorrow needs to head elsewhere in Europe.

The most western point of Iceland, a tiny part of Portugal and a large chunk of northern Spain are in its path.



To celebrate, Bjork is headlining a rave near Iceland’s capital, Reykjavik, and there are seven festivals in Spain.

Other fanatics will be out in the Atlantic on specially chartered ships to catch the historic moment.

A solar eclipse does happen once every 18 months somewhere on Earth and there are obsessives who try to witness as many as possible, though not all are as dramatic as tomorrow’s.



Dr Opitom, who saw a full one on the horizon from an observatory in Chile in 2019, says: “It is absolutely spectacular.”

Back in 1999, two Concordes were sent up by British Airways so that 200 passengers paying £1,500 per seat had the best chance of getting a clear view of the event from the air.

On the ground, a total eclipse lasts for around two minutes, but due to the supersonic craft travelling at twice the speed of sound, they got to enjoy it for some six minutes.

The number of people on the tiny Channel island of Alderney swelled fivefold, from 2,000 to 10,000, because it was one of the best spots to see the incredible sight.

Around 250,000 extra tourists headed for Devon and Cornwall 27 years ago, and there were traffic jams on the way to Land’s End, one of the first places in Europe to go fully dark at 11.11am.



As the eclipse started, the birds went quiet and ducks tucked their heads in their wing feathers, believing it was night-time.

Once it was over, the air was filled with a “dawn chorus” as they woke up again.

The temperature also dropped, but the South West was largely cloudy so onlookers only caught glimpses of the total eclipse.

There were some parts of the British Isles where the skies were clear enough to fully enjoy the eerie moment, particularly the North East of England.



Tomorrow, there is far more chance of the clouds parting as the heatwave continues.

Most of Britain should be sunny until the moon begins to obscure the rays just after 6pm.

Whether it is cloudy or not, one rule always applies — never look at the sun with the naked eye.

Even with the moon covering most of the giant fireball, it can still blind onlookers.



Wearing regular sunglasses is no protection at all and only eclipse glasses bearing the ISO 12312-2 safety standard should be used.

Make sure they are bought from a trusted retailer because fake ones are being sold online.

Despite repeated warnings about the risk in 1999, hospitals across the country received hundreds of calls from people complaining about eye problems in the aftermath of the eclipse.

If you want to keep the party going this year, then there is a good reason to stay out beyond 6pm.



That is because there is the added bonus of the Perseid meteor shower.

With the moon in its new moon phase, and its light diminished, during the Perseid’s peak it should be much more visible over the UK.

Keep your eyes peeled between midnight tomorrow and 5.30am on Thursday.

The eclipse will also be a far more relaxing occasion this time around.



In 1999, with the turn of the millennium just over four months away, there were a lot of predictions that the darkened skies heralded the end of the world.

Verses from the 16th century French astrologer Nostradamus had been interpreted to predict “fire from heaven” in that year.

Fashion designer Paco Rabanne had even warned that the MIR space station would plummet to Earth and that Paris would be destroyed.

As with all the millennium scare stories, no disasters befell anyone.

In fact, after the eclipse passed Britain on its way towards the Middle East and India, everyone returned to their desks to switch back on their computers and make themselves a cup of tea.



The power surge was the biggest the UK had ever experienced.

With a peak demand of 36,150 megawatts, it was even higher than when the nation tuned in to watch Prince Charles marry Lady Diana Spencer in 1981.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And as the skies lightened there was one other lesson we learned from 1999.

Nothing can ever truly eclipse The Sun.

News.title: Residents of tiny Welsh community left ‘blindsided’ after migrant families are secretly moved into former village hall
News.content:
RESIDENTS of a tiny ­community say they have been blindsided by plans to house asylum seekers in their old village hall.

Locals were expecting the new homes to be put up for rent on the market but were shocked to discover the Home Office had already moved migrant families in.



Earlier this year, the Government promised to stop housing ­asylum seekers in newbuilds after The Sun revealed an entire street had been designated as migrant housing.

But out of the 15 new units in the North Wales ­village, 13 have been taken over by Clearsprings, the Government contractor run by asylum billionaire Graham King.



Gronant in Flintshire has a population of just 1,600, with residents fearing new arrivals will put pressure on stretched resources.

Kerrie Cox, 39, lives near the new asylum accommodation and said: “No-one was notified whatsoever.



“I was washing my car and a blacked out minibus arrived and seven people got out, five males and two females.

“We had been told the properties were to be leased out or sold with a promise of them going as social housing.

“Everyone is in shock. We have had the police here all day and night.

“We don’t normally have a police presence around here.



“I feel betrayed by the Government as a taxpayer.”

Julie Tuson, 65, said: “We want to know who is coming and vetted.

“If we want a better Britain, we all have to be involved. We were not told about it. I feel absolutely betrayed by the Government.”



Her partner Robert Bagshaw, 64, said: “They wouldn’t have a ­consultation beforehand because they would know the outcome. It’s definitely the wrong area.”

Laurie Gilmour, 29, said: “The feeling in the village is one of anger and uncertainty.

“It’s about not knowing who will be there. Who would want a load of random people moving into a village?

“It’s the wrong area. There’s nothing here.”

Keith Williams, 57, commented: “Our homeless people should get priority. You see ex-soldiers like myself on the street.”



Councillor Glyn Banks is seeking a meeting between the area’s Labour MP Becky Gittins, police and representatives of worried residents.

He told The Sun: “It’s just too big for a small village.”

Resident Joanne Gilmore has started a petition urging the council to reconsider.



She pointed to problems such as “limited access to healthcare, education and employment opportunities”.

Flintshire council said: “They are not illegal immigrants.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They are individuals exercising their legal right to claim asylum and deserve to be treated with compassion and respect.”

A ­Government spokesman said: “The concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms.”

News.title: More than two-thirds of England now in drought
News.content:
Chair of the National Drought Group, Tony Grayling, said that drought conditions will continue to worsen until "significant and sustained rainfall".

The week ahead is forecast to remain mostly dry, as the fifth heatwave of the year intensifies, although there are signs of some rain coming into the UK on Sunday.

"We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment," Grayling said in a statement, adding that "we need everyone's help in using a little less water to make sure our current water reserves last".

The National Drought Group said most of England is now experiencing a flash drought, which "develops very quickly" and is "brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures."

Yorkshire and north-east England have been moved to "prolonged dry weather" status, which is the stage before drought.

Nowhere in England is now under a "normal" status.

Hot weather is continuing, with the UK Health Security Agency issuing amber heat health alerts for all of England apart from the North East from Tuesday at 09:00 BST until Friday at 21:00 BST.

An amber alert means significant impacts "are likely" across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.

The continued hot and dry conditions increase the risk of wildfires. Dozens of firefighters are currently battling a fire in the New Forest, which earlier on Monday was estimated to be the size of 140 football pitches (247 acres).

Scotland and Northern Ireland have not been experiencing drought conditions and are expected to see spells of heavy rain over the week ahead.

Scotland does not declare drought, but monitors "water scarcity".

While conditions have improved in some parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some eastern areas remain in the two most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

News.title: New Forest firefighting to continue overnight as cars abandoned
News.content:
A firefighting operation will continue into the night to quell a blaze which began on Sunday and has affected one square kilometre (250 acres) of the New Forest national park in Hampshire.

It began when a van caught fire on the A31 near Bratley Wood, forcing motorists to abandon more than 20 vehicles.

Lindsey Legg was with her husband and three children when they were forced to stop by police and leave their car. She said "women and children were walking with buggies" on the road and it had been "pretty scary".

National Highways said the A31 dual carriageway through the New Forest would remain closed in both directions until further notice.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service said more than 120 firefighters had been working "in challenging conditions" to contain the blaze.

Forestry England said the blaze was under control, but it expected the firefighting operation to continue for several days.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to stop betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and "for many people, the high streets they grew up with have become unrecognisable".

BBC News has exposed organised crime on high streets across the country, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes and vapes, selling cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco or up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham said "the rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for".

He added: "That's not on. I said we would improve Britain's high streets, and that's exactly what we are starting to do.

"We're putting communities back in control and giving local people a real say over what opens on their high street."

News.title: GB's Amy Hunt wins European 100m gold
News.content:
Amy Hunt had her coming of age moment as she stormed to 100m glory to claim her first senior international title and deliver Britain's first gold medal of the European Athletics Championships.

Hunt announced herself on the sport's global stage last year with world 200m silver in Tokyo - the first individual international medal of her senior career.

Having backed that up with Commonwealth 100m silver two weeks ago, the 24-year-old would not be denied gold this time in Birmingham.

"I have had such a string of silvers and I was starting to get a bit fed up with it, so I thought it was time for gold," Hunt, who won in 11 seconds flat, told BBC Sport.

"My parents gifted me these gold earrings to finally level up, because I wear all-silver jewellery.

"They said it was time for gold - they left me that note two nights ago - so it made me quite emotional.

"It was definitely time for me to come of age here."

It was Britain's second medal on the opening day of action after the hosts took silver in the mixed 4x400m relay.

Yemi Mary John held off Dutch athlete Myrte van der Schoot on the home straight to bring a British quartet also featuring Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich and Toby Harries home in three minutes 10.47 seconds, behind winners Norway (3:09.62).

News.title: Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat
News.content:
A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel.

It breaks the previous record set in July, when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel.

The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday.

A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route.

A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels".

French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy".

The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added.

French maritime officials said 30 migrants were left stranded by the tide during a boarding attempt at Berck beach in northern France.

They were brought to safety by maritime and land-based rescue services, the statement from France's Channel and North Sea Maritime Prefecture said.

The boat carrying 232 people continued its journey, before two passengers requested assistance and were taken to Calais by a French Navy rescue ship, the statement added.

News.title: No evidence of data breach after Chinese-made component found in Navy drones, MoD says
News.content:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said there is no evidence to suggest a systems or data breach after the Royal Navy's new sea drones were found to include a Chinese-made component.

During what the MoD called a "routine cyber vulnerability assessment" of the drones, the cameras were found to have sent a squark â also known as a heartbeat communication â to a Chinese IP address.

A squark can signal when the system is switched on, is functioning properly, but it can also carry location information.

"A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally," an MoD spokesperson said.

"Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment," the MoD added.

This is embarrassing for the MoD which, like most Nato countries, has banned Chinese components from military equipment - not least over fears of spying.

The K3 Scout sea drones can remotely carry out surveillance, and according to their supplier, "support a wide range of mission profiles including maritime awareness, force protection, logistics and precision strike".

The supplier of the Royal Navy's 20 new K3 sea drones, Kraken, said it was given assurances about security. But a third party supplier of the drone camera still had Chinese-made components.

Kraken has said it is confident no sensitive information has been shared.

The story was first reported by The Telegraph., external

The security lapse has been addressed, but it is a reminder of the heavy dominance on Chinese supply chains.

Even the defence sector â which has taken measures to prevent espionage â still struggles to source materials, and technologies that are China free, or as cheap.

News.title: Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears
News.content:
The death of a Treasury worker who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers was "materially contributed" to by her employers, an inquest has heard.

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Surrey Coroner's Court heard the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy which would have made clear that if the allegations were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said it was "considering the findings carefully".

In a statement to the press, Moffat's family said they believed the Treasury failed in its duty of care.

"When she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced her career and reputation had been destroyed," they added.

The inquest, in which a conclusion of suicide was recorded, heard that on 19 May Moffat went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

She was told of allegations she had shared sensitive personal information about colleagues, obtained as part of her job.

Moffat, from London, denied this.

News.title: Cocaine worth £232m found in banana shipment
News.content:
Cocaine with a street value of Â£232m was discovered hidden in a large shipment of bananas from South America.

The 2.9-tonne (2,900kg) haul was smuggled into London Gateway Port in Thurrock, Essex, on Thursday.

The drugs were removed from the container and then delivered to an address near Buntingford, Hertfordshire, where Border Force officers swooped in.

They arrested nine men allegedly connected to the bust, who were later released on bail.

Border Force had been tipped off about the illegal consignment by the National Crime Agency.

News.title: Vandals target playground before it has even opened
News.content:
A play area that cost more than Â£178,000 was vandalised days before it was due to open.

Knowsley Council leader Graham Morgan said he was "absolutely furious" that every piece of play equipment at the Finch Woods play park in Halewood, Knowsley had been spray painted with graffiti over the weekend.

Trees and safety surfacing were also damaged and rubbish was left strewn across the site, with the cost of the damage estimated to run into thousands of pounds.

Morgan condemned the "mindless vandalism", saying "it is the cost to the community that sickens me the most".

News.title: Antiques stolen in 16th Century manor house raid
News.content:
More than 20 antiques were stolen from a National Trust (NT) property during a break-in last month, it has been revealed.

The silver, pewter and brass items were taken from the 16th Century manor house at Baddesley Clinton in Warwickshire, on 30 July.

The most notable piece of the 25 taken was a Georgian silver salver engraved with the coat of arms of the Ferrers, the family who resided at the house for about five centuries, the NT said.

"We very much hope the objects will be returned, so they can be enjoyed by everyone," a spokesperson added.

News.title: MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments
News.content:
A newly-elected MSP has apologised for the hurt caused by comments in which they talked of the "demonisation" of rape.

Scottish Green Party politician Q Manivannan has also faced criticism for suggesting rape is a "spectrum of things" during a podcast recorded before they were elected to the Scottish Parliament.

Earlier, the Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) - which represents four rape crisis centres - said there is "no hierarchy of rape" and warned the MSP not to minimise sexual violence.

In a statement, Manivannan said clips from the podcast had been "selectively edited" but said they were "sorry" for the upset, and insisted they would never seek to diminish a rape survivor's experience.

The comments, which were made during The Subjective Space podcast , externalrecorded last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.

News.title: Owner of 250-year-old Grade II-listed windmill gave it colourful makeover without permission
News.content:
Dr Eiddwen Jones, 85, is the great-great-great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Jones, who she said was the first miller at Llynon mill in 1776.

He managed the property in the village of Llanddeusant, Anglesey, until he died in his nineties.

She said the windmill should be repainted in whitewash as it is a historical building, and traditionally "that's how the mills were".

The author, whose family moved from Anglesey to Flintshire 150 years ago, said she did not agree that the windmill was painted in the first place to celebrate the Eisteddfod.

She has visited the windmill several times throughout her life where Thomas Jones' name is painted inside, and said he "would have turned in his grave, I believe," if he had known about its new appearance.

Jones added that it looked "very impressive in its original colour" when driving towards it.

"It's been made fun of now rather than kept the fact that it was a historical building and that people have been working there for a couple of centuries," she said.

Holt said the mill can be hard to find for visitors, as it is not close to the A55 road.

But the new colours have sparked a lot of interest.

With winters especially proving difficult with fewer people coming, he added: "I have a duty to ensure the future of the mill for the next generation."

He apologised to the local authority, saying he "realises that they [the council] are only doing their job and I know that I have broken the rules".

But he added: "I'm struggling and the winter is hard, but painting the mill has attracted more visitors here and helped me pay the bills."

He is gathering the opinions of visitors to the mill this summer to make a case to the council.

News.title: Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
News.content:
Nigel Farage said an incident at his London home last year was "directly linked" to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, after counter-terror police reopened an inquiry into it last week.

It relates to what Farage described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025, the BBC understands.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation was handled.

At a Monday press conference, the Reform UK leader said: "I understand this is a completely unprecedented move, and yes, this is directly linked to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, and I'm afraid I just can't tell you any more than that at this stage."

News.title: Consortium advances talks for stake in Liverpool
News.content:
A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.

The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed last month that the group had "expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club".

Bhatia is the son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal and had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.

American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world.

According to Forbes, the 62-year-old has an estimated net worth of $256bn (Â£192bn).

FSG, who bought Liverpool in a Â£300m deal in 2010, previously sold a minority stake in the Anfield side to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity.

BBC Sport contacted FSG about the latest developments, but they had no further comment.

In January, Liverpool became the top-earning Premier League club for the first time, according to analysis from financial firm Deloitte.

The following month the club announced record revenues of Â£703m for 2024-25 financial year.

News.title: Bungalow destroyed in explosion captured on camera
News.content:
A suspected gas explosion that destroyed a bungalow and left a man injured has been caught on camera.

It happened on Cobb Hall Road, Newton Longville, near Milton Keynes on Sunday morning.

Additional footage showed flames and smoke rising from the property afterwards.

Jackie, the California bald eagle who became an internet sensation, died from illness on Monday, weeks after being injured in an attack by two other eagles, officials announced.

For more than a decade, nature lovers watched via an online video feed as Jackie and her partner Shadow tended to their nest each year atop trees near Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains east of Los Angeles.

The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015 and documented the successes and failures of each breeding season. In 2024, Jackie diligently sat on her eggs for more than two and a half days straight after a winter storm blanketed the nest with snow.

The Los Angeles County Department of Parks and Recreation’s San Dimas Raptor Rescue team found Jackie on July 17 following reports that the bird had been involved in a fight with two other eagles and was found to be ill.

Jackie had been receiving medical treatment for three weeks at the Ojai Raptor Center, where she was treated for a variety of ailments including anemia. Despite undergoing a blood transfusion and oxygen therapy, her condition worsened and the center announced the animal's death Monday.

Jackie the bald eagle has died after mystery illness

“We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her,” the center's statement said. “Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her.”

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife is caring for the remains.

Among those who enjoyed monitoring Jackie's nests from afar was biologist Kelly Sorenson, executive director of the Ventana Wildlife Society in central California. While his group was not involved with the Big Bear eagles, he sees their breeding as emblematic of the comeback the species has made in the state over the past decades.

American bald eagles teetered on the brink of extinction until the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were established, leading the species to rebound and be removed from the federal endangered list.

“You want to see a success story like that,” Sorenson said Monday. “Having access to a live cam to see the nesting first hand is very powerful. It brings people in on an emotional level.”

The Associated Press contributed to this article.

President Donald Trump appeared to zone out during an Oval Office announcement on vaccines, prompting a fresh round of mockery online.

On Monday, Trump signed an executive order that calls for reducing the number of vaccines recommended for children and splitting the MMR shot — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — into three individual vaccines.

The order is the latest step in the administration’s campaign to remake the childhood vaccination schedule, led by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long questioned vaccine safety.

During the ceremony, the 80-year-old president appeared to repeatedly close his eyes while seated behind the Resolute Desk — including as Kennedy and National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya spoke beside him.

Videos of the moments quickly circulated on social media.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump appeared to zone out during a vaccine announcement in the Oval Office on Monday with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr ( AFP via Getty Images )

“I love how he pops out of it for a few seconds then closes his eyes again and he's right back in dream land. This is getting ridiculous,” wrote one X user. Another chimed in: “Why doesn't the assembled media speak out about this...they all see it.”

“What a loser,” a third user wrote. “After years of listening to those ‘sleepy joe’ comments…” The remark referred to Trump’s longtime nickname for former President Joe Biden, whom he repeatedly accused of being mentally and physically unfit for office.

Some commenters, however, were more supportive of the president. “In Trump's defense, good Lord, the speaker is boring,” one wrote.

The White House defended Trump, saying: “President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people. President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible President in American history who is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises.”

Trump, the oldest person ever inaugurated as president, has faced persistent scrutiny over his health since returning to the White House, including over moments during official events in which he has appeared to close his eyes for extended periods. One such moment came during Lindsey Graham’s funeral last month.

“The president has severe daytime somnolence,” CNN medical analyst Dr. Jonathan Reiner said in May. “He falls asleep very often. He’s fallen asleep in the Oval Office on multiple occasions with people talking to him, in the cabinet room,” he said. “And chronic insomnia is a severe illness. It can result in an increase in risk of dementia, a decrease in cognitive effects in older people.”

open image in gallery Director of the National Institutes of Health Jay Bhattacharya (L) speaks before President Donald Trump signs an executive order calling for more research and flexibility on vaccines ( AFP via Getty Images )

Trump, for his part, has repeatedly insisted that he is in excellent health. After a physical at Walter Reed in May, the president wrote on Truth Social that “everything” had “checked out PERFECTLY.”

In a YouGov survey conducted last year, 78 percent of respondents said they believed Trump had not been transparent about his physical health.

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

MAGA firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert’s eldest son, Tyler, has been arrested on child exploitation charges.

The Colorado Republican’s 21-year-old son has faced public scrutiny for several years amid multiple run-ins with the law, including past allegations of child abuse relating to his young son.

On Sunday, the Garfield County Sheriff’s Office arrested Tyler, from New Castle, for sexual exploitation of a child and other charges. The sheriff’s office didn’t specify what the charges were related to in a Monday Facebook post, but said he made a $10,000 bond the day of his arrest.

“I love my son. We take these allegations very seriously and pray for everyone affected during this challenging time,” Boebert told The Independent in reaction to the new charges.

Tyler is the oldest of four sons that the Republican shares with ex-husband Jayson Boebert.

open image in gallery Congresswoman Lauren Boebert’s eldest son, Tyler, 21, is facing a new round of child exploitation charges ( Garfield County Sheriff's Office )

The new charges were first reported by the political watchdog group American Muckrakers.

Tyler was charged with sexual exploitation of a child, induce/entice; sexual exploitation of a child, possession with intent; sexual exploitation of a child, video and two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, multiple outlets reported, citing court records filed Thursday.

The alleged offenses began in January 2024, when Tyler was 18. His next court appearance is scheduled for August 19.

Tyler has already been accused of child abuse twice, once in July 2025 and again this past February.

open image in gallery The Congresswoman’s 21-year-old son has been accused of child abuse in the past, relating to his young son ( Getty Images )

On July 11, 2025, Tyler was cited by the Windsor Police Department on a misdemeanor charge of child abuse, Westword, a Denver-based independent news site, reported at the time.

Boebert told Westword that the citation stems from “a miscommunication on monitoring my young grandson that recently led to him getting out of our house.”

Tyler, whose son was born in June 2023, has been “doing a great job getting his life on track as a father and citizen over the past year,” the congresswoman said in her 2025 statement.

“As the citation states, there was absolutely no injury or physical abuse involved,” Boebert said, adding that Child Protective Services met with her family “to ensure we are continuing to provide a safe environment for my boys and my grandson.”

“I am confident this is a one-time incident that we have addressed as a family,” she added.

open image in gallery 'We take these allegations very seriously and pray for everyone affected during this challenging time,' Boebert said in reaction to the new charges ( Getty Images )

On February 15 this year, Tyler was cited on a misdemeanor charge of child abuse without injury again, 9News reported, citing Windsor Police.

Boebert told the local outlet at the time that Tyler was watching his son at her home while she was at an event in her district and the toddler got out of the house.

"A kind woman quickly and safely secured him, and authorities were called as a precaution," Boebert said, adding that there’s “no excuse” for the incident and that she’s “very frustrated” it happened.

A first responder has accused Andy Burnham’s government of “spitting in the faces of police officers” after Downing Street claimed it cannot stop the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.

Former officer Chris Bushnell, who met with PC Harper on the day he died while responding to a quad bike theft in Berkshire in 2019, said he finds the possibility of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers being released early “absolutely outrageous”.

Downing Street faces immense backlash over the situation, with more than 880,000 people signing a petition calling for the pair to remain in jail, while Thames Valley Police Federation is weighing legal action to prevent their release.

On Monday night, PC Harper’s “really angry” mother Debbie Adlam told ITV News she had not heard from the prime minister: “My message is that you want to tour the country, you want to meet the people. You haven’t even got in touch with me. How about coming to see me?”

Newlywed PC Harper, 28, was caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary. Mr Bushnell, then a police constable, was waiting in a lay-by for the suspects’ vehicle when he saw it dragging his colleague’s body behind.

The officer pursued but was ordered to stop through the radio. Minutes later, he was told PC Harper had been killed.

In a statement issued through the Thames Valley Police Federation (TVPF), Mr Bushnell said: “I will never get over it. The guilt. That feeling of ‘what if?’ Today, I feel pretty much how I felt the day after it happened.

“This news about the sentencing – and the offenders being released early – has brought it all back again.”

open image in gallery Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers will be eligible for release from January under current plans ( Thames Valley Police )

Cole and Bowers were convicted of manslaughter in 2020. But under current early release plans, they remain eligible to be freed in January – halfway through their 13-year sentences. The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and would not be eligible for early release.

Some 5,000 inmates are expected to be released early under sentencing changes, down from 6,000 after the exemptions announced as part of an urgent review of the scheme.

Despite growing pressure, Downing Street said yesterday it is “not possible” to exempt “one or two offenders” convicted of manslaughter from early release.

No 10 insisted Mr Burnham is “far from accepting the situation” but played down the prospect of a carve-out to keep Cole and Bowers behind bars.

“He understands the public wants him to go further, and he wanted to go further, but on the wider issue that prisons would have run out of space, police would stop making arrests, it would be impossible to lock up convicted offenders and that would put public safety at untold risk,” the prime minister’s spokesperson said.

But late on Monday night Sky News reported, via a spokesperson at No 10, that Mr Burnham has asked justice secretary Alex Norris to “work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper”, conflicting with Downing Street’s position throughout the day.

Mr Bushnell, who was serving in the West Berkshire dog unit when PC Harper was killed, said: “I’ve seen people die before. I’ve seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful.”

Recounting the court hearings he had to attend, Mr Bushnell said: “They were mocking it. The second time they were in the cells, but we heard they weren’t even paying attention.

open image in gallery Pc Harper, 28, was caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary ( PA Media )

“There was no remorse at all. It was almost a joke to them. Nothing serious. If you have an accident, if you kill someone, you show remorse. I just can’t comprehend it.

“And for all this to be coming up again now is unbelievable. It stirs up all those emotions once more.”

Mr Bushnell, who retired from Thames Valley Police in 2022, added: “We can’t change the verdict. They got their sentences, which were pretty pitiful, to be fair.

“When I first heard a couple of weeks ago there was a chance they could be let out early, I was shaking. It brought everything back.

“To think they could be released early is absolutely outrageous. I’m angry with them, but I’m also angry with the government. They’re spitting in the face of police officers.”

“They have got to serve their full sentence. Andy did his duty that night. The least they can do is show him some respect.”

The national chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, Mark Fairhurst, said he is “positive we could free up additional space and block anybody convicted of manslaughter from early release”.

He added: “You only have to look at the remand population. We’re knocking on to some 17,000 people on remand. I’m sure we could get a couple of thousands of them bailed or tagged with the GPS tag to monitor them electronically. That’s an easy win for this government and I can’t understand why they don’t consider it.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham is facing mounting backlash over the early release scheme ( PA Wire )

It comes despite Mr Burnham earlier this week saying he had “pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do without risking the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing” by excluding sentences for “rape, serious child sex offences and other grooming offences” from eligibility.

Reforms in the Sentencing Act came after prisons came close to running out of space entirely last year, risking the “total breakdown of law and order”, which would leave police unable to make arrests and courts unable to send offenders to custody, the then justice secretary Shabana Mahmood said.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The death of PC Andrew Harper was a horrific crime. Our thoughts are with his family and friends, and we share the anger from the police community that we are in this position.

“Thanks to tireless campaigning by Andrew’s family, Harper’s Law means that anyone convicted of killing an emergency worker whilst committing a crime now gets a mandatory life sentence. This government has gone further by introducing a presumption that anyone convicted of murdering a police, prison or probation officer is handed a whole-life order.

“We have been clear that we wanted to go further and block more offenders from getting out sooner into their sentence but could not do so without risking prisons reaching capacity and collapsing.

“If that happened, police could not make arrests, courts could not remand offenders and there would be unchecked criminality on our streets.”

Sitting in her car one morning before work, Sabrina Javellana was frantically scrolling through photos of herself online that someone anonymously sent her a link to, with an ominous warning of their explicit content.

As she sifted through the dozens of images, posted on 4chan, she came across one that made her freeze.

“I recognized one from when I was 17 in high school, just taking a cute picture in a mirror of my outfit, about to go hang out with my friends…except my clothes were totally removed,” she recalled.

“It was the same exact photo, except they used this AI-generated technology to remove my clothes, and it looked hyper-realistic. But I knew this wasn't real. From that day on, my world turned upside down.”

Javellana was 23, working in local politics in Florida, when she fell victim to AI deepfake pornography in 2021, which she describes as an act of sexual violence.

open image in gallery Sabrina Javellana was 23 and working in local politics when she fell victim to AI deepfake pornography in 2021. She said it turned her life ‘upside down’ ( Sabrina Javellana/Getty )

With the unstoppable rise of AI technology, it has never been easier for perpetrators to create and share nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfakes. The estimated number of deepfakes rose from approximately 500,000 in 2023 to 8 million in 2025, according to analysis. And 99 percent of deepfakes target women.

Still, it remains unclear how serious tech bosses are about tackling the problem. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared unaware of the latest deepfake bill being pushed by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle when The Independent quizzed him on it in Washington, D.C. recently, while Elon Musk’s xAI is suing Minnesota over its attempts to ban so-called “nudification” apps in the state.

Momentum to tackle nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfakes by the U.S. government had been picking up steam after Congress passed the TAKE IT DOWN Act last year. It prohibits the publication of authentic and AI-generated sexual images published without a person’s consent, and requires online platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a complaint.

The DEFIANCE Act would allow victims to file civil lawsuits against people who produce, distribute, and solicit nonconsensual deepfake AI pornography, as well as those who intend to distribute such images.

It was cleared the Senate by unanimous consent in January but is languishing in the House, with time running out. The bipartisan bill, introduced by New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and co-sponsored by Republican Rep. Laurel Lee of Florida.

But some Republicans, it seems, do not want to hand Ocasio-Cortez a win so close to the midterms in November, when she is up for election.

When The Independent recently asked Ocasio-Cortez about the GOP lawmakers reportedly blocking the bill because her name is attached to it, her response was blunt. “I don't think that we should be emboldening child pornographers and helping abusers just because of some personal beef that they may have,” she said.

open image in gallery Paris Hilton told The Independent: ‘Every day the DEFIANCE Act isn’t put on the calendar in the House, more women and girls become victims without a meaningful path to justice’ ( Getty Images )

Ocasio-Cortez said that she would welcome the assistance of first lady Melania Trump, who supported the TAKE IT DOWN Act.

“I think that this is a really great opportunity, just as we have in the House, to be able to champion and for women to uplift one another across party lines,” she told The Independent.

Javellana said the issue transcends party politics and described the blockage as “petty.”

“It feels like a slap in the face to the women and girls who have spoken so bravely to tell their stories,” Javellana, 28, told The Independent. “This is not about making AOC's star even brighter.”

At a January press conference, Ocasio-Cortez teamed up with Paris Hilton, where the pair spoke of what it feels like to be a victim of deepfake AI pornography. Hilton said that more than 100,000 deepfake images of her exist online and has urged lawmakers to pass the DEFIANCE Act.

“Every day the DEFIANCE Act isn’t put on the calendar in the House, more women and girls become victims without a meaningful path to justice,” Hilton exclusively told The Independent.

I felt fear for my family, my home. It impacted my stress, my health, everything. It crushed me to step away, but I had to for my sanity, for my survival, for my health, for my safety Sabrina Javellana

Hilton added that there is “no legitimate policy reason” for the bill to be stalled and hit out at Rep. Jim Jordan, Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. “Representative Jim Jordan and House leadership have an opportunity to protect millions and send a clear message that people who knowingly create or distribute nonconsensual explicit deepfakes to cause harm will be held accountable,” Hilton said.

Jordan’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

As AI technology advances at pace, the law is yet to catch up on holding perpetrators and Big Tech accountable for sexually explicit deepfakes and other online harms. And while the DEFIANCE Act “isn’t perfect,” Javellana said, introducing civil penalties provides victims with “more tools in the toolbox.”

In 2018, then aged 21, Javellana became one of the youngest elected officials in Florida when she won a seat on the Hallandale Beach city commission in Broward County, located between Miami and Fort Lauderdale. The young politician threw herself into issues she cares about deeply, which her critics deemed progressive.

“I'm speaking about climate change, I'm speaking about police reform, I'm speaking about government corruption,” she said.

open image in gallery Javellana suffered in silence for a year, not wanting to tell her family or friends about the images. After speaking out, she has joined advocates like Paris Hilton to call for legislation to stop AI deepfake pornography ( Getty Images for The Ford Founda )

The online abuse soon followed. “Because I was outspoken, because I was a young woman and an easy target,” Javellana said.

Everything changed on the day she received the first AI deepfake, depicting her nude. More popped up, and still do to this day, she said. “It’s not just the photos, but the comments from all these anonymous users. I would do her, I would rape her... just disgusting, vulgar comments.”

She served her four years in office but decided not to run for re-election following the ordeal.

“I felt fear for my family, my home,” she said. “It impacted my stress, my health, everything. It crushed me to step away, but I had to for my sanity, for my survival, for my health, for my safety.”

She had limited options for recourse but reached out to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and consulted with a New York-based attorney. Due to a lack of state and federal legislation about AI deepfakes at the time, neither resulted in any morsel of justice. It was baffling to Javellana that what happened to her did not constitute a crime.

“It wasn't illegal to do this to people, to take their own likeness and make it into a new nude image and put their face on it and destroy their life, their career,” she said. “I totally lost my sense of self. I felt like I had no agency over my own body…I felt like this was a new form of sexual violence.”

open image in gallery Hilton has hit out at Republican leadership for stalling on the bill. ‘Representative Jim Jordan and House leadership have an opportunity to protect millions and send a clear message that people who knowingly create or distribute nonconsensual explicit deepfakes to cause harm will be held accountable,’ she said ( Getty Images )

Javellana suffered in silence for a year, not wanting to tell her family or friends about the images.

“It felt like a losing battle,” she said. “I decided maybe no one will ever see these. I'll never talk about it to anyone. I'll just, you know, compartmentalize it and try to move on with my life.”

Then, in January 2022, then-Florida Democratic state senator Lauren Book introduced a bill making it a felony to create sexually explicit deepfakes without consent. Book went public with her own experience where she was blackmailed with sexually explicit deepfake AI images.

Javellana reached out to Book to share her story and testified about her ordeal in the Florida Senate, marking the beginning of her public fight for women and girls. “I reached out to [Book’s] office and I told her, ‘Hey, this happened to me, and I want to help support your bill and make sure it gets passed.’”

With Javellana’s help, the Florida bill was swiftly signed into law by Governor Ron DeSantis. She hopes the DEFIANCE Act will follow suit, stressing that federal lawmakers can’t afford to delay.

open image in gallery First lady Melania Trump supported the TAKE IT DOWN Act last year, which prohibits the publication of authentic and AI-generated sexual images published without a person’s consent, and requires online platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a complaint ( Getty Images )

Prince Harry and Meghan are the latest high-profile names to back the bill. The couple criticized House lawmakers given the bill has been passed by the Senate.

“This begs the question: why the delay?” a release last week from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex asked. “The answer may lie in the deepest offense to families and children: the tech industry’s commitment to pushback on these bills to protect their bottom line.”

It isn’t only high-profile women and girls who are being targeted, as instances of deepfakes are cropping up more and more in schools, an issue Hilton has also raised.

“Around 99 percent of nonconsensual explicit deepfakes target women. But anyone can become a victim,” she told The Independent. “These AI tools and nudification apps are becoming cheaper, faster, and easier to use. All it takes is a single photo, and within seconds a coworker, stranger, classmate, or ex-partner can create realistic explicit images that can devastate someone’s reputation, career, relationships, and mental health.”

Javellana added: “Big tech has started this revolution where it's growing so fast, our laws are not catching up to it. It's going to continue to grow, impacting women and girls in all different aspects of life, not just public figures, politicians, celebrities. It's impacting more and more every single day, [including] girls in school.”

The bill is flailing even though it enjoys the support of House Speaker Mike Johnson as well as right-wing firebrands like GOP Reps. Nancy Mace of South Carolina and Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, in addition to progressive Democrats like Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Ro Khanna of California.

It has not so much as come up for a vote in the Judiciary Committee - which handles legislation relating to legal affairs and votes on whether to put a bill on the House floor - which is galling to many survivors.

open image in gallery The DEFIANCE Act is flailing in the House and time is running out to pass it. Javellana is calling on lawmakers to get it done ( AFP via Getty Images )

“AOC is a very powerful force, but it's so much bigger than her,” Javellana said. “And I know that these [Republican] leaders see that. It would be a win for them just as much as for her, as for President Trump.”

“This is common sense and to survivors, to victims...it's upsetting.”

But Javellana and other advocates remain confident that the DEFIANCE Act will become law. She is already looking ahead to the next fight.

“We're still not going to be done because this is still very reactive and not preventative,” she said of the bill. “And the preventative is once we start talking big tech, once we start talking about holding the platforms liable.”

“They are not good at all about responding to inquiries and reports of people asking to take this [content] down or regulating their users,” she added.

Indeed, when The Independent asked OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for his take on the DEFIANCE Act last week, he said he was “unfamiliar” with it. This was the same week the entrepreneur was in Washington, D.C., to talk with lawmakers about AI policy.

Javellana doesn’t believe she will ever discover the identities of the people who created the deepfake pornographic images of her, but whatever happens, she won’t be silent anymore.

“I wanted to hide for a while, but you know what? I can't do that,” she said. “That's letting them win.”

If you need support, call the Rainn National Sexual Assault Hotline at 800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit rainn.org

News.title: Used EV sales jump 67% as Britain’s second-hand car market gets its spark back
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Britain’s used car market has returned to growth, with electric cars providing much of the extra spark as used EV sales jumped by 67 per cent.

More than two million used cars changed hands between April and June, according to new figures from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). The total of 2,009,318 transactions was up 0.7 per cent on the same period last year.

It was the first time since 2021 that second-quarter sales had passed the two million mark, leaving the market just 1.2 per cent below its pre-pandemic level. That small rise helped to make up for a slight fall during the first three months of the year. In total across the first half of 2026, 4,025,550 used cars found new homes, an increase of 0.2 per cent.

open image in gallery 110,761 used EVs changed hands during the second quarter of 2026 taking a record 5.5 per cent share of the used market ( Kia )

The biggest movement came from fully-electric cars. A total of 110,761 used EVs changed hands during the quarter, up 67 per cent and representing the strongest quarterly growth since the start of 2024. Electric cars also took a record 5.5 per cent share of the used market. That means more than one in every 18 second-hand car buyers chose an EV, compared with around one in 30 during the same period last year, when their share stood at 3.3 per cent.

It’s still a relatively small slice of Britain’s enormous used car market, but the direction of travel is clear: more electric models are reaching the second-hand market as cars originally bought or leased new are traded in, giving used buyers a broader range of ages, sizes and prices to choose from.

Growth was especially strong during April, when used EV transactions more than doubled with a 110.9 per cent rise. They increased by 57.6 per cent in May and 37.8 per cent in June. SMMT said the sharp rises in April and May coincided with higher fuel prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The figures were also compared with a weaker period last year, when changes to vehicle excise duty came into force.

Regular hybrids had a busy quarter too. Sales rose by 31.2 per cent to 130,825, lifting their share of the market from 5 per cent to 6.5 per cent. Plug-in hybrids didn’t join the growth, however. Transactions fell by 6.8 per cent to 22,856, leaving them with 1.1 per cent of all used car sales, down slightly from 1.2 per cent a year earlier.

Despite the rapid rise in electric and hybrid sales, petrol and diesel cars remain comfortably dominant. Together, they accounted for 86.7 per cent of all transactions during the quarter, or almost nine out of every 10 used cars sold. Petrol was still the country’s favourite fuel type, with 1,121,243 cars changing hands, although that figure was down by 1.2 per cent. Diesel transactions dropped by 7.2 per cent to 620,045, reflecting the falling number of new diesel cars feeding into the used market.

Mike Hawes, SMMT chief executive, said: “A return to growth is good news for motorists and the wider automotive sector, with sales of used EVs rising particularly strongly as more choice reaches more buyers. As the used market is where most people buy their cars, plentiful and affordable supply is vital, however, increasingly unrealistic targets in the new car market risk constraining that supply and pushing up costs. Urgent regulatory reform is needed to deliver a transition that works for every driver.”

open image in gallery The Ford Fiesta remained Britain's favourite used car in the second quarter of 2026 ( Ford )

Smaller cars continued to rule the used market. Superminis accounted for 31.7 per cent of all transactions, with sales edging up by 0.2 per cent. Lower-medium cars, another familiar source of everyday hatchbacks and family models, followed with a 26.6 per cent share and the same 0.2 per cent rise. Dual-purpose cars including SUVs recorded the strongest growth, climbing by 7.4 per cent to take 17.7 per cent of the market.

Used car buyers weren’t feeling especially adventurous when it came to colour. More than 1.1 million of the cars sold during the quarter were black, grey or white, with the three shades accounting for 56.5 per cent of the market. Sales of black cars rose by 0.7 per cent, grey increased by 4.1 per cent and white was up by 4.7 per cent. Blue remained the fourth most popular colour despite a 1.1 per cent decline, while silver held on to fifth place even as sales fell by 6.4 per cent.
