Crooked Media’s "Pod Save America" was accused by a former Biden staffer of deleting a social media clip that was critical of far-left streamer Hasan Piker, and the liberal podcast reposted a longer version after hours of backlash.

"Pod Save America," the popular progressive podcast helmed by ex-Obama staffers, welcomed MS NOW's Chris Hayes for Sunday’s episode to discuss the state of Democratic politics with guest host Alex Wagner. Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s ties to Piker came up, and the liberal pundits pleased moderates by speaking critically about the controversial streamer.

El-Sayed has taken heat for campaigning with Piker, who has blamed America for the terror attacks of September 11, 2001, and praised dictators ranging from Mao Zedong to Fidel Castro. Now Democrats are trying to figure out if Piker can help them in general elections while grappling with his incendiary rhetoric, which has also included dismissing Hamas rapes on Oct. 7 as essentially irrelevant.

HASAN PIKER STANDS BY 'INTENTIONALLY PROVOCATIVE' CLAIMS THAT HAMAS IS 'A THOUSAND TIMES BETTER' THAN ISRAEL

"I don’t think it makes a ton of sense in a general election, frankly, to campaign with Hasan Piker. I think you also can’t control what a 35-year-old streamer is going to say," Hayes said.

"I also think he is learning the lesson that, with great power comes great responsibility," Hayes continued. "This is a dude that streams like seven days a week for years, do you know the amount of words he said? Like, you’re going to say some stuff."

Hayes then suggested that Piker needs to make a minor change going forward.

"If Hasan Piker wants to contribute to the success of the movement, he’s probably going to have to watch what he says a lot more," Hayes said.

The "Pod Save America" episode remains live on other platforms, but former special assistant to President Biden Michael LaRosa noticed the clip was oddly deleted from X.

UNEARTHED CLIP OF EL-SAYED REVEALING HIS 'HATE' FOR ICONIC MICHIGAN TOWN SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'DARK HEART'

Others also noted the deletion, including gun control activist Shannon Watts.

LaRosa, who served as press secretary to former first lady Jill Biden, recently made an unusually sharp break with his party in a post responding to reports that he was supporting Republican Mike Rogers over El-Sayed. At the center of LaRosa’s criticism is El-Sayed’s association with Piker, who drew widespread condemnation after saying during a 2019 livestream that " America deserved 9/11. "

LaRosa, who quoted the clip to celebrate Democrats debating what to do with Piker, noticed it was removed and called out the podcast.

"WOW. This is remarkable. @PodSave America appears to have deleted the clip they themselves posted of @Chrislhayes and @alexwagner telling the truth about why Hasan Piker is a major liability and problem for El-Sayed," LaRosa wrote, adding, "Apparently, their candor was refreshing right up until moderates like me started amplifying and celebrating it."

Crooked Media did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.

Hours later, following backlash online, a new post appeared with a longer version of the clip.

Larosa accused Crooked Media of deleting the clip before 9 a.m. ET on Monday but the longer version wasn’t posted until after 3 p.m. ET. Shannon Watts, who had criticized the clip removal, said the podcast "wanted to make the clip longer and add more context."

"Which means somebody from Piker's camp or El-Sayed's camp probably wined and cried and forced them to take down and recreate the content. Truly hysterical. But how embarrassing for ‘Pod Save America," LaRosa responded to Watts’ post.

DEM ATTORNEY BACKS GOP HOPEFUL IN MICHIGAN RACE AGAINST EL-SAYED, 'JUMPING SHIP' FROM HIS PARTY'S 'LUNATICS'

Julian Epstein, who served as the chief legal counsel for House Democrats during the Clinton impeachment hearing and worked for Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign, recently said he would support the Republican candidate against El-Sayed after he campaigned with Piker.

"I don’t understand why people keep talking about Hasan Piker in the media because I think the guy is a lunatic," Epstein told Fox News Digital.

"I don’t think he’s ever said anything, to me, that’s particularly interesting. He’s a shock jock, but he’s never demonstrated any understanding of economic or history in my mind," Epstein continued. "What he understands is influencer culture and how to say shocking things."

"Pod Save America" famously irked Biden allies when the podcast co-hosts were among the first prominent Democrats to call for then-President Joe Biden to step aside during the 2024 presidential election.

The show, which consists of ex-Obama White House staffers, had previously pushed the "cheap fakes" narrative that Biden's mental health decline was being promoted by misleading video clips.

World.title: Michigan Dem Senate nominee comes under fire over resurfaced blog post linking football to 'toxic masculinity'
World.content:
Michigan's Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, is taking heat after resurfaced writings exposed his sweeping attacks on traditional masculinity and U.S. sports culture.

According to a report by The Midwesterner, El-Sayed authored a 2021 Substack post taking aim at the gridiron in the wake of former Las Vegas Raiders coach Jon Gruden's resignation over leaked emails.

In the post, the progressive favorite laid out an aggressive critique of male sports culture, writing that "the toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport, and men’s sports culture more generally, is way deeper than a few emails or a Jay-Z turnaround."

El-Sayed, who played high school football as a starting center at Andover High School, used his past experience to argue that traditional athletics breed bigotry. While noting he felt free on the field, El-Sayed claimed that "on the sidelines and in the locker room, I was fed a hefty dose of the worst kinds of racist taunting," adding that within men's sports, "racism, misogyny, and homophobia were lingua franca." He also unloaded on the NFL directly, accusing the league of "deep-rooted racism."

‘SPECIAL SAUCE OF CRAZY’ — MIDWEST DEM CANDIDATE’S POLICIES TOO EXTREME FOR VOTERS: OPPONENT

Rather than leaning into classic athletic grit, the Democratic nominee pushed a soft-spoken, progressive rebrand of manhood centered on Hollywood fiction.

El-Sayed urged coaches to abandon traditional toughness and instead copy the lead character from the soccer comedy "Ted Lasso," praising the fictional soccer coach because "Ted cries. He talks through his problems. He encourages his players. He bakes biscuits for his boss. He smiles ... like, all the time."

His political theories on sports extend beyond American boundaries. In a separate 2021 Substack entry cited by The Midwesterner, El-Sayed explicitly tied his sports preferences to his far-left ideology, writing, "European soccer also speaks to my politics. Compared to American sports leagues, the sport is also deeply egalitarian."

The resurfaced posts expose a massive gap between El-Sayed's academic gender theories and his recent campaign trail efforts to build street cred with young male voters by bragging about his own high school wrestling and football history.

Now facing Republican Mike Rogers in the general election after narrowing out Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, El-Sayed has some explaining to do to working-class Midwesterners who prefer football over progressive lecturing.

World.title: Iran installs new war chiefs as Tehran signals ‘prolonged confrontation,’ expert warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei formally appointed six senior military commanders Monday, cementing a wartime reshuffle as Tehran rebuilds a command structure impacted by months of U.S. and Israeli strikes.

The appointments, announced by Khamenei’s office and promoted on social media, fill posts across Iran’s armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij paramilitary force, with a counterterrorism expert warning the timing and language of the decrees signal Tehran is preparing for "prolonged confrontation" and not a settlement with Washington.

"Strategically, the announcements made were issued in English, on X, while Iranian and Omani negotiators finalize the coordinates of a proposed shipping route through Hormuz, which is deliberate sequencing," Dr. Omar Mohammed, director of the Antisemitism Research Initiative at George Washington University’s Program on Extremism, told Fox News Digital.

"Tehran is establishing its command structure as a fact on the ground before it signs anything."

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

Mohammed also pointed to language in the appointment announcements blaming the deaths of predecessors on what Iran called the "Zionist-American enemy."

"That phrase, in formal state documents, codifies the United States as a co-belligerent," Mohammed said.

Khamenei appointed Ali Abdollahi as chief of staff of the armed forces and Kioumars Heydari as his deputy. He also formally named Ahmad Vahidi commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, promoting him to the rank of major general.

Mostafa Izadi was named deputy IRGC commander, Ali Azmaei as commander of the IRGC Navy and Hossein Taeb as commander of the Basij.

Mohammed said Vahidi was also instructed to maintain readiness for "powerful offensive operations against the enemy," by the Supreme Leader, while Abdollahi was tasked with completing the integration of the General Staff into the Khatam al-Anbiya wartime joint command.

"States exiting a conflict dismantle their wartime command arrangements, but Iran is now institutionalizing its own," Mohammed said. "The decrees here describe a leadership planning for a prolonged confrontation, not a settlement."

Several of the newly appointed commanders have previously faced U.S. or European sanctions or allegations tied to terrorism and violent crackdowns.

Vahidi is the subject of an Interpol Red Notice requested by Argentina over his alleged involvement in the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people.

Taeb, a former chief of the IRGC Intelligence Organization and former Basij commander, is on the U.S. Treasury Department’s sanctions list.

The United States first designated him in 2010 over serious human rights abuses following Iran’s disputed 2009 presidential election.

Heydari was also sanctioned by the United States in 2022 after the Treasury Department said he had publicly acknowledged his forces’ involvement in the violent response to Iran’s November 2019 protests, in which hundreds of protesters were killed.

The European Union has also sanctioned him.

IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY

The reshuffle comes as Iran continues rebuilding its political and military leadership after a series of U.S. and Israeli strikes killed senior figures across the regime.

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had served as supreme leader since 1989, was killed in a Feb. 28 strike at the start of the war. Mojtaba Khamenei, was selected as Iran’s new supreme leader in March.

Ali Larijani, then secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and a major figure in the country’s security and foreign policy establishment, and Gholamreza Soleimani, commander of the Basij, were killed in strikes on March 17.

The latest appointments come amid continuing questions about Mojtaba Khamenei’s health and public absence.

President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Monday that he had held a nearly seven-hour meeting with Khamenei, only the second meeting the president has publicly disclosed since the new supreme leader took office, Iran International reported.

Khamenei has not appeared publicly since being selected in March and is believed to have been wounded in the Feb. 28 strike that killed his father.

Pezeshkian said the two discussed economic conditions, sanctions and other domestic challenges and that Khamenei emphasized the need for "unity and cohesion."

The military rebuild, however, has not extended fully into Iran’s sensitive intelligence apparatus, according to Mohammed.

"The IRGC Intelligence Organization and its counterintelligence arm have no announced chiefs, and Iran has no permanent defense or intelligence ministers," the expert said.

"The appointments require assigning responsibility for the counterintelligence failures that enabled the February decapitation.

World.title: Unlicensed NYC boat operator allegedly ignored safety warnings before mother, baby died in capsizing: feds
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A New Jersey man accused of running illegal boat tours allegedly ignored multiple safety warnings before an overcrowded New York Harbor excursion turned deadly, killing a 5-month-old baby and her 27-year-old mother.

Manuel Hernandez, 46, of Manville, was charged Monday with two counts of misconduct and neglect of a ship officer resulting in death after the Yamaha AR210 he was piloting capsized Saturday night.

Hernandez appeared Monday before U.S. Magistrate Judge Valerie Figueredo on the two charges, each of which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

DRUNK REPEAT OFFENDER CALLED A 'TICKING TIME-BOMB' BEFORE 80-MPH BOATING COLLISION KILLED WOMAN: PROSECUTORS

Federal prosecutors say Hernandez was not licensed to carry paying passengers, had 14 people aboard a boat with a maximum capacity of 10 and knowingly took the infant out without an appropriate life vest.

According to the federal complaint, it was not Hernandez’s first time allegedly taking paying customers onto New York Harbor without the required credentials.

After his arrest, Hernandez allegedly told investigators he had previously piloted at least two other boat tours for the same tour company using his own vessel.

He allegedly acknowledged he lacked the required Merchant Mariner Credential and Coast Guard Certificate of Inspection for those trips and said he was paid about $1,000 for each.

COAST GUARD OPENS FIRE ON BOAT SMUGGLING 25 CHINESE NATIONALS NEAR FLORIDA AFTER IT REFUSED TO STOP

Coast Guard Investigative Service Assistant Director Josh Packer said illegal charter operations "gamble with human life."

"In this case, the alleged conduct led to an unthinkable tragedy," Packer said.

Before Saturday’s fatal trip even began, Hernandez allegedly asked the baby’s parents whether they had an infant-sized flotation device. When they said they did not, Hernandez told them the boat did not have one either, according to the complaint.

Despite that, Hernandez allegedly instructed one parent to wear a life vest and hold the baby throughout the tour. The child’s mother did so.

OVERCROWDED MIGRANT VESSEL WITH 240 PEOPLE ON BOARD INTERCEPTED NEAR TURKS AND CAICOS

About three hours and 20 minutes into the excursion, Hernandez allegedly made a U-turn while heading toward the Statue of Liberty, bringing the vessel into a swell that may have been caused by the wake of a larger passing boat.

Hernandez tried to accelerate through the swell, but it swamped the bow and the vessel "immediately capsized," prosecutors allege.

All 14 people were thrown into the harbor. Eleven passengers and Hernandez survived, while the mother and baby were recovered unresponsive and later pronounced dead at a Brooklyn hospital.

"The defendant allegedly flouted those regulations when he transported paying customers on a commercial vessel without appropriate licenses, overcrowded the vessel, and took on a five-month-old infant passenger, with no infant life vests onboard," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said.

The boat used in the fatal trip belonged to a friend and was smaller than Hernandez’s own vessel, which needed mechanical repairs, according to the complaint.

CARNIVAL CRUISE PASSENGER, 67, FOUND DEAD WHILE SNORKELING OFF THE COAST OF AUSTRALIA DURING EXCURSION

Hernandez allegedly told investigators he did not know the borrowed boat’s maximum capacity and had expected 12 passengers before ultimately agreeing to take 13.

The victims were identified in a GoFundMe organized by friends and colleagues as Sara Sanchez, 27, and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia. Sanchez’s partner and Antonella’s father, Andres Garcia, was also aboard the boat and survived.

Garcia is now grieving their deaths while caring for the couple’s 6-year-old son, Salvador, according to the fundraiser, which is raising money for funeral expenses and other costs. "No amount of money can replace Sara or Antonella," organizers wrote.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Hernandez showed "a complete disregard for the safety of his passengers."

"This tragedy could have been prevented, and now a family is left to grieve the unimaginable loss of a mother and her five-month-old daughter because of his negligence," Tisch said.

World.title: RFK Jr. wants to fix loophole that allows additives into food. Critics say it doesn’t go far enough.
World.content:
The Trump administration said it’s taking first steps in strengthening rules over ingredients food companies have long added to their products with minimal oversight.

Under a proposed rule announced Monday, manufacturers will have to notify the Food and Drug Administration when they deem additives as “generally recognized as safe,” also known as GRAS, as well as provide information on existing additives.

But critics say that while this is a good first step, the proposed rule won’t prevent manufacturers from adding new ingredients to foods, nor will it remove the many thousands of additives already in foods.

The GRAS designation, which began in the 1950s, was meant to simplify the use of common ingredients like paprika, garlic and vanilla and avoid a lengthy approval process while also freeing up the FDA’s limited resources. Companies are not required to tell the FDA when deciding what they consider GRAS.

Critics, including public health experts and food scientists, have long said the industry has exploited the rule to introduce thousands of unstudied chemicals into the nation’s food supply, potentially endangering public health.

Deeming an ingredient GRAS does not necessarily make it so, and the FDA has banned certain ingredients from food after evidence emerged that they might harm health. These include Red No. 3, a synthetic dye that gives foods and drinks a bright cherry red color but has been linked to cancer in animals, and brominated vegetable oil, often used in citrus-flavored drinks, which has been linked to liver, heart and brain damage.

“Over time, that exemption has become the loophole, and the vast majority of substances have been submitted via that loophole without public disclosure or of the information safety,” Dr. Dariush Mozaffarian, director of the Food Is Medicine Institute at Tufts University, said during a media event Monday with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The proposed rule would require companies to notify the FDA when they deem substances as GRAS. The notices would be made public. For substances that already have GRAS designations, the proposed rule would ask companies to submit data about how those ingredients are used.

“The new rule does not prevent companies from self-affirming the safety of their ingredients,” said Alyssa Moran, deputy director of the Center for Food and Nutrition Policy at the University of Pennsylvania. “It does require mandatory notification, but my understanding is that there’s not even a timeline for notification, so companies can introduce these ingredients and then eventually notify FDA.”

Thousands of ingredients have been designated “generally recognized as safe” since the 1950s. Joe Raedle / Getty Images file

“It’s just quite misleading to say we’re going to close the GRAS loophole, and then to still allow companies to self-affirm the safety of their ingredients,” Moran added.

Jennifer Pomeranz, associate professor of public health policy and management at the New York University School of Global Public Health, said the proposed rule was “an incredibly important first step” but said more work is needed.

“What data is going to be required to be submitted about the ingredients already in the food supply?” Pomeranz said. “It has to be enough for us to see that it’s safe. It can’t just be a name of an ingredient and its uses.”

Stephanie Harris, chief public policy officer for the Food Industry Association, which represents grocers and other food suppliers, said that the GRAS proposal is “an important step” but shows limits of what the FDA can do to make such reforms, legally.

“Congress should act this year to establish a nationally uniform, science-based framework for ingredient transparency that strengthens FDA’s role, avoids a fragmented state-by-state patchwork and provides consumers and the food industry with clarity and confidence,” Harris said in a statement.

During the media event, Kennedy also announced a federally recognized definition for ultraprocessed foods is under “final review” but did not provide the text of the definition. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services did not give a timeline for when that would be made public.

World.title: N.C. GOP committee picks Jennifer Balkcom to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on November ballot
World.content:
A panel of Republican officials in North Carolina selected a state lawmaker on Monday as their nominee for a House race after embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his re-election bid following sexual harassment allegations.

Jennifer Balkcom, who represents a state legislative district in Henderson County, will face Jamie Ager, who won the Democratic primary in March.

North Carolina GOP’s Executive Committee for the 11th Congressional District picked Balkcom to replace Edwards in compliance with state law given how late in the campaign he dropped out.

Balkcom faces a sprint to Election Day, which is less than three months away. Absentee ballots are set to start going out on Sept. 4, giving her just a few weeks to make her case to some voters.

She announced her intention to seek the nomination less than 24 hours ago.

“This race is too important to sit out,” Balkcom wrote in a statement Sunday posted to X, adding that Western North Carolina “needs a strong voice right now” as it continues to rebuild after Hurricane Helene.

Her candidacy was heavily boosted by power players in the state. North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, a Republican, endorsed Balkcom on social media Monday afternoon, calling her “the right person at the right time.”

“Jennifer is a principled conservative, a tireless advocate for her district, and a leader who gets things done,” Hall wrote on X.

The state GOP’s executive director Zachary Almond congratulated Balkcom on X following the announcement of her nomination, saying he was “excited to work alongside her and her team throughout the election cycle.”

Rep. Chuck Edwards in Washington in 2025. Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images file

Edwards, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump, announced last week that he would serve out his term in Congress but would not seek a third term in the House. His decision came days after the House Ethics Committee recommended a censure following a probe that found “substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.”

He has repeatedly denied wrongdoing, and the Ethics Committee said Edwards, who cooperated with the panel’s investigation, had denied that any of his actions were meant to be sexual or romantic in nature. Attorneys for Edwards wrote a 15-page response to the committee’s findings, calling them “unfounded.”

Edwards previously called the allegations “baseless,” and in May he said he welcomed an investigation.

Edwards was elected to the House in 2022 after having ousted the scandal-ridden Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary. Before that, the district was represented by Mark Meadows, who led the House Freedom Caucus before he stepped down to become White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term.

Edwards won his seat by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, but Democrats are hopeful they can flip it as Republicans seek to defend their narrow majority in the House heading into the midterm elections.

Ager, a farmer who significantly outraised Edwards in the race, was previously listed as “Likely Republican” by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report. The rating was downgraded to “Lean Republican” before the House Ethics Committee report was released.

World.title: The U.S. just had its hottest month on record
World.content:
For much of the country, it was a hot and dry month. At the end of July, around 40% of the U.S. and Puerto Rico was in the grips of drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor, which tracks conditions nationwide and releases weekly updates.

Despite widespread drought, several regions experienced heavy rainfall in July that caused damaging flash flooding. Intense rain fell across the Texas Hill Country from July 13 to 17, producing rainfall totals of more than 28 inches near the town of Knippa, in Uvalde County, according to NOAA. Later in the month, from July 28 to 30, slow-moving thunderstorms dumped nearly 12 inches of rain over eastern New York, causing major flash flooding.

July is typically one of the hottest months of the year, and last month was no exception. It was among the top five warmest Julys for 13 states, while Wyoming experienced its warmest July and warmest month on record, with temperatures a whopping 5.1 degrees above average, according to NOAA.

Heat waves baked almost every part of the U.S. last month, including much of the West, Southwest, Rockies, northern Plains, Upper Midwest, mid-Atlantic, Gulf Coast and Southeast. NOAA said multiple sites across Idaho, Utah, Wyoming and Montana set new all-time high temperature records July 12, including 109 degrees in Salt Lake City; 109 degrees in Sheridan, Wyoming; 111 degrees in Billings, Montana; and 115 degrees in Miles City, Montana.

Several large wildfires also broke out in the Pacific Northwest last month, continuing into August. More than 140,000 acres were scorched in Oregon in July, prompting thousands of residents to evacuate from mostly small towns across the central and eastern parts of the state. Devastating wildfires also burned in Canada and Europe, and fast-moving blazes this month have destroyed hundreds of structures in Washington state and Oregon.

00:00 00:00 Chinese air conditioners are in hot demand in Europe 01:44

NOAA’s latest figures add to other grim climate findings: A report released Monday by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service found that Western Europe had its hottest June-July period on record. The continent has suffered through four brutal heat waves since May, with temperatures smashing several national records and plunging the region further into drought.

The Copernicus report also said that average sea surface temperatures reached their highest levels for July across extrapolar oceans — the bodies of water between latitudes 60 degrees south and 60 degrees north that are free of seasonal sea ice.

A separate “state of the climate” report released Monday in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society indicated that last year was similarly extreme. The report found that greenhouse gas concentrations, global sea level and ocean heat content all reached their highest levels on record in 2025.

World.title: 5 takeaways from Zuckerberg's essay on his vision for superintelligence
World.content:
Mark Zuckerberg said in an essay published on Meta's website on Monday that artificial intelligence tools should be shared with "as many people and businesses as possible."

In a 6,500-word post outlining the Meta founder's vision of AI, Zuckerberg also expressed his belief that "superintelligence" — a theoretical form of AI with superior cognitive abilities to those of humans — will advance national security, lead to greater economic prosperity, and promote scientific and creative achievement.

"Humanity has witnessed many transformative advances. Each time there is fear that people will be left behind," Zuckerberg wrote. "But each time humanity has come out with more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom. We believe this will be true with AI as well, and the abundance of the future can be shared by everyone."

Zuckerberg touts the potential upsides of superintelligence — and Meta's place in advancing it — but also warns that action is needed to maintain America's competitive edge and ensure humanity retains control over the technology.

Here are five takeaways from Zuckerberg's essay.

"Free or affordable access" to AI for all

Zuckerberg envisions a future in which individuals have a personal agent designed to assist them with everyday needs related to their health, careers, finances and relationships.

To encourage AI use, the tech billionaire said Meta will provide free versions of its tools to "billions of people" and seek to offer access to its AI technology for the "lowest price possible."

Zuckerberg also committed to building a "fully private mode" for personal AI agents that will prevent Meta and other providers from seeing people's information.

Jobs won't disappear

Disputing widespread concerns that AI will displace workers, Zuckerberg said the technology will create new kinds of jobs that don't exist today and allow people to do more with less. In his essay, he referred to superintelligence as a "tool of invention" rather than of automation.

"Company sizes may shrink — just as they did in the transition from industrial giants to tech companies," Zuckerberg said. "But this doesn't mean fewer jobs overall. It implies a larger number of companies with fewer people each."

Data center community investments

Meta is among the so-called hyperscalers, along with rivals such as Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, rushing to build data centers as growing AI demand spurs a need for more computing power. Yet the push is drawing intense public opposition over environmental, economic and other concerns.

Seeking to address such concerns, Zuckerberg said Monday that Meta will create an investment fund called the "Future is for Everyone Fund" to benefit communities where data centers are being built. The fund size will be $1 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Zuckerberg also committed to keeping electricity prices low, restoring local water supply and training workers to support its data center buildout. Meta's 2026 capital spending budget of $145 billion will be used "largely to build data centers," he noted.

Releasing open-source models

Zuckerberg argues in his essay that the U.S. should lower barriers that he said make it harder for U.S. open-source AI models to compete with those of foreign competitors. While there are risks to releasing models, allowing AI labs to keep them under lock and key as proprietary AI tools would be worse, he said.

To that end, Zuckerberg said Meta will "resume releasing some open source models soon." According to The Wall Street Journal, Meta is planning to launch a new model with open weights — numerical values that determine a model's behavior — called Muse Glimmer, as well as an open-weight version of Muse Spark 1.2, its most advanced AI coding model.

Working with the authorities

Zuckerberg also offered policy suggestions for how AI companies and the government can work together to advance AI safely. Those include sharing "intermediate training checkpoints of new models" with the government — allowing it to tackle potential security issues early on. AI labs should also work with law enforcement to prevent bad actors from misusing the models, he said.

World.title: Captain of boat that capsized in New York facing federal charges after mom, infant die
World.content:
A woman and her 5-month-old baby died after a vessel carrying 14 people overturned in New York Harbor on Saturday night, according to police, and the boat's captain now faces federal charges.

Manuel Hernandez, 46, was arrested on 13 counts of reckless endangerment, police said Sunday, and authorities are investigating whether the vessel was operating illegally as a charter, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

Hernandez also appeared in federal court in Manhattan on Monday and was charged with two counts of misconduct and neglect of ship officer resulting in death, according to a federal complaint. He was not required to enter a plea and was released on $50,000 bail, The Associated Press reported. Hernandez has been transferred to federal custody, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Hernandez and his lawyer, Amy Gallicchio, declined to comment outside court on Monday, The AP reported.

Manuel Hernandez leaves U.S. District Court in Manhattan with his lawyer, Amy Gallicchio, on Aug. 10, 2026, after being charged in the deaths of two people in a boating accident in New York Harbor. AP Photo/Larry Neumeister

According to the federal charging documents, Hernandez was operating the vessel with 14 people onboard, which exceeded the maximum allowable capacity of 10. Hernandez "knowingly operated the Vessel with an infant onboard, knowing that the infant was not wearing a personal floatation device," the documents state.

Hernandez was allegedly operating the vessel without a valid Coast Guard Certificate of Inspection, "which is required for a vessel to operate with paying customers onboard, and, in fact, the Vessel was of a type and size that made it ineligible to receive a COI for the type of operation conducted by Hernandez," according to the charging documents.

An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that lacks Coast Guard credentials, safety equipment and inspection certificates, the Coast Guard said.

The New York Police Department said it was called to an overturned vessel near Liberty Island, home to the Statue of Liberty, at 10:55 p.m. on Saturday. The department deployed a harbor unit, a scuba team and an aviation team to the scene, where 12 people had already been rescued from the water.

A 27-year-old woman and a 5-month-old baby girl were located and taken to NYU Langone Hospital, where they were declared deceased on arrival, according to authorities. Law enforcement sources identified to CBS News the 27-year-old woman as Sara Sanchez and her baby as Antonella Garcia.

Il Punto Ristorante, an Italian restaurant in Midtown Manhattan, said on social media that Sanchez and Garcia were the wife and daughter of one of their employees, Andres Garcia, who was also on the boat.

"What was meant to be a joyful family outing ended in unimaginable tragedy," the restaurant wrote on Instagram.

A coworker told CBS New York that Andres Garcia and Sanchez also have a 6-year-old son, but it was not clear if he was also on the boat. Police said the family lived in College Point, Queens, and neighbors told CBS New York they had just moved there about two months ago.

A Sea the City boat initially saw the capsized boat and people in the water and helped 11 people out of the water, according to the company's founder, Adam Schwartz.

The remaining survivors were taken to a local hospital and, according to police, had minor injuries.

"We are deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life last night, and our thoughts are with the victims' family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time," Captain Doreen McCarthy, the Coast Guard Sector New York commander, said in a statement. "We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water."

Police said they are investigating the cause of the deadly incident.

World.title: Man who allegedly arranged Tupac Shakur's 1996 killing is on trial in Las Vegas
World.content:
Las Vegas — The man who prosecutors say orchestrated the 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur went on trial Monday, almost 30 years after the fatal drive-by shooting in Las Vegas.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, faces a single count of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang in Shakur's death. He's been jailed since late 2023 and has pleaded not guilty.

Family members of Shakur were among those who gathered at a Las Vegas courthouse for the beginning of jury selection, which could continue through much of this week.

"Whoever had anything to do with it, whoever set it up, whoever had any hand in it should be locked up in prison," said Shakur's cousin, Kendrick Lesane.

For decades, Shakur's unsolved killing has gripped hip-hop fans. He's considered one of the most influential rappers of all time with songs that speak to the human experience of love, heartache and familial relationships. When Shakur died, he was in the midst of a fierce battle for dominance in a music scene increasingly shaped by rival gangs.

The trial, which is expected to last about a month, likely won't reveal who pulled the trigger. Instead, prosecutors hope to prove that Davis was the shot caller and provided the weapon.

Gunfire came from the Cadillac that Davis was in, and he's one of the only people there that night who is still alive. Prosecutors say if Davis hadn't written explicitly about the killing, or talked about it in interviews, it's likely no one would have been charged.

Tupac Shakur, left, and Duane "Keffe D" Davis CBS News

How Shakur's killing unfolded

On Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW and Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight was driving. They had just watched Mike Tyson knock out Bruce Seldon and were headed to a nightclub where Shakur was scheduled to perform. But at a red light near the Las Vegas Strip, a white Cadillac pulled up beside them and gunfire erupted.

Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived with minor injuries. Knight is serving a 28-year prison sentence for a fatal hit-and-run.

The case went cold until Davis began making public statements about his involvement as a leader of the South Side Compton Crips. In 2019, he published a tell-all memoir. The book, along with interviews Davis gave, revived the police investigation.

Duane Davis appears in Clark County District Court on Aug. 10, 2026, in Las Vegas. David Becker/Pool Photo via AP

Davis' defense attorneys argue there is no evidence he directed the shooting and the state relies on witnesses who weren't there. The defense said Davis left the narcotics trade in 2009 and worked a steady job before illness forced him to retire in 2014.

For Shakur's family, the last 30 years have been exhausting and stressful, his stepbrother Maurice "Mopreme" Shakur said. Sitting through the trial will be retraumatizing, Shakur said, but he's "cautiously optimistic" justice will come.

"I hope that the trial is fair, and we find out the truth," he said.

Gang rivalry behind slaying?

Hundreds of pages of grand jury transcripts portray Tupac Shakur's shooting as a culmination of a longstanding feud between rival record labels Death Row Records and Bad Boy Records and rival gang sects Mob Piru and South Side Compton Crips.

Witnesses said South Side Compton Crips hung out with and provided protection to Bad Boy Records, which was founded by Sean "Diddy" Combs and included rappers like The Notorious B.I.G., or Christopher Wallace. Mob Piru, part of the larger Bloods gang, was associated with Death Row Records, which featured rappers like Shakur, Snoop Dogg and Dr. Dre.

The rival gangs fought and retaliated against each other both before and after Shakur's death.

Prosecutors allege Davis orchestrated the shooting to get revenge after Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis' nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, at the MGM Grand hours before Shakur was killed.

Davis denied any involvement in an interview with CBS Las Vegas affiliate KLAS-TV.

The prosecutors' case relies on "Compton Street Legend," the book Davis co-authored about the shooting and his time in the Crips, as well as police and media interviews he participated in.

Davis' attorneys unsuccessfully fought to block the use of the book and a recording of a 2008 police interview in the trial. They argued the book was fictionalized and had a co-author, making it impossible to know which parts Davis wrote. They also argued Davis' interview with a federal task force investigating the deaths of Wallace and Shakur was supposed to be confidential and not used against him.

The memoir says that Shakur and his entourage "crossed the line" when they beat up Anderson.

"We couldn't let no record company studio gangsters do us like that," the book says.

Davis was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed a gun to the back seat earlier that night, according to the book. When they encountered Shakur and Knight, Davis claimed to see Shakur reach for a weapon and wrote that "one of my guys from the back seat grabbed the Glock and started bustin' back."

No weapon was found in Knight and Shakur's car, according to retired Las Vegas police Detective Clifford Mogg, who was assigned to the investigation in early 2018.

Shakur relative says justice "unattainable"

Mopreme Shakur said nothing would bring back his stepbrother.

"That would be justice for me," he said. "But we all know that is unattainable."

Mopreme Shakur said he wants allegations that Combs was involved to be explored further. In his book, Davis claims that Combs wanted Knight and Shakur killed. Combs has denied having any involvement in Shakur's death.

He's serving roughly four years in prison after being convicted of prostitution-related charges. Combs' attorney did not return emailed requests from The Associated Press for comment.

Shakur sold over 75 million records worldwide with hits like "California Love," "Changes" and "Dear Mama." His songs spanned from party anthems to deep social commentary. The issues he discussed still resonate with people 30 years later, history professor Jeffrey O.G. Ogbar said.

"I can't think of anyone else in the history of hip-hop who's had a greater impact in such a short period of time," said Ogbar, who is the founding director of the Center for the Study of Popular Music at the University of Connecticut.

Lottery system for courtroom seating

There's so much public interest in the trial, the Eighth Judicial District Court will implement a lottery system to determine who will get to watch in the main courtroom, KLAS reports, and the court will provide an overflow room with live video of the proceedings during both jury selection and the trial itself. Seating in the overflow room will be limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis.
