World.title: Former Miss Universe Canada calls out 'Feathered Headdress' and 'Arctic Beauty' costumes at pageant
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former Miss Universe Canada winner Ashley Callingbull interrupted her own duties hosting the 2026 Miss Universe Canada pageant on the weekend to call out multiple instances of what she described as cultural appropriation at this year's event.

Just as director Sonny Borrelli was about to announce the top 20 contestants, Callingbull took the opportunity to speak.

"Sometimes there are mistakes that are made," said Callingbull.

"It's 2026. We should know better, but most importantly a part of reconciliation is that we educate and learn and understand and move on from these things in a good way."

On Aug. 4, Miss Universe Canada hosted its national pageantry costume competition in Windsor, Ont., where 35 contestants were competing for this year's crown.

During the costume portion, Karisa Haverkamp walked on stage wearing a turquoise, black and white feathered headdress and a small red painted hand on her cheek.

Jasleen Kaily, another contestant, walked out wearing a two-piece "Arctic Beauty" costume with brown fringes on the thighs, two braids and a maple leaf cutout on her back.

Organizers of the Miss Universe Canada pageant issued a statement saying the costume segment of the pageant will have guidelines in the future after Indigenous people reacted negatively to some of the contestants' outfits. (Miss Universe Canada/YouTube)

In an interview with CBC Indigenous on Friday, Callingbull said "my jaw just dropped on the floor."

"This cannot be real. I just couldn't get over that this was happening. Who allowed this on stage? Who approved this?" she said.

"Anything traditional or sacred should not be allowed. I was very, very upset."

On stage, Callingbull told the audience that Borrelli assured her there will be guidelines implemented and cultural liaisons moving forward.

Callingbull then spoke on stage to the Indigenous community, adding that the organizers released a statement earlier in the week but noting that the statement needed an apology.

"On behalf of all of us at Miss Universe Canada, it was not our intent to offend anybody and if we did, we take full responsibility, we will learn from it," said Borrelli, adding that Callingbull will be their cultural liaison moving forward.

Callingbull then spoke again.

"We're going to make sure that everyone is going to be respected and honoured properly," she said.

"And thank you for teaching us and we'll learn from it, we apologize again, we love you," said Borrelli.

Miss World Canada 2022 Emma Morrison said the costumes were culturally inappropriate and sexualized Indigenous people.

Morrison also said the hand print on Haverkamp's cheek, which she believes represented Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG), was not "the time or place" to make a MMIWG statement.

"When you're on stage, you're smiling to the judges and it just doesn't fit," added Morrison, who is Mushkegowuk Cree from Chapleau Cree First Nation in northern Ontario.

"The stage that we celebrated Ashley Callingbull on just two years ago is the same stage she is being disrespected on," said Morrison, adding that she believes the incident stems from a lack of Indigenous education.

Callingbull, who is Plains Cree and is from the Enoch Cree Nation in Alberta, is also the first Canadian and first Indigenous woman to win Mrs. Universe in 2015 and has championed accurate Indigenous representation in her modelling, acting and hosting career.

Callingbull said she immediately called the organizers the moment she saw the costumes.

"They were very apologetic and said they were being ignorant and that they didn't know any better. I told them, 'Unless you were living under a rock, we know that headdresses are not OK at Coachella, so they're not OK on stage,'" said Callingbull.

Both costumes can be found on the e-commerce websites Etsy and Fashion Nova. Etsy calls the headdress "perfect for music festivals, Burning Man style outfits, Halloween, carnival, parades and themed parties."

Statements and apologies come in

In a Friday statement, Miss Universe Canada said, "if any costume caused offense, hurt, or misunderstanding, please know that it was never our intention."

CBC Indigenous also contacted Borrelli for comment but was unable to schedule an interview.

The pageant said it is actively implementing a comprehensive costume guide that will establish clear guidelines and standards for all future pageant cycles.

"Within that statement there was really no direct apology," Morrison told CBC Indigenous on Friday.

In a post on her Instagram page, Haverkamp wrote she acknowledged and recognized that her outfit caused "hurt and offence" to the Indigenous community.

Haverkamp wrote she has learned from the incident and is committed to stand up and speak "for all women who have lost their voice because of violence, trauma and oppression."

Kaily also took to Instagram and apologized, saying, "My intention was never to disrespect or misrepresent Indigenous culture" and upon developing her costume she wanted to "recognize and celebrate one of the First Peoples of Canada."

CBC Indigenous attempted to contact Kaily and Miss Universe Canada but did not hear back.

CBC Indigenous reached out to Haverkamp for comment. She said she would talk to the Miss Universe Canada organization leadership before speaking and hasn't responded since.

Aleria McKay, the founder/director of Miss Indigenous Canada, is from Six Nations of the Grand River. (Submitted by Aleria McKay)

Aleria McKay, who is Onondaga from Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario and the founder of Miss Indigenous Canada, said Miss Universe Canada has a history of cultural appropriation around Indigenous people, both on the national and international stage.

"The fact that they're just allowing those types of things on their stage is in my opinion shameful," said McKay.

Callingbull said the costume incident reminded her of her grandfather, who previously defended her when she faced racism in person.

"When he did that, he looked at me and said, 'You know if you never speak up, nothing's going to change.'"

World.title: Trump signs executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. ‌President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday calling for fewer childhood vaccinations by limiting the inoculation schedule to 11 immunizations, ‌which he said would give U.S. children "gold-standard" protection and align the country with peer nations that recommend fewer shots.

The order advances a long-standing goal of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an anti-vaccine activist who has promoted a link between vaccines and autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked.

Public health experts say the U.S. schedule reflects decades of evidence and the specific health needs of Americans, and that fewer recommended ​shots will leave more children exposed to preventable diseases.

The order also ​recommended splitting the childhood measles, mumps ​and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering the shots at separate medical visits.

Kennedy ​had in January cut the U.S. immunization schedule to remove shots against six out of 17 diseases — a move halted ​by a federal court ruling. The Trump order says ⁠that the federal ⁠government will now only support the ‌remaining 11 shots.

'This executive order ​is wrong'

The American Academy of Pediatrics and vaccine-maker Merck criticized the order.

"We are evaluating our next steps," said Richard Hughes IV, lead counsel for ‌the American Academy of Pediatrics, which sued earlier this year over Kennedy's changes to the childhood immunization schedule.

A nurse prepares to inoculate a child in Easley in March 2026. (Mary Conlon/The Associated Press)

Merck said there is no published scientific evidence showing any benefit to splitting the combination MMR shot into three, and that using the individual components increases the number of injections and can lead to delayed or missed immunizations.

"Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations ‌for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR, which hopefully will be split up," Trump said during ​a White House signing ceremony.

Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, said breaking up combination vaccines and downgrading recommendations would deepen disparities and worsen vaccine coverage, warning that the resulting recommendations ‌in practice cannot be implemented.

Kennedy has previously led efforts to drop universal recommendations for hepatitis B shots for children and reduce the list of recommended vaccines, citing links to autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked.

U.S. President Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks on in the Oval Office of the White House on Monday. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

The executive order reaffirms Kennedy's overhaul despite the ongoing litigation.

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician who chairs the Senate health committee, condemned the order.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order ​is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that breaking up vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Cassidy, however, ⁠has shepherded Trump's slate of health agency leaders through confirmation despite his own warnings about vaccine skepticism. He cast a decisive vote to confirm Kennedy in 2025. ⁠Cassidy lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-endorsed challenger and will leave office in January.

Trump, Kennedy and other White House ⁠officials said ⁠the order means U.S. children would receive far fewer than ​the 72 injections recommended under the previous schedule.

Vaccine experts say that figure is inflated, because it counts combination shots such as MMR as multiple injections even though they ​are given in one shot, and assumes annual ⁠flu and COVID-19 doses.

WATCH | Winnipeg microbiology lab expanding to produce test vaccines: Winnipeg microbiology lab expanding to produce test vaccines | Duration 2:00 The National Microbiology Lab in Winnipeg, currently the only facility in Canada that can handle the most extreme infectious pathogens, is expanding. A new medical countermeasures lab, expected to open in 2033, will aim to better defend against the threat of future pandemics.

Dr. Elizabeth Mack, a pediatric critical care physician in Charleston, South Carolina, said breaking up the shots would increase the number of injections children receive, because they are currently given in combination.

She also said there were no licensed single-antigen measles, mumps or rubella vaccines available in the United States, making the recommendation unfeasible as written.

"We don't have a system that supports this," Mack said, questioning whether parents would be asked to make more visits and whether those visits would be reimbursed.

World.title: Hiker escapes after being attacked by grizzly bear in backcountry near Pemberton, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A man managed to escape without being seriously injured after a grizzly bear attacked him while he was hiking alone near Pemberton, B.C.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) responded to the backcountry area of Rutherford Creek drainage on Sunday evening.

“The investigation determined the attack was defensive in nature and resulted from a close-range surprise encounter,” said BCCOS.

The man suffered non-life-threatening injuries, officials said, adding that he self-rescued and sought medical attention on his own.

“Officers have confirmed there is no ongoing threat to other backcountry users,” said BCCOS.

A predator attack team conducted an investigation and said anyone recreating in the area is encouraged to remain vigilant and be prepared for potential wildlife encounters.

Multiple first responder agencies collaborated on the rescue of a woman attacked by a grizzly bear including BC EHS, Pemberton SAR, RCMP, Conservation Officer Service and B.C. Wildfire Service on Aug. 2, 2026 (Pemberton Search and Rescue)

Grizzly bear breaks woman’s neck

Sunday's incident marks the second grizzly bear attack in the region within a week — and both individuals were hiking alone.

A 72-year-old woman suffered a broken neck after a grizzly bear attacked her while she was hiking on Aug. 2 in the South Chilcotin near Pearson Ridge, roughly 70 kilometres north of Pemberton.

The woman was taken to the hospital by air ambulance in serious condition.

B.C. Emergency Health Services received a call at 3:20 p.m. PT on Aug. 2 for a person requiring medical attention near Tyaughton Lake, in the South Chilcotin area, after being attacked by a grizzly bear. (Pemberton Search and Rescue)

Pemberton Search and Rescue president David McKenzie said the woman also suffered several lacerations to her face, arms and neck.

“The bear was batting them around in the altercation,” McKenzie said.

The Ministry of Environment said the attack was defensive in nature, from a female grizzly with at least one cub.

The bear was not removed nor killed, and no capture devices were set up.

Preventing grizzly bear encounters

Bear biologist and researcher Wayne McCrory said having campsites and trails that overlap with grizzly bear feeding areas will create a high level of conflict.

He’s done bear risk assessments for many national and provincial parks in the province over the last 40 years.

Conservation officer said anyone recreating in the area of the attack on Aug. 9, is encouraged to remain vigilant and be prepared for potential wildlife encounters. (Wayne McCrory)

“Where you have trails and campsites that avoid those areas, the conflict level goes way down,” McCrory said.

Grizzlies feed in riparian spaces, such as moist spots along rivers or subalpine areas in high-elevation, he said.

“Most of the grizzly bear injury incidents occur after July, when the bears are more intensely feeding to gain a third of their body weight before hibernation."

McCrory said the trails where the attacks occurred should be assessed.

“Do more bear habitat mapping and professional risk assessments and look at readjusting some of the historic trails and campsites that are in high hazard areas,” he said.

Research scientist Lana Ciarniello specializes in human-bear conflicts, and said trails should not go through grizzly habitat and closing areas during berry season can help.

“It's hard on bears,” Ciarniello said. “We are taking up a lot of habitat and bears need a home.”

Research scientist Lana Ciarniello has been in the field for 30 years and is pictured with a grizzly bear that has been immobilized to be prepared for release into the wild in May 2022. (Lana Ciarniello)

A current proposal from Recreation Sites and Trails B.C. would prohibit camping and motorized vehicles for the Brandywine Meadows area from June 1 to Nov. 1, as they say it is important habitat for grizzlies to raise their cubs.

“Don't forget this isn't only for the bears; this is also to protect the people,” Ciarniello said.

Staying safe in the backcountry

McCory said grizzly bears are known to rub on trees and mark their territories.

“Grizzly bears are leaving their scent there,” McCrory said.

Field studies can be done to locate these tree markings, which are often visible with scratches or stumps on the tree that have been smoothed over and shiny from the rubbing.

“If you find more than four grizzly bear marked trees along a trail, you know, that's the main travel route,” McCrory said.

A grizzly bear seen on trail camera rubbing against a tree marking its territory, which alerts other bears and researchers of the animal. (Submitted: Wayne McCrory)

To avoid encounters with grizzlies, he said people should avoid travelling at dusk and dawn, and know how to use bear spray.

“That will help you survive a close, serious encounter,” McCrory said.

Ciarniello said people should use their voice when in bear habitat, and travelling in a group also helps prevent attacks.

“Having a group of you, staying together [and] making noise, your chances are very, very reduced,” Ciarniello said.

World.title: N.Y. jury convicts Montreal father of murder in death of 9-year-old daughter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Melina Frattolin's loved ones and family members sobbed in a New York courthouse on Monday after a jury found the girl's father guilty of drowning her and hiding her body in a marsh last summer.

A group of family members held onto each other as the jury read out "Guilty" and convicted Luciano Frattolin, 46, of second-degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of nine-year-old Melina.

Standing between his two attorneys, Frattolin kept a neutral expression, shaking his head slightly, before sitting down. He was taken away in handcuffs minutes later.

Once the trial was officially over, the family members hugged and cried between the benches.

Michael Langey, the Essex County District Attorney, said it felt good to hear the verdict after a year of working on this case.

"The grandparents were here, the aunts were here. They had to sit in the courtroom and there was a possibility, obviously, that he wasn't gonna get convicted. So it was a relief for them, and hopefully this could be some type of closure for them," he said outside the courthouse.

'Her daughter never came home'

Melina's mother, Kali Galanis, was not in the courtroom on Monday. She had not wanted to be there in case Frattolin testified, said Langey. Galanis lost her only daughter when Melina died, he added.

"She waited for her daughter to come home all night, looked out the window ... Her daughter never came home, and she had to get the call the next day that she was dead in a brook in Essex County, in New York," he said.

Melina's body was found last year in a marsh in a rural area of New York, partially covered by a fallen tree with a large rock on her chest.

The girl and her father were nearing the end of a weeklong trip in the United States when Frattolin reported his daughter missing on July 19, 2025.

Her body was found the next day near Ticonderoga, N.Y., about 400 kilometres north of New York City. The autopsy found she died from asphyxia due to drowning.

Frattolin reported his daughter had been kidnapped by two men who drove off in a white van, but investigators later arrested him for the child's murder.

Electronic data key to verdict

Electronic data played a big role in finding Melina's body and in the outcome of the trial, both through location data from Frattolin's phone and car, and through records of text messages and calls.

The prosecution called several police officers and experts over the trial who used car location data, cell phone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin's movements on the day Melina died and prove the story he told to investigators was false.

"I think every second there was data in this case. We could see exactly where his vehicle was during the entire trip, and that was huge. Knowing that he wasn't where he was telling people he was was a big factor in them starting to turn the focus away from the abduction to, 'why are you telling us you're here when you're not here?"' said Langey.

Documents found in Frattolin's car helped prove intent, which was necessary in both charges the jury convicted him on. In the documents, Frattolin writes disparaging remarks about Galanis and mentions bringing his daughter to "the end."

"It was something that when you read it, there definitely was a plan. He definitely knew a life was coming to an end somewhere on this vacation, no matter where he went," said Langey.

"It was a tough case," said Eric Weyand, one of Frattolin's lawyers, walking out of the courtroom.

The jury deliberated for about an hour following a trial that lasted about three weeks.

Earlier in the day, the defence rested its case after Frattolin announced he would not testify in his defence.

"I really want to, but I was advised not to," he told the judge earlier.

The defence presented a single witness. The prosecution, who had the legal responsibility to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt, presented over two dozen witnesses.

Defence argues inconsistencies

In the defence's closing argument, Brian Pilatzke, Frattolin's other lawyer, went back through the evidence presented over the last three weeks to fit it into Frattolin's version of events.

He argued that the inconsistent statements Frattolin made the night he reported Melina missing were due to English not being his first language, to stress and to exhaustion.

He added the police did not do enough to track the van when Frattolin reported the abduction, instead turning immediately to him as their suspect, and that they overlooked key evidence. The rock found on Melina's body was never tested for DNA, sweat or blood, he said.

Frattolin is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 14, and will remain in custody in Essex County in the meantime. He has a month to appeal the jury's decision.

Melina touched the hearts of people in the area, said Langey after the verdict was announced. Residents even adopted a section of the highway near Ticonderoga in her name.

"She really had no connection to the county, but I think whenever a child is murdered — everyone's got parents, they have children…. The community has rallied around it," he said.

He approached the case with the same energy as he would have for a community member, he said.

"It doesn't make a difference, whether she was from Essex County or Montreal or anywhere else. She was a nine-year-old that lost her life in our county, so I felt responsible for getting some type of justice for her," he said.

World.title: Heated Rivalry Season 2 cast announcement sparks criticism from some fans over body diversity
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two new faces are joining the world of Heated Rivalry — but the casting announcement for Season 2 is sparking some criticism among fans who were hoping to see more book-accurate body diversity.

Crave confirmed on Friday that the cast of the wildly popular hockey romance will be expanding in its second season to include Justice Smith and Charlie Gillespie.

Gillespie, who hails from New Brunswick and recently appeared in the movie One Night Only, has been tapped to play Troy Barrett, a forward on the Ottawa Centaurs. He also previously starred in the Netflix show Julie and the Phantoms, which was cancelled after only one season.

Smith, known for his roles in I Saw the TV Glow, Pokémon Detective Pikachu and Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, will be playing Harris Drover, who is the Centaurs' social media manager.

Troy and Harris are the central characters of Role Model, the fifth book in Rachel Reid's Game Changers series, which the show Heated Rivalry is based on. Crave has stated the second season of the show will continue following the first season's main characters Ilya Rozanov and Shane Hollander, while incorporating Troy and Harris's story.

"From the start of the casting process, we knew we were looking for actors who could create something truly special together and bring that same depth and heart to the screen," director Jacob Tierney and producer Brendan Brady wrote in the casting announcement.

"Justice and Charlie do exactly that. They immediately connected with the vulnerability and resilience at the core of these characters, bringing an instinctive understanding of who Harris and Troy are.”

Fan reaction split

While some fans are excited by the announcement, other fans are expressing disappointment with Smith's casting as Harris, calling it a missed opportunity to have more inclusivity in the types of bodies presented as desirable on screen.

"Harris in the book is described by himself as being a little pudgy, unathletic, and is described by Troy as having a broad chest, solid body, soft belly, being stocky and rugged, and I am just so sad that we're losing that piece of Harris," BookTok content creator Taylor Layne, who posts under Taylor Just Reads, shared in a TikTok on Sunday.

"As a big gay Libra myself, I related so much to Harris, and I was so excited to see more body diversity, especially in a show about jacked athletes. [...] I believe that the show will be amazing and that the actors will be fantastic, but at the same time, I'm heartbroken."

Justice Smith attends the world premiere of Now You See Me: Now You Don't at The Lighthouse Pier 61 on Nov. 10, 2025, in New York. Smith is set to play Harris Drover in the second season of Heated Rivalry. (CJ Rivera/Invision/The Associated Press)

The comments on Crave's Instagram and TikTok posts revealing the casting are filled with fans expressing mixed feelings.

"Justice Smith has been 10/10 in everything I have ever seen him in! I’m very excited to see him in HR," @geeky_spice wrote in an Instagram comment.

"I love Justice as an actor, but as a bigger guy, I really wanted a character in a romantic role who had a body type like mine," user @Jax wrote in a TikTok comment on the show's casting announcement, adding, "While I'm disappointed in the lack of representation I'm sure Justice was the right choice."

CBC News reached out to the producers of Heated Rivalry for comment, and were referred to the casting announcement.

This image released by Universal Pictures shows Charlie Gillespie in a scene from One Night Only. Gillespie has been tapped to play Troy Barrett in the second season of Heated Rivalry. (Nicole Rivelli/Universal Pictures/The Associated Press)

Other fans pointed out that the casting of Ilya and Shane also sparked controversy when it was first announced — and now actors Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams have skyrocketed to fame in the wake of the show's massive international success.

Reid appeared to echo this on Instagram over the weekend.

She shared a selfie of her side-eying heavily on her Instagram story, along with the caption, "Thinking about all the people last summer who told me the casting for Ilya and Shane was wrong and bad…"

WATCH | Canadian Tire tote bag flies off shelves due to Hudson Williams:

Smith expressed his excitement to tackle the role in a story post on his Instagram on Sunday, writing that he is "moved by the support and love i’m getting from fans in my dms, fans who have welcomed me with open arms and who already feel a responsibility to protect me."

"i am honored to play a character you all care about deeply and i promise i will take good care of him if you give me the chance," the post continued.

The second season is slated to come out in Spring 2027, and filming has already begun, much to the excitement of fans feverishly following every development. After Storrie and Williams were spotted in Toronto, fans flocked to Canadian Tire to purchase a reusable bag Williams was carrying.

As the shooting continues, Tierney posted a request last week for fans to give cast and crew space at filming locations.

World.title: Trump says Iran should pay compensation, including for past actions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday responded to Iran's conditions for a peace deal with his own demands that Iran pay compensation for people killed in wars, attacks and protests, in a rhetorical escalation likely ‌to complicate efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump's proposal, which has not been raised before, was a response to Tehran's demands for compensation and an end to sanctions. This are largely in line with the terms of a preliminary peace deal signed in June, which has since broken down.

Since the war began in February, Trump has repeatedly oscillated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.

"We're going to ask for ​money for the damage they've done over a 50-year period," Trump said at the White House, ​saying payments would cover deaths among both civilian demonstrators and U.S. forces in the region.

"So if there's damages to be paid, I think Iran should pay those damages," Trump said.

Oil prices settled five per cent higher on Monday after the demands dimmed prospects for a deal to reopen the ​strait.

Vehicles drive past a banner in Tehran on Monday, which carries a message in English and Farsi that says: 'We will kill Trump.' (Vahid Salemi/The Associated Press)

Trump cites attack blamed on al-Qaeda

Referring to Tehran's crackdown on demonstrations in late 2025 and 2026, Trump said Iran had ⁠killed some 52,000 protesters as of six ⁠weeks ago. While some Iranian opposition and exile groups have claimed tens of thousands killed, ‌the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) in February reported around 7,000 deaths, including 6,500 protesters.

Trump encouraged protesters to overthrow the Iranian government when the war began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes in February. Rights groups say the Iranian government has continued to crack down on opponents since then.

Trump also said Iran should compensate families of the 17 U.S. sailors killed in an October 2000 attack in Yemen on the naval vessel USS Cole, which has been ⁠blamed on al-Qaeda, not Iran.

WATCH | Margaret Evans crosses into Iran: Reporting from inside Iran | Duration 6:46 In June, CBC senior international correspondent Margaret Evans and videographer Lyza Sale were granted rare access to report from inside Iran. Where they could travel and what they could report on was tightly controlled, but Iranian authorities had no editorial influence on the content and were not given access to CBC News material before it was published.

"Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!" Trump wrote in a social media post.

Iran earlier said it was nearing ‌a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz but repeated that the U.S. must meet conditions, including compensation and an end to sanctions and military threats before the key waterway is reopened.

The strait, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flowed prior to the conflict, has been effectively blocked since the war began, pushing up oil prices and inflation.

An unpopular war at home

Ironically, ​the agreement with Oman would give Tehran more leverage over the key waterway than it had before the war began.

A bird flies past ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Monday. (Ali Saeedi/Getty Images)

Trump is under pressure to end a war that is deeply unpopular at home ahead of midterm elections ⁠in November, and high fuel prices are a top issue in rural areas that have backed him in the past.

"What you're seeing here is the beginning ⁠of a capitulation," Democratic U.S. Rep. Bill Keating said on CNN. "This is reality. It's sinking in."

Earlier on Monday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said talks with ⁠Oman were "progressing ⁠smoothly and constructively," with an agreement reached on a shipping route map, ​while some technical issues remained unresolved.

Baghaei said the discussions also covered services which would normally involve payment, such as safe navigation, environmental protection, maritime services and combating crime.

U.S. ​officials have repeatedly ruled out any deal ⁠that would allow Tehran to charge fees for access to the strait.

But months of U.S. military efforts, including a two-week campaign of strikes in July, have not broken Iran's grip on the strait, despite Trump's misleading claim, ⁠repeated on Monday, that the strait was open and, "the only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now is the United States navy."

Washington and Tehran agreed to a ceasefire in June, but the U.S. reimposed a blockade on Iranian shipping in July, a move that Tehran said violated the truce.

Iran has been striking back with missiles and drones against Washington's allies in the region, while also targeting commercial ships transiting the strait without its permission.

World.title: Man charged with arranging Tupac Shakur's murder heads to trial 30 years after hip-hop legend's death
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A former gang member's murder trial concerning the unsolved shooting death of hip-hop legend Tupac Shakur began with jury selection on Monday, almost 30 years after the influential rapper was shot and killed.

Duane (Keffe D) Davis, 63, faces a single count of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang in Shakur's death in 1996. Davis, who has been in custody since 2023, has pleaded not guilty. The trial, which is taking place in Las Vegas, where the shooting took place, starts with jury selection, and is expected to last about a month.

Prosecutors in the trial will not attempt to prove that Davis pulled the trigger. Instead, they'll try to convince a jury that he was the "shot caller" — slang for a leader or decision maker — of the group that targeted Shakur in the Sept. 7, 1996, shooting on the Las Vegas Strip.

Wearing a blue dress shirt and tie, Davis sat quietly next to his attorney Monday while Nevada Judge Carli Kierny asked a group of 75 potential jurors questions, including if they have any medical issues, language barriers or conflicts with serving.

'Justice is a little bit weakened'

William Leslane, Shakur's cousin, said the trial may bring accountability, but that it's too little, too late to bring justice.

"Justice has been foregone years ago. The night my cousin was murdered — there should have been an intense investigation at that time," he said in an interview.

"We're here 30 years later, so justice is a little bit weakened."

WATCH | Shakur's cousin discusses the murder trial: Justice in murder of Tupac 'foregone years ago': cousin | Duration 0:52 Thirty years after his death, jury selection is underway in the murder trial of rapper Tupac Shakur. Being charged with Shakur's murder is former gang leader Duane (Keffe D) Davis, who prosecutors say ordered the killing and provided the gun in the shooting. Shakur's cousin William Lesane says he thinks 63-year-old Davis is the killer, claiming he was 'screaming it out publicly' but says justice was 'foregone' the day Shakur was killed.

Much of the evidence in the case will come from a book Davis co-wrote. In his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, the former high-ranking member of the South Side Compton Crips gang wrote about his alleged role in the shooting.

Shakur, who was 25 when he died, was one of rap's brightest rising stars, known for hits such as Dear Mama and California Love. Though born in New York City, Shakur was associated with West Coast hip-hop. He released four solo albums during his life, followed by six posthumous albums.

At the time of his death, Tupac was signed with Death Row Records, which was one of rap's most notorious labels.

Marion (Suge) Knight, the co-founder and then-CEO of Death Row Records, was with Shakur when he was shot. Knight, the only other living witness to the shooting, told ABC News last week that he will not co-operate with law enforcement and does not want to testify.

Knight is serving a 28-year prison sentence in California for running over and killing a Compton businessman outside a burger stand in January 2015.

Fans hold up a poster of Shakur during a ceremony honouring the late rapper with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on June 7, 2023, in Los Angeles. Davis was arrested and charged that year for his alleged role in Shakur's 1996 shooting death. (Chris Pizzello/Invision/The Associated Press)

The night of the shooting

Shakur and Knight were in Las Vegas the night of Sept. 7 to watch a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon. Following the fight, the pair drove around Las Vegas in a Death Row-owned BMW.

At approximately 11:15 p.m., a Cadillac pulled up next to them and fired multiple shots, hitting Shakur four times. Though Knight was also injured in the shooting, he managed to drive the car away and got the attention of emergency services. Shakur died from his injuries six days later on Sept. 13.

The murder spurred intense speculation and conspiracy theories about the perpetrators and the circumstances of the shooting, including theories that Shakur had not died.

Tensions were high at the time between East and West Coast rappers. The rivalry fuelled theories that rapper Notorious B.I.G. — Shakur's New York-based adversary — was involved. He died in a shooting less than a year later.

Shakur spits in the direction of reporters as he leaves state Supreme Court in New York, July 5, 1994. Two years later, Shakur was shot and killed on the Las Vegas Strip. (The Associated Press)

What Davis wrote about the shooting

In his book, Davis said the shooting of Shakur was about revenge. Earlier that evening, he wrote, his nephew, Baby Lane, said people from Death Row had attacked him.

He wrote in his book that Shakur, Knight and others "didn't have any business putting their hands on Baby Lane. Them jumping on my nephew gave us the green light to want to do something to their ass."

Davis also said that Shakur was "a guppy that got swallowed up by some ferocious sharks. He shouldn't have ever got involved in that bullshit of trying to be a thug."

Davis and his gang were able to find Shakur's car because he was greeting fans and waving to them from the window of the BMW. Had he not been hanging out of the window, Davis said, the gang would not have seen him.

Davis recalled the shooting in detail. He did not mention who fired the fatal shots, but said he threw the pistol that killed Shakur into the back seat.

He said Knight immediately recognized them when their Cadillac pulled up to the BMW.

"Tupac made an erratic move and began to reach down beneath his seat," Davis wrote.

He said he saw Tupac pull out a gun. "That's when the fireworks started. One of my guys from the back seat grabbed the Glock and started bustin' back," Davis wrote.

Case hinges on 3 pieces of evidence: law prof

Lucius Outlaw III, an associate law professor at Howard University, said three pieces of evidence will be key at the trial — the memoir, the interviews Davis gave to promote the memoir, and the interview Davis gave to investigators.

He expects Yusuf Jah, who co-wrote Davis's book, will be an important witness.

Davis appears in Clark County District Court on Monday in Las Vegas. Davis wrote about his alleged role in Shakur's murder in a 2019 book. (David Becker/Pool AFP/The Associated Press)

"The defence is going to lean heavily into the involvement of the co-writer to say, look, jury, you can't take this as face value, because these really aren't Mr. Davis's words," he said.

"The prosecution, on the other side, are going to say '[Davis] gave interviews saying it's 100 per cent accurate.' "

Shakur's legacy

Davis wrote in his book that he regrets the shooting.

"At this point in my life, I can say that I have a deep sense of remorse for what happened to Tupac," he said. "Pac was a talented artist with tons of potential."

Shakur's music often had political themes. He was primarily raised by his mother, Afeni Shakur, who was a member of the Black Panther Party. He was an avid reader and often went by the name "Makaveli" as a tribute to political philosopher Niccolò Machiavelli.

Shakur was also an actor, starring in the 1992 film Juice and and 1993's Poetic Justice among other movies. He also wrote poetry and previously worked as a backup dancer.

For A.D. Carson, a rapper and associate professor of h ip-hop and the Global South at the University of Virginia, Shakur's talent across so many different fields stands out.

"You couldn't say that Tupac was static. He was an incredibly dynamic artist," said Carson.

"He was doing this dynamic thing in hip-hop, at a time where hip-hop was not the globally recognized set of art forms that it is currently."

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: As De la Espriella takes office, his US-backed security policy for Colombia is raising questions
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella assumes office on Friday, after elections with a razor-thin margin. He brings with him promises to wield “iron fist” policies against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and organized criminal organizations in the country.

He has also promised to dismantle ongoing peace talks initiated by outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro, including groups that are currently disarming. De la Espriella made scores of hardline promises on the campaign trail, many of which he will likely not be able to achieve with a minority coalition in the legislature, such as withdrawing Colombia from the United Nations.

On security issues, however, Colombia’s constitution grants the president broad unilateral powers. De la Espriella has promised to “end” armed groups within a month, an extremely unlikely goal. Despite the broad powers of the presidential office, De la Espriella faces historical and logistical limitations.

Despite claims from right-wing parties that Petro has gone easy on armed groups, Colombia’s military has been fully deployed against NSAGs in the country for the last two years.

As conflict expert Thomas Garrison reported for news website Pirate Wire Services in June, Colombia has ongoing and large military operations against FARC dissident group Estado Mayor Central (EMC), the National Liberation Army (ELN), and EMC splinter-group EMBF.

Colombia’s security forces are “already operating on all cylinders,” and “stretched to their limit,” according to the International Crisis Group. It isn’t clear how deployments can be increased without increasing the numbers of security forces themselves — hardly a goal that can be achieved in his first month in office.

Nonetheless, there are strategic changes that de La Espriella can impose to chart a more aggressive course. As part of those plans, the president-elect has promised to implement a “Plan Patriota remixed”, an allusion to highly aggressive US-backed military operations against armed groups under then-President Alvaro Uribe in 2003.

Uribe’s allies to this day hail Plan Patriota as a great success that forced the FARC to the negotiating table in 2016.

Critics, however, point to rampant human and civil rights violations, including working with paramilitary forces to kill thousands of civilians and frame them as guerrilla fighters to increase casualty counts.

The US, however, is pushing Latin America towards increased military spending and Bukele-style crackdowns on organized crime, and de la Espriella plans to comply.

What was Plan Patriota and how will Abelardo’s version be ‘remixed’?

Plan Patriota involved aerial bombardments, large-scale military deployments in FARC-controlled areas, and aggressive intelligence gathering against FARC guerrillas at the height of Colombia’s civil war.

Although paramilitary groups were not officially part of Plan Patriota, they cooperated closely with regular military forces during the operation, functioning as spies, informants, and death squads — ostensibly killing alleged guerrillas, but just as often murdering leftists in general, as well as non-politically involved civilians.

The operation, which continued until 2010, weakened the FARC considerably, but at a great price: gross human rights violations including massacres, torture, and using sexual violence against civilians as a weapon of war.

Paramilitary structures were also greatly empowered across the country, sowing the seeds of groups that still exist today, such as the Ejercito Gaitanista Colombiano (EGC) — often referred to in Western media as ‘the Clan del Golfo.’

The full extent of the atrocities committed by both sides of the war would not become clear until Colombia launched its Truth Commission in 2017. (De la Espriella wants to disband the Truth Commission as well as the Colombian Peace Court, which prosecutes the worst offenders of the civil war.)

Any new version of Plan Patriota would look very different. Colombia is not the same country it was in the early 2000’s. Modern armed groups are not interested in clashing with state forces on the battlefield. Most are not interested in overthrowing the state at all, and certainly not via military victory.

Technology has also advanced considerably. Drone warfare is a dangerous new weapon in the arsenal of NSAGs who wage asymmetrical attacks on state forces as well as one another. Digital surveillance and satellite optics also mean that unlike the FARC, which often relied upon jungle canopies to hide large training and logistics camps, modern NSAGs instead blend into civil society in the communities where they operate.

They do not wear uniforms to distinguish themselves and avoid direct confrontations with the military, which means there are no large targets to bomb, nor columns of marching fighters for the state to confront.

Modern NSAGs are far more flexible, transnational, and relatively decentralized in their operations compared to FARC at the height of the civil war.

De la Espriella’s security program is more likely to look like Daniel Noboa’s policies in Ecuador than the 2002 Plan Patriota. It will likely include US cooperation on target-finding, naval cooperation on drug trafficking, and joint US-Colombia operations within the country.

Most of those dynamics already exist. Despite a rocky relationship with Washington, D.C, Petro continued to cooperate with the US on intelligence-sharing and anti-narcotics operations.

Critics of de la Espriella, however, fear that logistics won’t be the only similarity to Ecuadorian-US operations, which have resulted in the murder of civilians by security forces, torture, arbitrary detentions, and bombings of civilian infrastructure.

One factor that may keep de la Espriella somewhat in check is a lack of a clear mandate. He won elections by less than 1%, and has already clashed with more established right-wing political parties, who will not be forming part of his coalition in the legislature.

De la Espriella signals he will follow Washington’s lead

On a recent trip to the U.S, de la Espriella’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo, met with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph M. Humire, who spoke of investment by US companies in hydrocarbon and energy sectors as well as cooperation on security and migration issues.

“Colombia is historically one of the U.S. strongest security and defense partners,” he wrote on X on July 21. “Under the leadership of incoming President Abelardo De La Espriella, we plan to take this partnership to new levels with Plan Patriot 2.0.”

Before Humire joined the War Department, he worked as an anti-migration lobbyist propagating conspiracy theories that cartels have “weaponized” migrants as part of “asymmetrical warfare” against the U.S.

He falsely testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in February that Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua had “opened” the Darien Gap to migrants during the Biden administration as part of a Venezuelan plan to destabilize the US.

De la Espriella has already signalled that he looks forward to closer cooperation with the administration of US President Donald Trump and largely follow the US lead on regional issues. Trump has made migration a key facet of his domestic and foreign policy.

The ultra-right Colombian president-elect has also promised to “secure” the country’s borders. Migrants “who are here illegally, or committing crimes will be deported to their countries of origin without delay,” he said in a press conference on July 13.

He has agreed, however, to keep commercial and migratory pathways open on the Venezuelan border. Petro re-initiated diplomatic and commercial ties with Venezuela in 2022.

De la Espriella has not criticized Chavista governments as heavily as many other right-wing politicians in the country, and provided legal representation for Maduro loyalist Alex Saab, who has been extradited for a second time to the US to face money laundering and corruption charges.

Aggressive military strategies have failed in the past

The nature of conflict has changed drastically in Colombia since the civil war, and presidents have tried aggressive military tactics against criminal organizations and NSAGs before.

Former President Ivan Duque failed to slow the rapid growth of either during his time in office from 2018 to 2022.

The Colombian state failed to fulfill its promises to invest in legitimate economies and develop regions long ignored by Bogotá. Regions that had previously been governed by the FARC became power vacuums that were quickly filled by other criminal organizations and NSAGs.

Duque left office the least popular president in the country’s history since records have been kept, in part because of his security policy. Bombings on rebel camps that killed minors created significant public controversy. When Petro turned to similar strategies, the military inadvertently killed children in bombings in children as well.

Armed groups have continued to grow under Petro despite his employment of increasingly aggressive military strategies. De la Espriella has not offered details about his plans, and it is unclear what he could do that Duque and Petro did not, or why the results would be any different for his administration when similar tactics have failed before.

Trump, however, has gained a new ally in the region. The US president has often shown that projection of US power is an end in and of itself, and de la Espriella is likely to allow Trump to do exactly that.

World.title: At least 111 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia
World.content:
At least 111 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:51 UTC Full article

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead

At least 111 people were killed and 87 injured by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday, according to the official toll given by President Abelardo de la Espriella as of 12:30 local time. Authorities warned the figure is preliminary and that rescue work is continuing.

The quake struck at 07:34, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, at a depth of more than 80 kilometers, according to the Colombian Geological Service. It is the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead. Departmental tolls released by governors and mayors correspond to different cutoff times and do not match one another: Chocó governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi reported 12 dead and 84 injured in that department, while the mayor of Manizales confirmed two deaths. Fatalities were also reported in Valle del Cauca and Antioquia.

| URGENTE: Momento del derrumbe de un edificio de 3 pisos tras el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Pereira, Colombia. pic.twitter.com/r3v2lW5pU3 — Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) August 10, 2026

The government put the number of damaged homes at more than 1,500, with 37 destroyed and 61 buildings completely collapsed, along with damage to 18 health centers, 52 schools, 17 community centers and 18 roads. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at seven air terminals: Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.

Damage to the hospital network is among the most critical. In Cali, the Hospital Universitario del Valle partially collapsed and seven large health care institutions were closed and evacuated because of structural damage. Valle del Cauca governor Dilian Francisca Toro said at least five intensive care patients were trapped under rubble. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder reported at least twenty collapsed structures with people trapped inside and requested rescue teams from Bogotá and Medellín. The capital's mayor, Carlos Fernando Galán, dispatched a hundred rescue workers.

De la Espriella agreed to declare a national disaster situation and is leading a unified command post at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, with additional posts in Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry is coordinating international cooperation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was ready to provide assistance.

The Colombian Geological Service reported two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8. The agency also recorded an emission of ash and gases from the Puracé volcano, in Cauca department, on orange alert since July, coinciding in time with the earthquake.

World.title: Kast descarta impulsar el proyecto que condiciona el aborto a escuchar el latido fetal
World.content:
Kast descarta impulsar el proyecto que condiciona el aborto a escuchar el latido fetal

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:40 UTC Full article

“It is legitimate for lawmakers to introduce their bills and for a debate to be generated around that, but we are not going to move forward on this matter,” the president said

Chilean President José Antonio Kast said on Monday that his government would not push forward a bill introduced by lawmakers from his own coalition that would condition access to legal abortion on a woman agreeing to hear the fetus's cardiac activity.

“It is legitimate for lawmakers to introduce their bills and for a debate to be generated around that, but we are not going to move forward on this matter,” the president said in an interview with T13 Radio. He recalled that his campaign centered on an emergency government focused on the economy, security and social issues, and that he would not promote measures that generate tension.

Kast also drew a distinction about the text itself. “In other countries, the heartbeat is voluntary. The difference with the parliamentary bill in Chile is that it was made compulsory,” he said.

The initiative, named “Escucha su corazón,” was introduced in July by lawmaker Cristóbal Urruticoechea of the Partido Nacional Libertario, with signatures from members of that party and of the Partido Republicano, founded by Kast. It would amend the Health Code so that when a woman requests an abortion, the physician informs her whether cardiac activity is detectable and offers her the chance to hear it. If she declines the offer, the practitioner would have to refrain from carrying out the procedure.

Abortion has been legal in Chile since 2017 on three grounds: risk to the woman's life, fetal unviability and rape. The law was passed during Michelle Bachelet's second term, and the bill would not repeal it.

Objections also came from within the governing coalition. The president of the Unión Demócrata Independiente, Guillermo Ramírez, called the proposal ineffective and difficult to enforce. Health Minister May Chomali said last week there is no scientific basis for expecting a woman to change her decision. The World Health Organization recommends that ultrasounds not be a mandatory requirement for accessing an abortion and that information provided be objective and not aimed at influencing the decision. In late July, hundreds of women demonstrated in Santiago and about 30 other cities under the slogans “Hear my heart” and “Hear my decision.”

Kast's position drew discontent among the bill's sponsors. “We will not give up, we will keep up the fight, the battle, until we rebuild everything that former president Gabriel Boric's government tore down,” Urruticoechea said. His fellow party member Paulina Muñoz said: “The defense of innocent life has no timetable. I expected more from the president.” The head of the Partido Republicano, Arturo Squella, agreed with Kast that the debate should remain in Congress without executive involvement.

Similar measures have been in force in Hungary since 2022 and in Spain's Castilla y León region.

World.title: De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ
World.content:
De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:16 UTC Full article

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella reported 111 dead and 87 injured on Monday from the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck the west and center of the country, in an address containing extensive religious references. “I entrust our country to the Lord Jesus Christ,” he said after chairing a meeting of the unified command post set up at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit.

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary. The president listed 1,575 homes damaged and 37 destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, 18 health centers, 52 schools and 17 community centers damaged, 18 roads affected and six airports out of service. The priority, he said, is rescuing people trapped under rubble. The government agreed to declare a national disaster situation, to be signed during the day.

De la Espriella announced he would personally lead the response and issue updates every two or three hours. He will travel to Quibdó, capital of Chocó, with the health and defense ministers, while Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara Restrepo heads to the coffee-growing region and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera to Valle del Cauca. Command posts have been set up in Bogotá, Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry will coordinate international cooperation, and the president said the country's allies had offered assistance.

“Today all Colombians, without ideological distinctions, have to unite behind a single cause: the victims of this natural disaster,” he said. He argued that those affected would recover “with the help of God,” of the government and of the international community, and asked God to “protect Colombia.” Unlike his earlier appearances, he did not close with his customary slogan, “Firm for the Homeland.”

Religious language has been a constant feature since before he took office. The president was sworn in on Friday using the constitutional formula “I swear to God,” closed a speech to troops in Cali with “Long live Christ the King,” and included an interfaith segment in the ceremony. Days earlier he had gathered his incoming cabinet at a spiritual retreat, after which he said that “God must be placed at the center of every decision.”

Those statements have opened a debate over the scope of state secularism. The 1991 constitution established a non-confessional state, and in 1994 the Constitutional Court struck down a provision requiring the president to renew annually the country's official consecration to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Senator Jennifer Pedraza walked out of the inauguration session, saying the ceremony threatened the secular character of the state. Constitutional lawyer Juan Manuel Charry has argued, by contrast, that a public official retains personal convictions while exercising office.

World.title: Colombia records its strongest earthquake in a decade, geological service says
World.content:
Colombia records its strongest earthquake in a decade, geological service says

10th Monday, August 2026 - 14:29 UTC Full article

The quake struck at 07:34 local time (12:34 GMT), with its epicenter about five kilometers east of the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, some 240 kilometers west of Bogotá

A magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western and central Colombia on Monday, causing damage in several cities and affecting six airports. It is the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in the past decade, according to the Colombian Geological Service (SGC). No official casualty figures have been released so far.

The quake struck at 07:34 local time (12:34 GMT), with its epicenter about five kilometers east of the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, some 240 kilometers west of Bogotá. The SGC initially reported magnitudes of 6.6 and 6.7 before raising the figure to 7.4 in a later bulletin. The focus was located at more than 80 kilometers depth, an intermediate range that explains why the tremor was felt across such a wide area. The agency has recorded two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8, the second widely felt.

The earthquake was felt in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín, Popayán, Manizales, Armenia and Pereira, as well as in Panama, Ecuador and Venezuela. Buildings and hospitals were evacuated in the Panamanian capital. The National Disaster Risk Management Unit ruled out a tsunami threat along the Pacific coast.

In Manizales, one of the cathedral towers was severely damaged and left leaning against the main body of the church. At Pereira's Matecaña international airport, part of the roof came down in a passenger transit area. The civil aviation authority reported damage at the Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura terminals and suspended air operations at all of them pending structural assessment.

In Cali, the country's third city, facades came away, buildings collapsed and power, gas and water services were cut. Firefighters and rescue teams deployed to inspect structures while the municipal risk management council carries out its damage assessment. Injuries have been reported in Quibdó and at Pereira airport, without confirmed figures.

President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on Friday, ordered the establishment of a unified command post to coordinate the response and announced he would travel to Pereira. “You are not alone. The state is present and acting,” he wrote on his X account. He also requested a detailed report from the head of the national disaster risk management unit.

Colombia is one of the few countries in the world where three tectonic plates converge, and it records an average of 50,000 earthquakes a month, most of them imperceptible. The deadliest events in its recent history were the 1999 Armenia quake, magnitude 6.2 with close to 1,000 dead; the 1994 Páez quake, with about 800; and the 1983 Popayán quake, with 287.

World.title: Reform UK in talks with El Salvador over sending foreign prisoners to Bukele's jails
World.content:
Reform UK in talks with El Salvador over sending foreign prisoners to Bukele's jails

10th Monday, August 2026 - 09:23 UTC Full article

The precedent invoked by Reform UK is the arrangement reached by Donald Trump's administration with El Salvador

Britain's Reform UK party, led by Nigel Farage, has opened contacts with the government of El Salvador to transfer foreign prisoners to jails in that country should it win the next United Kingdom general election, which must be held by 2029 at the latest. The report was published on Monday by the newspaper The Sun and has not been confirmed by San Salvador.

The party's home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf, set out its prisons policy on Sunday night. “We will deport all foreign nationals from our jails. If their home countries won't take them back we will send them to serve their sentences in countries like El Salvador and Kosovo,” he said.
