World.title: Russia: Top court bans opposition anti-war party from vote
World.content:
Yabloko, Russia's only anti-war party, has been barred from September's parliamentary elections. The motion to bar Yabloko was filed by the nationalist pro-Kremlin party Rodina.

The Supreme Court of Russia on Monday ruled in favor of the nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina (Motherland) party and barred Yabloko (Apple) — Russia's only anti-war party — from participating in September parliamentary elections.

Rodina accuses Yabloko of receiving undeclared financial support from Western sources, among other things.

Arguing before the court, Yabloko vehemently denied the accusations and railed against Rodina's lack of supporting evidence.

The nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina party brought the case, accusing Yabloko of receiving foreign funding, yet without providing evidence to support the claim Image: Pavel Seleznev/TASS/picture alliance

On Monday, Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said, "The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted."

The court's decision means citizens opposed to Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine — or "special military operation" as it has been legally deemed under penalty of imprisonment — have no opportunity to vote for representatives willing to articulate that opposition.

Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov told the hundred or so supporters gathered outside the court, "Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing dialog with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities."

"We have a long road ahead and we have a big and important task — to stop deaths and bring back peace. Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added, vowing to appeal the decision.

Yabloko — the only liberal party still operating in Russia since most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents have been jailed, exiled or murdered — has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.

Yabloko was once a strong liberal force in Russia but like other opposition outfits it has been systematically sidelined by the Kremlin.

The party is currently only polling around three percent — short of the five percent threshold for entry into parliament — and has not won a seat in the federal State Duma since 2003.

Putin-backing United Russia has won every single election since then and that is expected to again be the case in September.

Yabloko supporters ignored the threat of repression to show support for the party's anti-war stance at the Supreme Court Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance

But despite barring political opposition to the war, public opinion toward the conflict has soured, more so since Ukraine has intensified its attacks on energy and logistics infrastructure inside Russia.

The non-governmental Levada Center — which is on the Kremlin's "foreign agents" list — charts support at around 66%, the lowest since Russia launched its attack against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

The Kremlin has cracked down on opposition to the war with strict censorship rules and mass arrests, with many activists and journalists preferring to flee than to face potentially deadly persecution by staying in Russia.

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
World.content:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.

Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

What is the latest?

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.

"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.

Multiple deaths after major earthquake in Colombia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.

"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

What's happening on the ground?

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.

Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors .

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

World.title: Why the Rhine drought is bad news for Germany's recovery
World.content:
Germany’s inland waterways still move around 5% of the nation's goods. With the Rhine at a critically low level, DW explores how the drought is hitting the economy where it hurts most.

Water levels on the Rhine River — a small but critical artery for goods vital to Germany’s industry — remain critically low as a result of weeks of drought.

At one of the river's shallowest stretches, Kaub — between Mainz and Koblenz — the water level stood at around 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) at Monday lunchtime, according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV).

Although the real navigable channel is roughly a meter deeper, 40 centimeters is regarded as the lowest for standard commercial vessels at Kaub.

Ship operators use the reading at Kaub to decide how much cargo their barges can safely carry and whether a passage is feasible at all.

According to local media, in recent weeks, carriers have significantly cut their cargoes along the Rhine — in many cases to as little as one-fifth of normal capacity.

The problem isn't just limited to the Middle Rhine, the 130-kilometer (80-mile) stretch between Mainz and Bonn that is the narrowest and shallowest section of the river.

Areas around Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg-Ruhrort and Emmerich are also at historic lows.

Jens Schwanen, the head of the BDB association of inland shipping, told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Monday that the Rhine may become impassable at Kaub before the end of the week.

This would effectively split the river in two for commercial traffic.

What effect will the drought have on the German economy?

The drought could not come at a worse time for Germany’s economy, which is already grappling with weak growth, high energy costs and fading industrial competitiveness.

Germany still relies on its long rivers and waterways to transport some 5% of goods around the country, most of them bulk materials, including iron ore, coal, sand and petroleum products.

Out of 3.28 billion tons of goods transported in 2024, 173 million tons were carried by inland water, including the Rhine, according to BDB.

Eurostat, the European Union's statistics agency, calculated in 2023 that the Rhine corridor — from the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands to the German-Swiss border — accounts for around 40% of freight by ton-kilometers.

After two previous droughts, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated in 2023 that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

In an economy that has barely grown for the past two years, even a temporary 1% hit to industrial output is highly damaging.

The German Economic Institute (IW) now predicts a 0.4% drop in gross domestic product, effectively wiping out this year's economic growth, which was expected at 0.5%.

"A prolonged disruption of navigability on the Rhine could completely stifle the tiny seed of growth we have," warned IW economist Thilo Schäfer in an interview with Bild newspaper last week.

Other experts have warned of losses of €1 to €2 billion ($1.2 to $2.3 billion) in the third quarter alone, with the steel, chemicals and energy sectors hit especially hard.

What happens if the River Rhine is effectively split in two?

The BDB's Schwanen warned that "due to the lack of rainfall, a single-digit reading is forecast for the first time this week at the Kaub gauge."

"In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer navigable along its entire length and is therefore effectively divided in two," he told the Rheinische Post.

This would result in two separate areas. On the one hand, shipping traffic would continue between the North Sea ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp and the Cologne region via the Rhine and the Western German canal system.

Further south, shipping would operate on the tributaries of the Neckar, Moselle, and Main, as well as the Main-Danube Canal, which is regarded as a key global link on the route to and from Southeast Europe.

Between the two sections, shipping companies would then try to move cargo onto trucks and freight rail services.

However, Germany's roads cannot absorb the typical 50 to 150 truckloads that a single large barge can handle without severe congestion and substantially higher costs.

Baden-Württemberg said Monday it would join four other German states in easing restrictions on truck movements on Sundays to help ease congestion.

Following urgent talks last Thursday, Transport Minister Steffen Bilger announced several other measures to shore up Germany's supply chain.

These include cutting red tape for heavy loads shifted to the road network, stopping unnecessary roadworks and better coordination with DB Cargo, the rail freight arm of Deutsche Bahn.

Many vessels are carrying a fifth of their normal cargo volumes Image: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO

Are regular droughts a new reality for Europe's waterways?

Extremely low water on the Rhine and other major European rivers used to be rare events.

Yet, many scientists believe climate change is now making them more frequent, longer and more severe.

According to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, western Europe has just experienced its warmest June and July on record, with exceptionally low rainfall driving much lower than average water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Seine.

The current crisis marks the third major low‑water episode in eight years, after major droughts in 2018 and 2022.

The Rhine has traditionally been supported during dry summer months by meltwater from Alpine snow and glaciers. As those glaciers retreat and snow cover declines, this natural buffer is weakening.

Germany’s Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) projected in 2023 that severe low-water events like 2018 could strike every five to 10 years by mid-century.

Can shipping adapt as Germany's busiest river runs dry? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: India news: Jharkhand police use tear gas, water cannons to disperse student protesters
World.content:
08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Assam flood toll climbs to 100

As floodwaters recede in some areas, residents are returning to homes buried under thick layers of silt Image: Pitamber Newar/ANI

The situation in India's northeastern Assam state remained critical on Monday, with the death toll in the floods reaching 100, officials said.

Two more people died overnight on Sunday after weeks of heavy monsoon rain inundated villages, damaged roads and farmland and disrupted livelihoods.

More than 700,000 people have been displaced since the floods began last month, while about 49,000 remain in 125 relief camps and distribution centers, officials said.

Authorities are warning that, several rivers, including the Brahmaputra, remained above danger levels, raising the risk of further flooding in vulnerable areas.

Farukuddin Ahmed, a 47-year-old trader from Nazira town in Assam's worst-hit Sivasagar district, that in a nearby village of 100 houses only a few remain.

"The residents, mainly dairy farmers, have to rebuild their lives from scratch having lost all their cattle," he said, according to the Associated Press.

Authorities are assessing the damage and providing financial assistance to affected residents. According to the government about 50,000 people had already received interim compensation.

While flooding is a recurring problem in Assam during the monsoon, experts warn that climate change is making rainfall increasingly erratic and extreme.

World.title: Which country is the new Mecca defense pact targeting?
World.content:
Observers suggest the new alliance between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan won't result in any of the countries fighting for each other. Instead it's about preventing Iran and Israel from regional dominance, they say.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sealed a historic defense pact on Friday, signing an agreement "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The so-called "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" between the three Sunni Muslim-majority states is meant to increase cooperation during regional uncertainty and threats from the Iran war.

The agreement was signed in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

The alliance has been likened to a NATO-style alliance and on Friday, the Pakistani foreign ministry said that an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all.

But experts and analysts have been quick to point out that the deal is unlikely to work that way — at least at first.

On Saturday, Yemen's Houthi group targeted Saudi Arabian oil facilities in Jizan. A July attack on the same facility is seen here Image: Social Media/REUTERS

For example, on the weekend the Houthi rebel group in Yemen fired at Saudi Arabian oil facilities again. The Houthis consider Saudi Arabia their enemy and are also aligned with Iran. The latter has also targeted Saudi Arabia after the US and Israel attacked it, starting a war in late February, because it sees the Saudis as a US ally.

But following the Houthi attack on the weekend, neither Turkey nor Pakistan sprang to the Saudis' defense. Nor are they likely to attack Iran, analysts say. In fact, Pakistan is acting as a mediator between Iran and the US currently.

Mecca agreement an 'elastic defense pact'

This arrangement is meant as more of a deterrent and as an "elastic defense pact," Dania Thafer, executive director of the Washington-based think tank the Gulf International Forum, or GIF, told DW late last week.

"If you look at the parties in this agreement, you have Saudi Arabia, which is in the middle of this conflict. But you also have Turkey and Pakistan, who both have relations with Iran and both have relations with the US. So I think it's an extra layer of deterrence, if you will, for Saudi Arabia," Thafer explained. "I think Saudi Arabia is looking at a layered deterrence approach to regional threats as they emerge."

This new alliance is likely to work out in various stages with the short-term goal being a "stabilized region," Kamran Bokhari, a senior fellow at the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told DW.

Technology transfer and investment

Longer term goals will involve defense cooperation rather than fighting, other experts have said.

"The three countries complement each other unusually well," Andreas Krieg, a lecturer in security at King's College London, told news agency Agence France-Presse last week.

Saudi Arabia has oil wealth but limited defense technology and has been reliant on the US up until now. Meanwhile Turkey and Pakistan need investment and have strong armed forces, and in Turkey's case an advanced defense-industrial sector, Krieg explained. Pakistan is the only one with nuclear weapons of the three.

"Turkey has technology and production capacity but needs markets and investment. Pakistan has a workforce, military institutions and nuclear deterrent, but needs financing and industrial capabilities," Krieg noted.

Who does the Mecca pact target?

A Turkish official cited by Reuters said the agreement was purely defensive in nature and open to any regional neighbors who might want to sign on. Egypt is thought to be a potential partner but also has other allies to consider, including the United Arab Emirates. The latter have not joined and relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia are currently strained.

The Turkish official also said the pact does not replace or negate previous bilateral or multilateral agreements between signatories, nor is it directed at any one actor or threat.

Yet there's no doubt the agreement has been understood as a deterrent, mainly against two other nations, Iran and Israel.

The Mecca pact's objectives are not about some kind of military victory, Khalid al-Jaber, director of the Doha-based Middle East Council on Global Affairs wrote in a Sunday op-ed for Qatari news outlet, Al Jazeera . "It is the prevention of hegemony."

"Diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran," he continued. "The Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole — a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region."

Damage in Iran: The country was attacked by the US and Israel in late February and the war is ongoing, although peace talks also continue Image: Morteza Akhoondi/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

How does Israel feel about it?

Two of the signatories to the agreement — Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — don't recognize Israel and have no official relations with it, even though at least in Saudi Arabia's case there are likely some covert ties. Turkey does recognize Israel but the relationship is strained at the moment, due to Israel's activity in Gaza that Turkey has called genocide.

Turkish leader Erdogan said last week that Israel's actions in Syria and Lebanon also constitute a threat to Turkish security.

"The development [of the Mecca pact] poses significant challenges for Israel, pushes the prospect of normalization with Riyadh further out of reach and cuts short the vision of a 'new Middle East'," Oshrit Birvadker, a research fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, wrote in a Saturday editorial for the outlet Israel Hayom .

Birvadker also believes that the new trilateral alliance will increase the growing rivalry and tensions between Turkey and Israel.

Mixed reactions in Iran

The Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University looked at how the Iranians were reacting.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not seem too upset by the agreement. On the social media platform, X (formerly Twitter) he posted that "when Muslims stand together, we can face every challenge by malicious outsiders head-on."

Observers took this to be a positive, part of Iran's argument for pushing the US out of the region.

Some Iranian observers thought that the Saudis might be trying to leverage the better relations that the Turkish and Pakistanis have with the Iranians, to make itself safer from Iranian attacks. But other Iranian politicians were more critical, saying that Saudi Arabia wasn't safe with the US as an ally and wouldn't be safe with Turkey and Pakistan either.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: How climate change is reshaping Africa's malaria risk
World.content:
Researchers say warming temperatures are altering malaria transmission patterns across Africa, creating new challenges for health systems and disease control.

For decades, global efforts towards the eradication of malaria, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, have focused essentially on West and Central Africa, where the disease is most endemic.

The WHO African Region accounts for about 95% of global malaria cases and deaths. More than half of all malaria deaths in the region occur in Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%). Children under 5 years of age account for about 76% of malaria deaths in the region.

To stem the tide of malaria cases across Africa, the global health body has recommended a wider use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine among children living in regions with moderate to high malaria transmission by the Plasmodium falciparum — a parasite that causes 95% of all malaria infections in Africa. It's transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

The WHO warned in April 2025 that recent funding cuts were jeopardising malaria control efforts, with more than half of malaria-endemic countries surveyed reporting moderate or severe disruptions to malaria services.

A study published in The Lancet found that the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine reduced all-cause mortality among vaccine-eligible children by 13.2% in pilot programs in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.

A changing disease landscape

Malaria transmission is most efficient within temperature ranges common across many tropical regions of West and Central Africa, according to a new study published in the journal Nature .

Tanzania's bold experiment against malaria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Malaria transmission by mosquitoes usually peaks at temperatures of around 25 degrees Celsius (77 Fahrenheit) and becomes much less likely when temperatures drop below 16 degrees or rise above 34 degrees Celsius, largely because the malaria parasite must complete part of its life cycle inside the mosquito — a process that is highly temperature-dependent.

Because of this, malaria transmission has historically been most favourable across many tropical parts of West and Central Africa, where temperatures frequently fall within the range most suitable for transmission.

In contrast, some parts of Southern Africa and the highlands of East Africa have historically remained cool enough to keep the spread of malaria at bay, preventing the disease from becoming a major public health burden.

That, however, is beginning to change. The Nature study found that rising temperatures are making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for malaria transmission, while parts of West Africa are becoming too hot for optimal transmission.

What does this mean for the continent?

Climate change is not only heating up the continent, it's redistributing risks, says Olugbenga Mokuolu, professor of pediatrics at Nigeria's University of Ilorin.

Although West African countries like Nigeria fall under areas that are "too hot for malaria to thrive, this is not good news to celebrate either, because a world that's too hot for malaria is not a good world for children's health overall," Mokuolu, who also serves as an advisor to the Nigerian Minister of Health on malaria elimination, told DW.

"The same heat that's inconvenient for mosquitoes is dangerous for people," he added, noting that climate is "not the primary driving factor of malaria. Funding, drug and insecticide resistance, and health system strength still matter more."

Olugbenga continued that the elimination and prevention of malaria on the continent could become "a story of two very different regions: West and Central Africa may get a small, unplanned assist from climate, while East and Southern Africa, historically lower-burden areas, face a growing new threat that could undo hard-won gains."

Are African health systems keeping pace?

Climate change is fundamentally changing the geography of disease on the continent, Olumide Idowu, founder of the International Climate Change Development Initiative, told DW.

Malaria research in Germany targets parasite’s life cycle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Idowu added that many African countries have developed adaptation plans but implementation has lagged behind the pace of climate change.

Although Africa is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, it remains one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change — posing systemic threats to the economy, infrastructure, and even its fragile health systems.

Idowu mentioned that without a significant increase in "investment at home, reinforcement of local institutional capacity and embedding health as a core pillar of climate resilience, many African countries risk being unprepared for the changing epidemiological landscape that climate change is creating."

The regions expected to be hardest hit are also regions less accustomed to fighting malaria today, the study revealed.

"Governments, health systems and communities must adapt to this evolving threat, including getting ready now to run more aggressive anti-malaria programs in cooler areas where risk is rising," Olugbenga said.

He also urged countries in West and Central Africa to sustain malaria elimination efforts, warning that resistance to insecticides and drugs, funding gaps and weak health systems could easily negate any reduction in malaria transmission associated with rising temperatures.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.content:

08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Trump says if Iran is demanding compensation, then he is too

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the US would demand compensation from Iran, in response to Tehran saying it would seek compensation over US and Israeli attacks.

Over the weekend, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over new shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz. But it said that reopening the waterway would depend on Washington meeting various conditions — including an end to sanctions, military threats and an agreement on compensation for damages resulting from the war.

Trump said that this was "never mentioned" in any negotiations with the US to date.

"But is an interesting idea because now ‌I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

He cited specifically a 2000 terrorist suicide bombing of the USS Cole ship, but alleged there were "thousands of others killed in combat."

Trump's remarks come a day after he said he was not engaging in major talks with Iran, telling US media outlet Axios that the US was "low-keying" its approach.

The US and Iran have frequently put out vastly contradictory claims and counterclaims about the status and details of their talks and terms.

El presidente colombiano, Abelardo de la Espriella, ha cifrado en más de 1.500 las viviendas afectadas y ha elevado a 61 el número de edificios completamente colapsados. “Le encomiendo nuestro país al señor Jesucristo”, ha dicho el mandatario, que ha declarado la emergencia nacional y se encuentra en Bogotá. Gran parte de los fallecidos se concentra en el área metropolitana de Pereira y también se han producido graves destrozos en la ciudad de Cali, la capital del Valle del Cauca, donde el regidor, Alejandro Eder, ha comunicado que al menos una treintena de estructuras se han derrumbado “con personas atrapadas”. Los aeropuertos de Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura suspenden sus operaciones tras sufrir daños por el seísmo.

World.title: Dos senderos idóneos para explorar el Valle de Arán en verano
World.content:
En la zona occidental de la comarca pirenaica esperan la Artiga de Lin y la Val de Toran. Cascadas, mariposas, pequeños pueblos y antiguos caminos para el contrabando que se disfrutan sin multitudes

Que levanten la mano quienes hayan estado en Baqueira, Salardú o Artíes. ¡Hala, cuánta gente! Ese es el Naut Aran (el Alto Arán, en aranés), al que más de un millón de personas acuden en invierno a esquiar. Que la levanten ahora quienes hayan estado en Es Bòrdes o en Canejan. Ni la décima parte. Esta zona occidental del Valle de Arán, por la que corren el río Garona y la carretera N230 poco antes de entrar en Francia, no es tan famosa como la oriental, pero por eso mismo está rodeada de montañas silenciosas, virginales, sin remontes ni aparcamientos para 1.600 vehículos.

Cuando la nieve se retira, aquí se ven flores, mariposas y cascadas. Hay dos senderos idóneos para explorarla: el que recorre el pasmoso valle de la Artiga de Lin, donde surgen a chorros las aguas del glaciar del Aneto después de circular casi cuatro kilómetros bajo tierra, y el camino del Contrabando, entre Canejan y Sant Joan de Toran, por el que los vecinos traficaban durante la posguerra con café y azúcar de la vecina Francia.

Los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío

La Artiga de Lin es el paraje natural más espectacular de la comarca. En este valle glaciar hay dos lugares difíciles de creer: a 1.370 metros de altura, se encuentra la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu (­los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío, que de las tres formas lo traducen), donde brotan 1.580 litros de agua por segundo —y hasta 10.000 en pleno deshielo—. Cien metros más arriba, a 1.470, está el Plan dera Artiga, una gran pradera alpina rodeada de hayedos, abetales y escarpadas montañas calizas a casi 3.000 metros de altura donde lindan el Valle de Arán y el de Benasque, Lleida y Huesca, Cataluña y Aragón.

Surgencia de los Uhels deth Joèu, en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

A diferencia de lo que ocurre en la zona oriental del Valle de Arán, aquí no se puede aparcar a pie de pista porque no hay ninguna. Tampoco hay atascos porque los meses de mayor afluencia de visitantes en esta zona, los estivales, es obligatorio estacionar junto a la ermita dera Mair de Diu dera Artiga de Lin, tres kilómetros antes de llegar al final de la estrecha carretera que sube culebreando por el valle desde el pueblo de Es Bòrdes. Luego se puede continuar subiendo por el asfalto en un trenecito turístico o hacerlo a pie por el camino del Agua, que es una senda ribereña fácil y preciosa.

Siguiendo el camino, antes de una hora se verá la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu. “¿De dónde sale tanta agua?“, se preguntan todos los que examinan por primera vez este nacedero torrencial, porque aunque su caudal medio se reduce en verano a 250 litros por segundo, sigue siendo mucha fuente. Pues resulta que sale del Aneto, el techo de los Pirineos, en la vecina Huesca. Y se sabe porque, en 1931, el espeleólogo francés Norbert Casteret vertió 60 kilos de colorante inocuo en el Forau d’Aigualluts —un sumidero kárstico del valle de Benasque donde las aguas recién fundidas del glaciar del Aneto desaparecen bajo tierra después de pegar un buen salto—, y comprobó que estas aparecían teñidas en los Uelhs. Así que estas aguas nacidas al sur de los Pirineos, en vez de ir al Ebro y al Mediterráneo, que sería lo lógico, corren cuatro kilómetros bajo las montañas para engrosar el río Garona y acabar en el Atlántico.

Indicador de rutas en la Artiga de Kin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Flores mil, más de 150 mariposas y dos guías excelentes

Al pie de la cascada tumultuosa, hay una pasarela metálica que permite cruzar el río Joèu para seguir subiendo por el abetal de la margen contraria y acabar saliendo, tras dos horas de paseo, al Plan dera Artiga de Lin. Es un rellano glaciar bellísimo, presidido por la mole rocosa del Malh dera Artiga (2.711 metros) y alfombrado de prados llenos de flores —gencianas, astrancias, violetas de los Pirineos, geranios silvestres, consueldas mayores, malvas moscadas…— y mariposas de montaña: la apolo, la mnemosine, la colias alpina, la erebia oeme, la común, la dentada…

Para distinguir las más de 150 especies que viven en este Shangri-La de las mariposas, es sumamente útil la guía ilustrada que ha publicado el Conselh Generau d’Aran. Otra guía excelente para explorar la Artiga de Lin es Sara Arjó, bióloga que dirige la empresa de ecoturismo y educación ambiental Verd e Blu y que es la autora de Parpalhòles dera Val d’Aran, un juego didáctico de papiroflexia con 14 recortables de mariposas de siete especies, las más llamativas del lugar.

Mariposa zygaena osterodensis en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

Todo es bonito en la Artiga de Lin, hasta el espléndido refugio donde Arjó se toma un refresco y algún tentempié con sus clientes, dejándolos disfrutar un rato largo de este paisaje embobador antes de acercarse al siguiente lugar destacado de la ruta: la cascada de Pomèro. En esta última, a solo 300 metros del refugio, les presenta la amapola amarilla (Papaver cambricum), una flor rara en España, pero muy abundante y estimada en las islas británicas, a tal punto que la usa como emblema Plaid Cymru, el partido nacionalista que ahora gobierna en Gales. Una microcentral eléctrica produce en este florido salto la energía de la que se abastece el refugio, que es grandecito, con habitaciones para 27 montañeros y un buen restaurante para cualquiera que pase.

Vista al Aneto desde el mirador de Vilamòs

Desde el refugio se baja cómodamente por la carretera asfaltada hasta la ermita donde se aparcó al principio. Como no se tarda mucho en completar la vuelta a pie (la ruta circular descrita, de algo menos de ocho kilómetros, lleva hacerla unas tres horas, cuatro con paradas contemplativas y de refresco), hay tiempo para acercarse en coche al mirador de Vilamòs, que está a solo siete kilómetros de la Artiga de Lin en línea recta, pero a 17 por una carretera loca (la LV5055) que sube desde El Pont d’Arròs trazando 16 revueltas. El mirador no está señalizado en la carretera, pero sí en Google Maps.

Vista del refugio de la Artiga de Lin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Desde aquí, con la ayuda del móvil y de la aplicación AR AlpineGuide (disponible en Google Play y en Apple Store), pueden identificarse las montañas que se alzan alrededor de la Artiga de Lin, arropando su formidable recuenco glaciar: la doble cima de la Forcanada, el Malh dera Artiga, la Tuca Blanca de Pomèro… Detrás de esta última cumbre asoman las nieves perpetuas y los riscos estratosféricos del macizo de la Maladeta, señoreados por el Aneto (3.404 metros).

Después de este atracón de montañas, apetece bajar a El Pont d’Arròs para darse otro de cocina aranesa en el restaurante del hotel Peña. Este es un cuatro estrellas cómodo y hogareño a más no poder, al que solo le falta aire acondicionado en las habitaciones para ser extraordinario. Pronto lo instalarán: el cambio climático obliga. Luego, un baño en la piscina climatizada y a la cama, que mañana hay que madrugar para explorar otra cara oculta de Arán, su rincón más desconocido y solitario: la Val de Toran.

Republicanos, judíos, maquis y contrabandistas

En Puntaut, poco antes de que el río Garona se cuele en Francia y de que la carretera N230 española se convierta en la N125 gala, se desvía a la derecha otra muy estrecha, sin eje central y sumamente virada que se adentra en la recóndita Val de Toran. Seis kilómetros y 38 curvas más arriba, se llega a Canejan, un pueblecito-balcón que domina desde su altura un inmenso panorama ­de las montañas donde España y Francia se besan.

Una cruz occitana en en suelo de la Plaça dera Castra, en Canejan. Andrés Campos

En la Plaça dera Castra, la mayor y más cuidada, la del Ayuntamiento, de pavimento decorado con una gran cruz occitana —la enseña aranesa—, dos paneles informativos recuerdan que por Canejan pasaban a Francia no pocos republicanos que huían de la represión franquista tras la Guerra Civil y judíos que escapaban en dirección contraria, de la Europa ocupada por los nazis, durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. También recuerdan que esta fue la primera localidad atacada y tomada por los guerrilleros antifranquistas en octubre de 1944 durante la llamada Operación Reconquista de España, que pretendía deponer al dictador y restaurar la República. No dicen nada, en cambio, de los contrabandistas que trajinaban aquí en los años del hambre y del racionamiento, entre 1939 y 1952. Para decirlo, están los vecinos. No es que haya muchos en la Val de Toran (unos cien), pero casi todos están en Canejan. Una de ellas, Generosa Marqués, cuenta al que quiera oírla el caso de sus padres, Pedro y Palmira, que una vez al mes iban a la comuna gala de Fos y volvían cargados de café y azúcar, productos que escaseaban en el mercado regulado español y por los que sacaban un buen pico. Hasta que una noche los sorprendieron y pasaron las 15 siguientes entre rejas.

Difícil saber qué caminos usaban los contrabandistas para cruzar la raya. Como dice Generosa, “el tiempo, el del reloj y el atmosférico, los ha borrado”. Sin embargo, se conservan bien algunos de los que seguían para trapichear en este valle fronterizo, como el histórico que une Canejan, Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran. Para andar por él solo hay que subir a lo más alto de Canejan y salir del pueblo siguiendo la calle Era Cau, que pronto se hace de tierra, asciende dejando a la derecha unas rústicas bordas y se vuelve prácticamente llana. Para más señas, hay indicadores de dirección y marcas de pintura blanca y roja a lo largo de todo el recorrido, pues coincide con el sendero GR-211. Y se puede consultar el mapa y descargar el track de la ruta en Wikiloc.

La soledad de Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran

Tras una hora de paseo por este camino alto y horizontal, contemplando cómo desde una terraza el callejón sin salida montañoso de la Val de Toran, se entra en Porcingles, una aldea fantasma con solo dos casas temporalmente habitadas, calles impracticables y un lavadero cuyas aguas llevan tanto tiempo sin reflejar a un humano, que las mariposas (los sátiros del bosque y los ocelados, por citar dos especies que aquí se ven), se posan sobre las manos del recién llegado, sin saber qué es. Las ruinas de Porcingles son un recuerdo escalofriante de cuando a la Val de Toran llegó para quedarse una muchedumbre de 500 personas poseída por la fiebre del oro o, más bien, del zinc y del plomo, que eran lo que se sacaba de las minas de Liat, en la cabecera del valle, durante el siglo XIX y a principios del XX. Había incluso un teleférico de 13 kilómetros que transportaba todo lo extraído valle abajo, hasta el lavadero de mineral de Puntaut.

El camino, bastante llano hasta Porcingles, gana luego altura, cruza el barranco de Gotèrs y la pierde para llegar, al cumplirse dos horas de marcha, a Sant Joan de Toran. Tampoco es un lugar donde viva una multitud: solo tres personas. Pero junto a los prados que alguien se ha tomado la molestia de segar, hay una iglesia con macetas floridas a cada lado de la puerta y una docena larga de casas y bordas tradicionales de piedra en perfecto estado, en cuyos tejados de afilado caballete no falta una sola losa de pizarra: señal de que aquí viene a pasar cortas temporadas gente harta del mundanal ruido, que sabe lo que es bueno y que puede permitírselo. En este pueblo de postal se encuentra uno de los pocos negocios turísticos de la Val de Toran, el restaurante Estupendet, buen sitio para tomarse una ensaladilla rusa de verdad y una cerveza artesanal Refu. Este pulcro pueblecito rodeado de prados y montañas es lo más encantador del Valle de Arán, con permiso de la Artiga de Lin.

World.title: Los veranos en que me enamoré
World.content:
Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las columnas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

Cuando eres niño, de un verano a otro pasan millones de cosas, como en el último día del año del calendario cósmico de Carl Sagan, que contiene nada menos que toda la historia de la humanidad. Los cambios físicos quedaban registrados en las fotografías de las vacaciones; en esas marcas que algunos padres iban haciendo en la pared para medir a su prole; en el bañador que ya no te servía… La playa era la misma, tú no. Y para observar los cambios internos, la televisión funcionaba como un microscopio de alta precisión.

Un verano te seguías despertando temprano para ver los dibujos animados. Al otro te aburrían y lo que te gustaba era ver los trompazos que se daban en Humor amarillo, y al siguiente los pobres concursantes de aquellas yincanas salvajes te daban una pena terrible y lo mejor que te podía pasar era que pusieran en la tele una serie o película de instituto con su buen baile de fin de curso; una de algún romance en vacaciones (tipo Dirty Dancing) o una que combinara ambas, como Grease. En el medio, es decir, durante el otoño, el invierno y la primavera, había sucedido algo muy importante: tu prioridad en la vida ya no era divertirte, sino enamorarte. En la playa, en el campamento, cinco minutos después de que sonara el timbre y dijeran: “¿Puede bajar Natalia a jugar?”. Y no de cualquiera, sino del protagonista: el malote.

El malote nos gustaba por culpa de la televisión y luego, en la vida adulta, había que dar muchas vueltas al calendario cósmico para salir de ahí. Era chulito, pero simpático. Sacaba malas notas, pero era listo y muy talentoso en algún deporte —con la excepción archiconocida de Danny Zuko—. Llevaba cazadora de cuero o beisbolera —cuando no se la dejaba a su novia, la capitana de las animadoras—; tenía un pelo de esos donde daban unas ganas locas de esconder la mano y, generalmente, se dedicaba a vacilar a la empollona con gafas hasta que, zas, se enamoraba de ella, o sea, de ti.

Olivia Newton-John y John Travolta, en 'Grease' (1978). Archive Photos (Getty Images)

Con 44 añazos, sigo siendo fiel al género. Es lo que ahora se llama, con algo de pedantería, el “placer culpable”. En mi descargo diré que en las películas y las series malas es mucho más fácil que haya final feliz que en las buenas y eso da mucha paz. Aunque me encanta La historia del camello que llora y todo lo que hicieron juntos Cassavetes y Rowlands, hay veces que lo que te pide el cuerpo es ver al capitán del equipo de rugby dejar a la rubia de ojos azules y llevar al baile de graduación a la chica del montón que previamente ha reformado al malote —aprueba el curso gracias a ella— y deja a todos epatados cuando aparece en la fiesta con un vestido precioso y lentillas. Al principio —como a Cenicienta—, de tan guapa que está, ni la reconocen, pero nosotros, los espectadores, sí, igual que sabemos todo el rato que Clark Kent es Superman aunque Lois Lane no se dé cuenta por culpa de las gafas. Es lo que suelo decirles, por cierto, a mis amigos cuando se quejan de la vista cansada: “Oye, que Superman también llevaba gafas”.

Trabajo para los psicólogos

Un rasgo para diferenciar las pelis y series malas de las buenas dentro del género es que, en las buenas, el malote guapo se enamora de la chica normal por su personalidad arrolladora, y en las malas, porque la chica normal se convierte en medio guapa. Quizá la culpabilidad del placer resida ahí: en que, según avanza la trama, te van entrando más ganas de que ella se transforme en un bellezón y se nos olvida un poco su personalidad arrolladora.

Supongo que un psicólogo tendría mucho que decir aquí, pero no debo ser la única afectada viendo el éxito que tuvo recientemente una serie titulada, nada más y nada menos, que The Summer I Turned Pretty —literalmente, “El verano que me volví guapa”, aunque en España se tradujo como El verano en que me enamoré—, la enésima vuelta de tuerca al cuento del patito feo y una imitación mainstream de Sabrina. Yo la devoré, naturalmente. Ya no las busco, pero si aparecen en la pantalla, me quedo a verlas. En diciembre te devuelven al verano. Y en cualquier momento, a ese interín maravilloso en el que has perdido la inocencia, pero aún no ha aparecido el cinismo de los adultos y crees que cualquier cosa es posible.

World.title: Police investigating three explosive attacks on pilates studio
World.content:
A pilates studio in Gelderland has been hit by three explosive attacks in six weeks, the most recent in the early hours of Monday, police have said.

The studio in Zevenaar, which opened a year ago, was first targeted on June 24, when a blast blew a window pane out of the front door and caused a fire to break out.

A witness saw a man in black clothing and a cap running from the scene immediately after the explosion, but police have not managed to trace him.

Five days later a second explosion blew a hole in the entrance. The word betalen (“pay”) was written three times on a window.

The most recent attack was at around 2.45am on Monday, when another explosion went off and a brick was hurled through a window, Omroep Gelderland reported. The explosion was heard throughout the neighbourhood.

The door and several windows of the building have been boarded up following the attacks. Police would not say if they were linked or if any arrests have been made.

World.title: Two men suspected of helping grave robber sell stolen valuables
World.content:
Two men have been questioned on suspicion of acting as accomplices for a man accused of stealing valuables from a cemetery in The Hague by selling the items to a gold dealer.

The 60-year-old man, who works as a shift manager at the city’s main cemetery on Kerkhoflaan, was arrested in June after police received a tip-off that items such as jewellery and gold fillings had been stolen during working hours.

The prosecution service confirmed on Monday that two other people who worked at the cemetery were suspected of money laundering “by selling valuable objects originating from the cemetery”.

The man was arrested after an inspection of the official register where second-hand and antique traders are required to log their purchases revealed that he had sold several items to a gold exchange bureau.

Prosecutors said there were no indications from the investigation so far that items had been stolen from other cemeteries in the city. The inquiry covers the period from 2023 until the man’s arrest.

The city council has launched its own internal inquiry and set up a hotline for families who were concerned that their relatives’ valuables may have been stolen. So far the hotline has received around 60 calls.

World.title: Scammers flood TikTok with fake student rental ads
World.content:
Hundreds of fake s for student rooms and rental homes are circulating on TikTok in an effort to defraud people looking for housing, according to an investigation by broadcaster NOS.

The scammers are also lifting listings from Pararius, one of the largest rental platforms in the Netherlands, and the company says it now wants TikTok to act. “We are completely fed up and want action from TikTok now,” Jasper de Groot, a Pararius spokesperson, told the broadcaster.

Some of the people who lose money come to Pararius believing they have rented through the site, De Groot said, because they have transferred a payment – only for it to reach a scammer instead.

Scams and complaints

The fraudsters copy photographs of real rooms from Pararius and reuse them in fake posts. Victims are typically asked to pay before they can view a property – a deposit, a viewing fee or a “reservation guarantee” – after which the money disappears.

The national student union, the LSVb, said it regularly hears from young people who get conned out of their money. “Sometimes a deposit is also demanded in advance and the room turns out not to exist at all,” said vice-chair Juliana Könning. “Students then lose their deposit of, say, three months’ rent.”

The Fraudehelpdesk, the national fraud reporting centre, received 175 reports in the first half of 2026 from people scammed through an , NOS Stories said, up from 21 in the previous six months.

International students are among those most exposed, unable to fall back on a parental home and often unfamiliar with their rights, the LSVb has warned in the past.

Platforms under pressure

TikTok said content used to defraud people is not allowed and that it removes such posts. The platform did not explain why it had not acted on the reports filed by Pararius.

After NOS Stories shared a number of fake s, the accounts behind them were taken down, but dozens of other scam accounts remained online.

Pararius said it had sent TikTok dossiers containing victims’ police reports and a registered letter, without success, and would take legal action against the platform. “It has to stop,” De Groot said.

Funda said it warns consumers but can do little because the fraud takes place elsewhere, while room-rental site Kamernet said it advises users to report suspicious posts and may pursue legal steps if they are not removed.

World.title: Perks of the job: making the most of your Dutch salary
World.content:
So you’ve got the job, you are moving to the Netherlands and you are ready to jump into your new life. Here is a guide from ABN Amro on some practical and financial matters you need to arrange, as well as some Dutch workplace benefits worth knowing about.

Get your finances set up

First things first – you need a current account so your employer can deposit your salary, and having a local account will make it easier to manage your day-to-day finances. Note, you must have a Dutch bank account to get paid by a Dutch employer.

ABN Amro, which has 25 years’ experience in helping expat clients, is currently offering up to €175 cashback to new account holders – a handy financial bonus, especially at the start of a new life in the Netherlands.

But what other financial things do you need to get sorted out? Apart from a current account, you might like to start saving, so opening a savings account at the same bank would be a sensible move.

You’ll also need insurance – you’ll find out very soon that the Dutch love insurance – and, of course, some insurance, such as health cover, is compulsory too. ABN Amro offers several insurance products that you should consider – from personal liability to contents and legal aid. If you take out three or more insurance policies with them, you will receive a 3% to 5% package discount. That’s another nice financial bonus.

Then there are work-related financial benefits.

Exploring Dutch employee benefits

One perk of a Dutch job that many people are not aware of to begin with is holiday pay, or vakantiegeld. All workers and benefit claimants in the Netherlands have the right to holiday pay, which is equivalent to 8% of their annual income.

The concept of holiday pay dates back to 1910 and the money was traditionally paid out at the end of May to make sure people actually used it to pay for a break.

By the way, by law you are entitled to at least 20 paid holiday days if you work a five-day week, but in most pay deals (CAOs), 25 paid days off or even more are the norm.

In some sectors you may also be entitled to a 13th month paid out in December. Some companies also have different ways of giving their staff a bonus, such as a fixed amount for reaching a performance target.

Travel allowances and company bikes

Your job may entitle you to help with the cost of getting to and from work. Employers are allowed to give staff a tax-free allowance of 23 cents per kilometre for using public transport or a car or bike to commute, or you may be entitled to a public transport card that offers discounted travel. You may even be able to get a company bike.

Every employer is different, so make sure you ask HR about the travel perks at your company.

Other job-related perks

You may find your company canteen is subsidised or even free. You may also be entitled to gym membership or other club activities, and by law, if you work remotely, you are entitled to €2.45 a day as a working-from-home allowance. Some companies also offer a training budget to keep your skills up to date or provide Dutch lessons for their international staff.

Many internationals are surprised by the extra payments and perks they are entitled to when working for a Dutch company, just as they are surprised by the strict Dutch work-life balance and the way most people head off home at 5pm and don’t answer their work phone at the weekend.

Make sure you don’t get any unwanted financial surprises by getting your money matters sorted out, and do feel free to put your questions to ABN Amro’s specialist support staff for internationals. Find out more about opening an ABN Amro bank account and how you can benefit from a €175 cashback offer. That’s a lot of takeaway lattes – also an essential part of Dutch working life!

World.title: Rotterdam night entry ban brings quiet, residents want it kept
World.content:
Residents of the Rotterdam neighbourhood De Esch say the nights have been quiet since a ban on entering the area took effect two weeks ago, but fear the disruption will return when it runs out in October.

A curfew for anyone without a good reason for being in the area was imposed on July 23, making it an offence to be on the streets from 11pm till 5am. The unprecedented move follows years of persistent anti-social behaviour in the area, usually by people who don’t live there.

Police stopped about 100 people during the first fortnight, though no fines have been issued yet – the penalty is expected to be more than €100.

Quiet nights

“The windows can just stay open all the time,” one resident told broadcaster NOS. “It was very quiet from night one.”

Another resident told regional broadcaster Rijnmond that before the ban she had been kept awake almost every night by shouting and car horns, even with earplugs, and had slept well for the first time in a long while.

The neighbourhood, home to more than 4,000 people, had put up with street races, drug use and prostitution at night for years. Police research found that most of those responsible came from outside De Esch.

Police and the council say the disruption has not moved to other areas, but both note that it is the holiday season and the picture may change.

After October

The ban runs for three months and can be extended by another three after consultation.

The residents’ committee wants the neighbourhood closed at night once it ends, with marshals at the entrances at weekends letting in only people with a reason to be there.

The neighbourhood council, which advises the city, is against that. “It restricts the movement of other Rotterdammers too much,” its chairman Christiaan de Jong told NOS.

He said he hoped instead that behaviour would change and the disruption would be less than before. The council says it is too early to discuss a permanent solution, and that no other part of Rotterdam needs the same measure.

World.title: German zeppelin takes to Dutch skies to measure air pollution
World.content:
People living in the Veluwe region near the German border have been surprised by the sight of a zeppelin hovering in the skies above their heads.

The airship took off from Essen, in the Ruhr area of North Rhine-Westphalia, and is being used to measure air pollution in an area on both sides of the border that covers Arnhem and Utrecht.

Scientists from Wageningen University & Research have equipped the balloon with instruments to measure levels of CO2 pollution, emissions and fine particles in the air, in a joint operation with German colleagues.

“The substances are partly produced by the forest and partly by traffic and industry,” researcher Michiel van der Molen told NOS. “Exactly how that works and how quickly it spreads is interesting, but mostly unknown.”

The zeppelin is due to pass over the area several times during the next week at a height of around 300 metres above ground level. Its path can be followed on Flightradar24 under the code DLZFN.

World.title: Thieves caught trying to retrieve cigarettes from police station
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Thieves broke into a police station in The Hague to try to retrieve a batch of illegal cigarettes that were seized in a raid on Friday.

Four suspects were arrested when they were caught while trying to throw boxes of cigarettes over the fence of the police compound on Zichtenburglaan at 4.45am on Saturday.

One of the boxes caught on the fence and burst open, scattering cigarettes over the ground just as officers arrived on the scene.

The suspects tried to escape by car, but were forced off the road and arrested within 15 minutes later. One man was injured and taken to hospital under a police escort.

The haul of 1.2 million cigarettes was confiscated on Mandelastraat in Delft on Friday. Earlier in the week police recovered 500,000 iillegal cigarettes in two vans in the town.

Officers are investigating whether the break-in at the police station is linked to the earlier raids in Delft.

World.content:

The A12 motorway heading out of The Hague was briefly closed on Monday morning following a crash involving six cars.

The multiple pile-up happened near the Prins Clausplein junction at Nootdorp at around 10am. Police are investigating the cause.

Two ambulances were seen at the scene, but no details have been released about whether any drivers or passengers were injured.

Traffic in the Utrecht direction was diverted via the A20 and A13 via Rotterdam. One lane has since reopened.

World.title: Kaczyński appeals to President Nawrocki to unify Poland’s right-wing opposition ahead of elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called on opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. His appeal comes as PiS, which for the last two decades has dominated the Polish right, is in crisis, amid falling polling numbers, a split by a breakaway faction, and a growing challenge from far-right parties that have long been critical of PiS. That has created a fragmented opposition, with parties competing against one another as much as or more than with the Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition. Some on the right hope that Nawrocki, who enjoys good relations with various parts of the opposition, could act as a unifying figurehead bridging those divides. 🔴 Jarosław Kaczyński ujawnił, o co osobiście poprosił Karola Nawrockiego. Podczas miesięcznicy smoleńskiej prezes PiS odniósł się do podziałów na prawicy i przyznał, że widzi dla prezydenta wyjątkowo ważną rolę: ma pomóc scalić zwaśnione środowiska. „Ja prezydenta swego czasu… pic.twitter.com/qwXhmccun2 — Super Express (@se_pl) August 10, 2026 Speaking on Sunday at a monthly commemoration of the 2010 Smolensk air disaster that killed his identical twin brother, then-President Lech Kaczyński, Jarosław was reported by a variety of Polish media outlets as saying that he had asked Nawrocki to act as a “patron” for a unified right. “I asked the president some time ago, and I hope he will do it,” said Kaczyński, quoted by newspaper Fakt. “It would be very good if the president took up this matter energetically.” “We could continue to develop – as we did during our years of government – not only in terms of achieving GDP growth, but also by undertaking major investments, by undertaking everything that would truly change Poland.” Kaczyński was referring to the period between 2015 and 2023 when a PiS-dominated coalition, known as the United Right (Zjednoczona Prawica), ruled Poland. In the latter year, it was ousted from power by a more liberal coalition led by Tusk, Kaczyński’s great rival. Since then, the landscape on the Polish right has changed dramatically. One of PiS’s partners in the United Right, the hard-right Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), merged with PiS in 2024. The other, the centre-right Agreement (Porozumienie), is now defunct. Meanwhile, support for PiS itself has collapsed. Having won 35% of the vote at the 2023 elections, it now averages only around 20% in polls – the party’s lowest figures for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, last month, around a fifth of the party’s MPs formed a breakaway group in parliament led by PiS deputy leader and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. They plan to soon form their own, separate party, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), with a more moderate, centre-right agenda than PiS. At the same time, PiS has found itself challenged by a growing far right. Confederation (Konfederacja), which won 7% of the vote in 2023, is now polling around 12-13%. The even more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which broke away from Confederation last year, is at 9%. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 That has resulted in a much more fragmented right, with four separate entities not only opposed to Tusk’s government but also competing with one another for overlapping electorates. With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, there have been questions over whether and to what extent the opposition should seek to cooperate with one another. One option would be an agreement not to stand candidates against one another for seats in the upper-house Senate, which are contested on a single-member-district system rather than through the proportional representation that decides the share of seats in the more powerful lower-house Sejm. Parties in Tusk’s current ruling coalition themselves formed such a “Senate pact” at the 2019 elections, helping them win control of the upper house, then repeated that in 2023, when they retained control. Although the Senate has a limited legislative role, it would be a significant prize for Nawrocki and the opposition, especially if Tusk’s coalition wins the Sejm, because the Senate has the power to approve or reject national referendums proposed by the president. An even more ambitious plan that has been rumoured is for some elements of the right-wing opposition to run joint electoral lists for the Sejm. That would require a far greater degree of programmatic consensus and longer negotiations over how to distribute places on lists. The government's majority in the Senate has, for the second time, rejected a proposal by opposition-aligned President Nawrocki to hold a referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the EU's climate policies, which he argues are too costly https://t.co/Idm6dnzQEH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Nawrocki is seen as key to any such plan coming to fruition. He was elected last year to the presidency as an independent, but with the formal backing of PiS. Ahead of the second-round run-off vote, he also received endorsements from defeated first-round rivals Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of Confederation, and Grzegorz Braun, the leader of KKP. Since taking office, Nawrocki has continued to cultivate good relations with PiS and Confederation, as well as with Morawiecki’s new breakaway faction. However, he has kept his distance from Braun, whose anti-Americanism, antisemitism and sympathy towards Russia makes him something of a pariah. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 Media reports have suggested that Nawrocki is planning to play a role in creating a “broad patriotic camp” among the opposition ahead of next year’s elections. Last week, during an event celebrating the first anniversary of his swearing in, the president also hinted at this role. He noted he will, in the coming months, be presenting “a presidential development strategy”, which “I believe will become a point of reference in the upcoming parliamentary elections for all those who aspire to govern Poland, a real plan for the future of the republic”. The strategy would be aimed in particular at “patriotic forces” who are “ready for dialogue between the offices of the president and future prime minister”. Given that Nawrocki and Tusk’s government are bitterly opposed to one another, that was a clear reference to opposition parties. A report on Sunday by Newsweek Polska, based on unnamed inside sources, claimed that Kaczyński is hoping to form a single electoral list for the Sejm elections compromising PiS, Development Plus and all or parts of Confederation, under the patronage of Nawrocki. 💥 Nowa obsesja Jarosława Kaczyńskiego, w jaki sposób odzyskać władzę. Prezes PiS naciska na Karola Nawrockiego, by prezydent stworzył "listę Nawrockiego" prawicy do Sejmu. To najbardziej ryzykowna, ale też o ogromnej stawce, decyzja prezydenta.https://t.co/sqRPFUuiZ7 — Jacek Gądek (@JacekGadek) August 9, 2026 Other leaders on the right have expressed varying degrees of willingness to work with one another. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Saturday, Krzystof Bosak, another of Confederation’s leaders, expressed support for the idea of a Senate pact. On Friday, Morawiecki said that he can “fully imagine working with Sławomir Mentzen”, who “I believe is absolutely part of the patriotic camp”. However, Mentzen himself quickly ruled out the idea, tweeting that he’d rather “quit politics than join this gang leading Poland to disaster”, adding that Tusk, Kaczyński and Morawiecki are “one and the same”. Whereas Bosak represents a nationalist faction of Confederation seen as more compatible with PiS, Mentzen represent’s a libertarian wing that is bitterly opposed to the former PiS’ government’s high social spending, support for Ukraine, and the restrictions it introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Tusk, Kaczyński, Morawiecki, Czarzasty, jeden pies. World.title: Protests against anti-Ukrainian violence held in 25 Polish cities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Demonstrations took place in around 25 Polish cities on Sunday against a “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. The protests came after police data showed a significant increase in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland so far this year, including a number of high-profile incidents of verbal and physical aggression. Sunday’s demonstrations, which took place under the slogan “Do Not Be Indifferent”, were organised by the Committee for the Defence of Democracy (KOD), an NGO, with support from other groups, including Amnesty International. “[This is] a nationwide campaign aimed at expressing opposition to the growing wave of hate, xenophobia, nationalism and violence directed against Ukrainians and members of other minorities,” wrote KOD ahead of the events. On Sunday, hundreds gathered on Warsaw’s Castle Square carrying Ukrainian and Polish flags and many waving signs saying “With U”, with the letter “U” coloured in Ukrainian national colours. #Siódemka Plac Zamkowy w Warszawie, protest w ramach: 🛑 NIE BĄDŹMY OBOJĘTNI! WSPÓLNIE PRZECIWKO NIENAWIŚCI! W wielu miastach Polski wyszliśmy na ulice, żeby jasno powiedzieć: nie ma zgody na hejt, przemoc i agresję wobec Ukraińców. W ostatnim czasie coraz częściej słyszymy… pic.twitter.com/kOfq4zBuGT — Piotr #FBPE Fijałkowski (@piotr4913) August 9, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, local media reported that around 150 people attended a demonstration, carrying placards saying “Let’s defend our neighbours from the aggression and stupidity of others” and “Putin is the enemy, Ukraine is our neighbour”. In Gdańsk, on Poland’s northern coast, around 300 people gathered, according to local media. However, they were also met with a small counter-demonstration of around a dozen people, led by the New Hope party that is part of Poland’s far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) opposition group. The counter-protesters held a banner declaring “Solidarity with victims of mass immigration” and “Down with Bandera”, a reference to historical Ukrainian nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, who in Poland is associated with the massacres of around 100,000 Poles by Ukrainians during World War Two. Separately, on Friday, a group of NGOs organised a demonstration against anti-Ukrainian violence outside the prime minister’s chancellery, during which they delivered a petition, signed by over 11,000 people, calling for the government to take “decisive action against xenophobic attacks”. Police data published last month showed that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025. Among those incidents have been a number of high-profile cases, including two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls being verbally abused by a man on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała and a violent attack on young Ukrainians by a group of Polish teenagers in Warsaw. Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. Tenions have been stoked further by a diplomatic crisis that began in May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after a group responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two. That prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Last week, PiS announced that, if it returns to power, one of its first actions would be to deport Ukrainian conscription-age men who are not in legal employment. At one of Sunday’s protests, in Kraków, a demonstrator responded with a placard declaring “Deport xenophobia”. Poland’s more liberal ruling coalition has condemned anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing opposition. Last month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for a “war against this violence”, saying that “thugs and hooligans have gained courage, audacity and political patronage” from the opposition. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative PiS, has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The idea was criticised by the government, which called it "absurd" and "disgusting" https://t.co/Z4kArDeLXl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
