Li Mingzhi, 30, leads the venture, which operates under the name SenJoy Mahjong. A former Alibaba employee, he saw American mahjong as a chance to sell a higher-value product overseas. He recruited his former colleague Wang Hao, his younger brother, and several childhood friends from northwestern China’s Gansu province to build the venture.

“I never imagined I’d move to such a remote village to start a business,” says Wang, 28.

Zhu estimates that nearly 30 new factories have sprung up in Taixing over the past year as entrepreneurs rush into American mahjong. The town’s fragmented supply chain has allowed outsiders to enter without building a factory from scratch.

“Here, you don’t need to build an entire production line yourself,” Li tells Sixth Tone. “You can outsource each step and focus on design and branding.”

In practice, however, the workshop became a crash course in manufacturing.

“Every day is unpredictable,” Li says. “Customers can call at any time, and problems can emerge at every stage — production, design, communication, quality inspection. Working until 3 or 4 a.m. is normal.”

The new equipment offered precision but no ready-made solution for mahjong production: sizes varied, hand-cut pieces did not match machine-cut ones, and every fault required another round of testing.

“Almost every step brought a different problem,” Wang says.

The UV printer proved especially difficult. Each design had to be aligned by hand, and a shift of just 1 millimeter could push the ink outside the engraved lines.

The night before Sixth Tone’s visit, all five stayed up until 3 a.m. trying to solve the problem. “Before entering the industry, I thought making mahjong would be simple,” says Wang. “Once I started, I realized American sets are closer to handicrafts.”

Despite the setbacks, the team produced and sold about 1,000 sets in its first few months, generating roughly 230,000 yuan in sales. Its customers included businesses selling on Amazon.

Li put 1.5 million yuan of his own savings into the venture. “Based on our current orders,” says Li, “we expect the business to recover that investment within six months.”

To avoid becoming another contract manufacturer in Taixing’s crowded supply chain, the team began working with outside designers to develop original sets. It also launched an independent website and overseas social media accounts.

“For us, building a brand starts with original design,” Li says. “We might become the first company in Taixing — and perhaps one of the first in China — to build a real mahjong brand instead of simply manufacturing for others.”

The team hopes to reach buyers directly through social media, influencers, online sellers, and brick-and-mortar retailers.

Their bestseller uses a coral-reef theme. Against a shimmering blue base, coral motifs represent bamboo tiles, shells stand in for circles, and small fish serve as jokers.

“As long as the designs aren’t ugly, we’re not worried about sales,” Li says. “Right now, demand far exceeds supply.”

Wang is more cautious. Today’s buyers, he says, remain a relatively small group with strong spending power. If American mahjong reaches a broader market, more manufacturers will follow, he says, adding: “Price wars are unavoidable.”

Hua, one of the first Chinese traders to bet on American mahjong, has watched competitors multiply within months.

When she launched the business, Hua handled every part of the operation herself, often staying up late to respond to customers in the U.S. and sleeping as little as two hours a night. Today, her Ningbo-based company employs about 10 people and provides customer service around the clock.

But the market that once seemed wide open has become more crowded. Designs that once sold out quickly are now easier to source, and more suppliers are competing for the same orders.

“The conversion rate isn’t as good as before,” Hua says. Her sales data show that fewer visitors become inquiries, and fewer inquiries turn into confirmed orders.

“The profit margins were much higher in the beginning, but now they have dropped significantly,” she says. “I think this is probably an inevitable stage for any viral product.”

She, too, has started developing designs of her own.

Last month, she began experimenting with AI to create early concepts before working with freelance designers to refine them. Her first ideas included themes inspired by witches, tennis, flowers, and Christmas.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Workers sort uncarved and unpainted mahjong tiles at Zhu Ronggen’s factory in Taixing, Jiangsu province, June 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.title: 14 dead as landslides, heavy rain batter Cordillera
World.content:
SEARCH. Emergency responders work through mud and debris during search and retrieval operations at the Guisad Surong landslide site in Baguio City.

Police say all the reported deaths were caused by landslides in Baguio City and Benguet

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – At least 14 people have died in landslides after days of relentless rain battered the Cordillera, while swollen rivers and continuing slope failures isolated communities and left at least 15 road sections impassable across the region.

Thirteen civilians were injured, while no one remained missing as of 6 am Tuesday, August 11, according to the Police Regional Office-Cordillera, citing data from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.

All the reported deaths were caused by landslides in Baguio City and Benguet, police said.

At least 10 people died in Guisad Surong, Baguio City; two were killed when a landslide buried a roadside eatery in Shilan, La Trinidad; and two relatives died after being buried while clearing mud near their home in Paoay, Atok.

The figures rose sharply from Monday morning, August 10, when authorities reported six deaths, 11 injuries and five missing people across the region.

Search and retrieval operations continued through Monday, particularly in Guisad Surong, where responders searched through mud and debris for those initially reported missing.

Police said four search, rescue and retrieval operations had been conducted across the region, with 13 people rescued and 14 bodies retrieved.

The names of the dead and injured were withheld out of consideration for the victims and their families.

Communities isolated

Police also reported that all six barangays of Lacub in Abra were isolated by swollen rivers and a series of landslides. They are Bacag, Buneg, Guinguinabang, Lan-ag, Pacoc and Poblacion.

Nineteen areas were also left without electricity, while 19 power lines were affected.

Authorities recorded damage to 52 houses, one school and one commercial building.

Roads cut off

At least 15 road sections in the Cordillera remained impassable as of 6 am Tuesday, down from 18 reported Monday morning. Nine were in Benguet, four in Abra, one in Kalinga and one in Mountain Province.

Affected routes in Benguet included Kennon Road, the Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road in Beckel, Lubas-Ambiong Road, and road sections in Atok, Itogon and Tublay.

In Abra, roads in Licuan-Baay, Boliney, Malibcong and Tubo remained blocked or unsafe because of landslides, erosion, road collapse or swollen waterways.

The Tabuk-Banaue Road via Tanudan-Barlig was also listed as impassable, while the Mountain Province-Ilocos Sur Road via Tue Road remained closed at Balaoa, Tadian, because of a soil collapse. Motorists were advised to use the route via Kayan instead.

Evacuations

Police reported 19 occupied evacuation centers across Abra, Baguio City and Benguet, sheltering 85 families, or 351 people.

Four occupied evacuation centers were in Abra, five in Baguio City and 10 in Benguet.

Police deployed 176 personnel for disaster response, including 138 for road monitoring and clearing and 19 each at evacuation centers and the Women and Children Protection Desk.

Another 1,074 personnel were listed under the Regional Standby Support Force.

Classes suspended

Classes remained suspended Tuesday as authorities continued to contend with rain and landslide risks.

Authorities said classes at all levels in public and private schools were suspended in 27 municipalities in Abra and all 13 municipalities in Benguet. Baguio City suspended classes from preschool through Grade 12 in public and private schools.

More rain expected

The state weather bureau Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) forecast 50 to 100 millimeters of rain over Benguet, La Union and Pangasinan through Tuesday evening, with another 50 to 100 mm expected over the same provinces from Tuesday evening through Wednesday evening, August 12.

It warned that rainfall could be higher in mountainous and elevated areas and that its impacts could be worsened by the significant amount of rain that had already fallen.

With slopes saturated and several roads and communities affected, authorities urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel, stay away from landslide-prone slopes and swollen waterways, and follow evacuation orders and local advisories – Rappler.com

World.title: The ‘provisional understanding’ with China that has caused misunderstanding
World.content:
A temporary agreement between Beijing and Manila on resupply missions has brought peace to Ayungin Shoal—until it unraveled

It was all smiles and handshakes when Maria Theresa Lazaro, then-foreign affairs undersecretary, concluded talks with her counterpart, Chinese Vice Foreign Minister Chen Xiaodong, to ease the tension during resupply missions to Ayungin Shoal. Both sides have called this a “provisional understanding” or a “provisional agreement”—and have kept the terms confidential.

The Philippines thereafter conducted 13 resupply missions, all untroubled.

The meeting was held in Manila in July 2024, weeks after machete-wielding China Coast Guard (CCG) personnel assaulted a Navy rubber boat that brought food and supplies to the BRP Sierra Madre and, in the melee, cut off a Filipino sailor’s thumb.

It was the first known violent encounter in the annals of rotation and resupply missions — known as RORE — to the aging Sierra Madre, which guards the Ayungin Shoal. A number of Navy and Marine personnel take turns keeping watch over the feature that China wants to control so that it can enforce its sweeping claims over the South China Sea.

But the fragile peace was shattered last month, two years after the “provisional understanding” took shape. A CCG ship came near the Sierra Madre, took anchor, and deployed a rigid hull inflatable boat with eight personnel aboard. They closed in on the Sierra Madre, sailed around it, and took videos and photos.

In response, the Sierra Madre crew deployed two rubber boats — one with two personnel and the other with five—and ordered the CCG vessel to leave, but the Chinese refused. A commotion ensued, and the Philippine personnel used their boat paddles to drive away the CCG. It was then that a CCG personnel hit a Filipino soldier with a long wooden pole, causing a gash on the latter’s head.

The smiles and the handshakes of July 2024 are no more.

He said, she said

Why did the CCG violate the peace?

China’s ambassador, Jing Quan, claimed that the RORE brought construction materials, particularly barrier nets, which the “provisional understanding” did not allow. “Our people found your soldiers… they’re building some kind of barrier nets… doing some kind of construction work on the ship,” Quan said. “That’s against the spirit of our provisional agreement. That is no new construction; keep the status quo…”

There is no such thing in the agreement, Lazaro, now the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) secretary, countered. In addition, the DFA said in a statement that the Philippines doesn’t need to seek permission for resupply missions, doesn’t allow the boarding or inspection of Philippine ships, and doesn’t “concede the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction” in Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea. (In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal declared Ayungin Shoal part of our Exclusive Economic Zone.)

The “provisional understanding,” the DFA further explained, is a “set of principles and approaches observed by both sides in order to avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation.”

Lazaro said a team at the DFA crafted the “provisional understanding” and was given the green light by then-national security adviser Eduardo Año. Left out was Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who said he was not consulted.

What happens during operations?

Apparently, something got lost between the high-minded “principles and approaches” and the actual nitty-gritty of operations.

Soon after the “provisional understanding” was set into motion, signs that both sides were not on the same page surfaced. A red flag.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson claimed that the Philippines notified China of its RORE before it was carried out, adding that “after confirming on-site that the Philippine vessel carried only humanitarian living necessities, the Chinese side let the vessel through.”

Then-foreign secretary Enrique Manalo clarified that Beijing and Manila agreed to an “exchange of information” rather than “prior notification.” Asked by a reporter when the “exchange of information” took place, Manalo replied: “It’s gotta be before. Otherwise, what’s the sense of exchanging (information) after?”

Well before this “provisional understanding” unraveled, I gathered from two sources with knowledge of the ROREs to Sierra Madre that our side would inform the Chinese of an upcoming resupply mission and allow the CCG to sail near our boats to check their contents — from a certain distance.

The sense I got was that it was better to keep this arrangement to de-escalate the tension and successfully resupply our troops rather than risk a conflict at sea. As we have seen, the Chinese have always blocked or water cannoned our ROREs when they learned that our boats were carrying construction materials to fortify the World War II-era Sierra Madre, effectively a shipwreck.

China sees Ayungin Shoal as an easy win once the dilapidated vessel is ravaged by time and the forces of nature, no longer able to serve as our country’s outpost.

Core issue

What next? The DFA could choose to make the “provisional understanding” public. Or it could go back to the table to iron out the misunderstandings with Beijing.

However, at the core of this issue is the fact that the Philippines has sovereign rights over Ayungin Shoal—which China will never accept.

That’s a fundamental divide that requires much more than a “provisional understanding” to resolve.

Let me know what you think. You can email me at: marites.vitug@rappler.com.

World.title: US court rules Meta, others must face thousands of social media addiction suits
World.content:
A US appeals court allows over 3,000 lawsuits against Meta, Google, TikTok, and Snapchat to proceed, claiming these companies designed their products to be addictive to young users

A US appeals court on Monday, August 10, allowed thousands of lawsuits to move forward against Meta Platforms, Alphabet’s Google, ByteDance’s TikTok and Snap Inc’s Snapchat over claims they designed their products to be addictive to young users.

The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an appeal by Meta and TikTok seeking to overturn a lower court ruling requiring them to face more than 3,000 lawsuits filed in federal court, saying the companies had appealed too early.

The companies had argued that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 — which generally shields online companies from claims over content posted by their users — also bars lawsuits claiming they failed to warn the public about the addictive nature of their platforms.

Most appeals come after a case has concluded with a ruling or a verdict. The companies contended that they should not have to wait until the litigation ends to challenge the lower court’s rejection of their immunity defense. But the 9th Circuit said Section 230 provides a defense to liability, not immunity from lawsuits, so the appeal was premature.

Meta loses bid to delay multistate trial

The court also denied Meta’s bid to postpone a trial beginning on Wednesday in a lawsuit brought by 29 state attorneys general alleging that the company illegally collected and used children’s data, designed its social media platforms to keep young users hooked, and misled consumers about their safety. The company had argued that the trial couldn’t go forward while the appeal had been outstanding.

The news comes days after a New Mexico judge found Meta had created a public nuisance in the state and ordered it to pay $567 million into a teen mental health fund and implement youth-safety measures.

A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment.

Representatives for TikTok did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Monday’s ruling.

In a statement, Lexi Hazam and Previn Warren, the attorneys representing the plaintiffs, said the ruling was Meta’s last “procedural off-ramp” before the trial starting this week.

“A trial is how the public finds out what Meta knew about its products’ impact on children, when it knew it, and what it chose to do with that knowledge,” the attorneys said. “Meta has fought to keep that evidence from the public.”

Thousands of lawsuits

Filed by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals, the lawsuits allege that social media companies intentionally addicted young users, contributing to surging depression, anxiety and body-image issues and a broader mental health crisis among American youth in recent years.

Parents, school districts, states and other plaintiffs had argued that the trial court’s ruling was not final and therefore could not be appealed. But they also objected to the companies’ arguments about Section 230, saying it does not cover claims related to how they operate and design their products.

The cases, which have been centralized before US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, California, seek damages, penalties and restitution from the companies. The companies appealed Rogers’ orders in 2023 and 2024 that largely allowed the litigation to move forward.

The companies are facing hundreds of additional lawsuits over similar claims in state court, with approximately 3,300 of them in a consolidated proceeding in California state court.

In the first lawsuit to go to trial in the California litigation, and a closely watched test of how juries might respond to similar claims, a Los Angeles jury in March found Meta and Google negligent for designing social media platforms that harm young people. The jury awarded $6 million to a young woman who says she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.

The New Mexico public nuisance ruling against Meta followed an earlier phase in the trial, in which a jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms.

Both Meta and Google, which have denied the claims in those cases, said they would appeal. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] The math behind Ramon Ang’s Lopez bet
World.content:
Ramon Ang may not have bought the entire Lopez empire, but through Illumina, he bought a place near its summit—and an invitation from Piki Lopez to help shape what comes next

Ramon Ang’s acquisition of 25.68% of Lopez Inc. is more than another billionaire buying into another corporate empire built on bricks, steel, and infrastructure.

Trace the investment through the layers of ownership and his economic interest reaches deep into First Philippine Holdings Corp. (FPH) and First Gen Corp. (First Gen), raising larger questions about valuation, financial capacity, and the continuing concentration of Philippine corporate power.

He did not buy the entire Lopez empire. But his acquisition of 25.68% of Lopez Inc. may prove bigger than the percentage suggests.

Ang has purchased a substantial stake in the privately held company sitting atop one of the Philippines’ oldest business dynasties. Consider the ownership structure beneath his investment and what appears to be a minority equity stake begins to carry much greater economic significance.

There is a crucial caveat. The buyer was not San Miguel Corp. (SMC). Ang invested through Illumina Investment Holdings Inc., his wholly owned investment vehicle. Crème Investment Corp., representing the Lopez family branch led by Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, sold its 25.68% interest, while the other Lopez branches retained control.

Illumina did not suddenly appear for this transaction. Cyber Bay Corp.’s 2024 and 2025 disclosures identify Ang’s lawyer, Maria Farah Z.G. Nicolas-Suchianco, as holding a directorship or officership in Illumina.

The same disclosures list her affiliations with Broadreach Media Holdings, Central Bay Reclamation and Development Corp., Global Titan Leisure Holdings, and several other companies.

That corporate trail suggests Illumina is not merely a special-purpose vehicle hastily created for the Lopez deal, but an established investment vehicle connected to Ang’s broader private corporate interests.

This distinction matters. Another major acquisition on SMC’s books would raise questions about financial capacity. San Miguel is enormously cash-generative but is simultaneously financing airports, tollways, railways, power plants and other infrastructure. It generated P262 billion in EBITDA in 2025, with operating income reaching P181.6 billion.

SMC possesses formidable earnings capacity, but its businesses require enormous continuing capital. Unless later disclosures reveal SMC financing, guarantees or participation, investors should not put Ang’s Lopez acquisition onto San Miguel’s balance sheet.

The more intriguing mathematics lies on the Lopez side.

Ramon Ang bought 25.68% of Lopez Inc., not direct stakes in its listed companies. Lopez Inc. owns 54.74% of listed Lopez Holdings. Lopez Holdings owns 60.67% of First Philippine Holdings (FPH), while FPH owns 67.84% of First Gen’s common shares. Run Ang’s investment through these layers and his 25.68% Lopez Inc. stake translates into a look-through economic interest of roughly 14.06% in Lopez Holdings, 8.53% in FPH and 5.79% in First Gen.

These are not direct shareholdings or voting rights. But the calculation reveals the economic reach buried underneath Ang’s investment. These are substantial businesses. Lopez Holdings ended 2025 with P581.5 billion in consolidated assets and P31.7 billion in consolidated net income, with P12.05 billion attributable to parent shareholders.

Now comes perhaps the most revealing number.

Ang has said Lopez Inc. was valued at P45 billion. That materially changes the arithmetic surrounding earlier reports that P45 billion represented the price for a combined 70.83% controlling interest.

At a P45-billion valuation for the whole company, Crème’s 25.68% block carries an implied value of approximately P11.56 billion.

That does not necessarily mean P11.56 billion was the precise cash consideration paid by Illumina. Until the deed of assignment or another primary document reveals the final consideration, it is best treated as the implied value of the stake.

The figure nevertheless gives investors something they previously lacked: a private-market valuation of the company sitting at the top of the Lopez ownership structure. Public investors have spent years valuing Lopez Holdings, FPH, and First Gen, separately. Ang has now effectively put a P45-billion value on something investors cannot buy directly on the Philippine Stock Exchange: Lopez Inc. itself.

This is where the transaction becomes bigger than either family.

The Philippine economy has historically revolved around a relatively small circle of conglomerates—Ayala, Sy, Aboitiz, Gokongwei, Lopez, San Miguel and, more recently, [Enrique] Razon. They supplied capital and built infrastructure where government and domestic capital markets sometimes could not.

But as ownership and influence increasingly overlap, another question emerges: are we witnessing more efficient allocation of Philippine capital, or increasing concentration of economic power?

Ang already operates across food, beverages, oil refining, electricity, cement, banking, tollways, airports and infrastructure. His Lopez investment gives him an indirect economic position near another major power platform, premium property interests, and ABS-CBN.

Federico “Piki” Lopez’s reaction makes Ang’s arrival more interesting. The Lopez Inc. president welcomed him and said he looked forward to “working together with him.” More revealingly, Piki described the transaction as the family’s entry into a “partnership” with Ang and said his expertise could contribute to the growth of their businesses.

Partnership is not synonymous with control, nor does Piki’s statement disclose board rights, veto powers or management arrangements. But it suggests Ang may be expected to bring more to Lopez Inc. than capital.

Piki also called the transaction “a great step toward resolving issues that have affected our family as well as our businesses.” Gabby’s branch obtained liquidity and exited a family conflict; the remaining branches retained control; and Ang entered as a substantial minority shareholder whom Piki welcomes as a partner.

There is one more number worth watching: 29.17%. First Gen financing documents contain change-of-management provisions tied to Piki and his family maintaining at least that ownership in Lopez Inc. Ang’s acquisition leaves it untouched, but demonstrates why movements inside the private parent can matter several corporate layers below.

If Ang remains merely a minority investor, this may be remembered as a settlement to an ugly family dispute. But Piki’s words suggest something potentially more ambitious: a partnership.

Ramon Ang may not have bought the entire Lopez empire, but through Illumina, he bought a place near its summit—and an invitation from Piki Lopez to help shape what comes next. – Rappler.com

World.title: Condo shopping? Expect better payment terms in best buyer’s market in decades
World.content:
Two of the country's biggest condo developers, Ayala Land and SM Prime, are holding back launches and working down inventories as they compete harder for cautious homebuyers

MANILA, Philippines – If you’ve been waiting for a better time to buy a condominium, the balance of power may be shifting in your favor.

Two of the country’s biggest property developers – Ayala Land and SM Prime – are sitting on sizable residential inventories, holding back new projects, and concentrating instead on selling units they already have.

For Ayala Land, that has meant stretching payment periods to as long as five years for some properties and offering selective discounts to buyers willing to pay faster.

Ayala Land chief operating officer Mikhail Cruz said the terms depend on the location, age of the project, and how quickly units are selling.

For projects with older inventory and slower sales, “we’re more aggressive and we give longer payment terms around five years,” Cruz said during the company’s first-half earnings briefing on Monday, August 10.

For other projects, Ayala may instead encourage buyers to pay over a shorter two- or three-year period through selective discounts.

The incentives come as Metro Manila’s condo market continues to carry the burden of excess supply. Leechiu Property Consultants said in its latest first half 2026 report that unsold condominium inventory reached an all-time high 82,900 units in the second quarter.

But demand has not disappeared. Buyers took up 7,255 units during the quarter, while residential demand grew 6% in the first half compared with the previous six months. Leechiu described the current environment as the “best buyer’s market in decades,” with ready for occupancy discounts being record-deep.

Developers are clearing stock

For Ayala, its aggressive strategy appears to be working well.

The developer has cut the value of its residential inventory from P214 billion in 2024 to just P110 billion by June, excluding its paused projects such as The Laurean. In other words, it has cleared nearly half the value of the unsold units it was carrying two years ago.

Ayala has also deliberately stopped the launch of new residential projects during the first half so its sales force could concentrate on existing units. Despite that, it recorded P22.3 billion in residential reservation sales in the second quarter alone.

Ayala Land president and CEO Anna Margarita Dy said that made the performance particularly encouraging because the sales team was selling entirely from existing inventory in what management described as a highly competitive market.

“We actually feel that to have achieved this kind of sales levels with no additional, no new launches in the market is quite a good performance for our sales organization,” Dy said.

Inventory has now fallen to around 15 months of sales, better than Ayala’s roughly 18-month level before the pandemic.

SM Prime is taking a similarly cautious approach to new residential supply, although its strategy is less about loosening payment terms and more about improving the quality of its sales while working through existing inventory.

The Sy-led developer had around 29,000 unsold units as of June, with 13% ready for occupancy. SM Prime said it would launch no new Metro Manila residential projects for the rest of 2026, with management instead taking a “wait and see” approach for boh their core and premium developments.

“We still have quite a bit of inventory to work through. So, we’re focusing on selling those inventories for the time being,” SM Prime executive vice president Cris Noel Torres said during a briefing on Monday.

Sales have nevertheless held up, with first-half reservation sales at around P25 billion, roughly level with the previous year.

Torres also said high-downpayment and spot-cash sales had increased “meaningfully” year on year, which SM Prime sees as a sign of a stronger buyer profile that could help reduce cancellations. – Rappler.com

World.title: At least 111 killed after magnitude 7.4 earthquake hits western Colombia
World.content:
AFTERMATH. Rescue workers and residents stand around a collapsed building in the aftermath of an earthquake in Cali, Colombia, on August 10, 2026, in this screengrab taken from a video.

(2nd UPDATE) Colombia's geological service says it was the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in the 21st century

BOGOTA, Colombia – At least 111 people were killed after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, August 10, toppling buildings across several cities, damaging hospitals and infrastructure and trapping people beneath the rubble in what authorities called the country’s strongest earthquake of the century.

The earthquake struck just days after Abelardo De La Espriella was sworn in as president, thrusting the new administration into its first major crisis, with memories still fresh of devastating twin earthquakes in neighboring Venezuela in June.

“The national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed,” he said in a national address around 1 pm local time, upon declaring a national state of emergency.

“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”

De La Espriella said preliminary reports indicated 111 dead and 87 injured, along with dozens of collapsed buildings and damaged homes.

The US Geological Survey said the magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck at a depth of 107 km. Colombia’s geological service said it was the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in the 21st century.

Reports from Choco, near the epicenter, were slowed by communications outages, with some areas still lacking cellphone service hours after the earthquake. Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said 12 people had been killed and 84 injured in the largely rural area.

The heaviest casualties appeared concentrated in Risaralda, part of Colombia’s coffee-growing region. Pereira, the department’s capital, suffered extensive damage, with rescue workers continuing to search collapsed buildings for survivors.

Buildings crumble, airports forced to close

A four-story building crumbled in Pereira during the earthquake, according to Reuters-verified video, while footage from Manizales showed one of the side towers of the city’s landmark neo-Gothic cathedral collapsing and scattering debris onto nearby streets.

Reuters footage showed rescue workers, police and volunteers shoveling debris by hand and loading rubble into trucks as they searched for survivors trapped beneath collapsed buildings. Other footage showed damage to residential towers and emergency-service facilities, with debris crashing onto ambulances parked below.

Mauricio Andrade, a firefighter in Cali, said his team had rescued two adult women and two children from a collapsed building. As he spoke to Reuters, his team was preparing to rescue more people from the rubble.

“They are alive,” he said. “We are making space so we can free them and get them out.”

Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television that the collapse of one building “sounded like a bomb,” as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali.

“All of us neighbors are working together, forming human chains. We need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped.”

Colombia’s civil aviation authority suspended operations at several airports in the country’s west, including Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura, while engineers carried out structural inspections.

EVACUATION. A woman prays as people gather outside a building following an earthquake in Bogota, Colombia, on August 10, 2026. Photo by Luisa Gonzalez/Reuters

Ring of fire

Colombia sits along the seismically active Pacific Ring of Fire and records thousands of mostly minor earthquakes each month.

Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the earthquake’s powerful magnitude, inland location and strike-slip motion may have amplified damage in populated valleys despite its considerable depth.

“This one was far below the crust, and in theory it shouldn’t cause as much shaking. At this magnitude, it did actually cause a lot of shaking,” she said.

The Colombian Geological Service said 21 aftershocks had been recorded by late Monday and warned that additional tremors were likely.

Colombia’s coffee region was devastated by a magnitude 6.2 earthquake in 1999 that killed more than 1,000 people, particularly around Armenia and Pereira. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sport’s Next Generation Won’t Choose Sides, Says Phygital International CEO
World.content:
ASTANA — Phygital sport’s future will depend on building lasting local ecosystems, developing a new generation of athletes skilled in both physical and digital competition, and establishing itself as a distinct international sporting movement, Phygital International CEO Daniel Merkley said in an exclusive interview with The Astana Times.

The Games of the Future 2026 powered by Samruk Kazyna (GOTF 2026) concluded in Astana on Aug. 9 after 12 days of competition across eight disciplines. With the event over, attention is turning to what comes next for phygital sport and how it can develop beyond major international tournaments.

Drawing on more than 20 years of experience working on Olympic and Paralympic events, Merkley said phygital sport has much to learn from established sporting institutions, particularly in governance, athlete-centered development and trust.

“One of the greatest lessons from the Olympic and Paralympic Movement is that lasting success comes from strong governance, clear values and a commitment to serving athletes first. Major sporting movements are built over decades through trust, consistency and collaboration, and those principles are just as relevant for phygital sport,” said Merkley.

“At the same time, we should not assume that because something has always been done a certain way, it is the right approach for a new generation,” he added.

For Merkley, strong governance – the rules, decision-making and accountability behind how a sport is organized – will be essential to building international credibility. However, he emphasized that the emerging movement should not simply reproduce the structures of traditional sport.

“Rather than asking young people to adapt to traditional sport, we can meet them where they already are. That means embracing technology, creating more engaging experiences for athletes and fans, and building a model that reflects how younger generations participate, compete and consume sport today,” said Merkley.

“Ultimately, our goal is not to replace traditional sport. It is to create something complementary that learns from its strengths while being confident enough to evolve in its own direction,” he said.

Astana’s legacy will be measured in years

According to Merkley, the most meaningful outcome for Kazakhstan will not be found in final scores, viewing figures or the scale of the event itself.

“The real measure of success won’t be what happens during these 12 days of competition. It will be what happens over the next three, five or even 10 years. If, in a few years’ time, Kazakhstan has more young people participating in phygital sport, a growing calendar of competitions, stronger links between sport, education and technology, and a new generation of athletes developing both physical and digital skills, then we’ll know these Games have created something that lasts,” he said.

He noted that impact could extend beyond organized competition, particularly as Kazakhstan places greater emphasis on innovation, technology and artificial intelligence. An event linking sport with digital skills can introduce young people to opportunities beyond the competition itself.

“If these Games encourage more young people to engage with technology, develop new skills and see opportunities at the intersection of sport and innovation, that is a powerful legacy in itself,” said Merkley.

He said Phygital International also works with host cities and partners to support continued development after the flagship event ends, to create local structures capable of sustaining participation and attracting future investment.

“Ultimately, success means leaving behind a stronger phygital ecosystem that continues to inspire young people, attract investment and create new opportunities long after the closing ceremony,” he said.

A new type of athlete

That distinction is also reflected in the demands placed on competitors themselves. In phygital sport, athletes compete across digital and physical stages within the same discipline. Depending on the format, a video game result can carry into football, basketball, combat sports or another physical contest, requiring competitors to perform effectively in both environments.

For Merkley, that combination is beginning to produce athletes who no longer fit neatly into the traditional distinction between gamers and sports competitors.

“What makes phygital athletes unique is that they cannot rely on excellence in just one environment. They have to combine elite gaming ability with high-level physical performance, while also being able to transition seamlessly between the two under competitive pressure. That demands technical skill, tactical intelligence, physical fitness, mental resilience and adaptability in equal measure,” said Merkley.

As competition develops, he expects training systems to become increasingly specialized around those combined demands. Coaches could prepare athletes for both stages, supported by sports science in areas such as physiology, biomechanics, psychology and performance analysis tailored specifically to phygital competition.

“I think we’re witnessing the emergence of a new type of athlete – one who develops physical excellence and digital mastery in parallel. (…) I also believe we’ll see more young athletes developing physical and digital skills side by side, rather than feeling they have to choose between traditional sport and gaming,” he said.

Becoming a category of its own

Phygital sport currently sits at the intersection of several industries, combining elements of international sport and entertainment while connecting traditional sports organizations, esports and technology companies.

“I don’t think those possibilities are mutually exclusive. Phygital sport has the potential to become a recognized international sporting movement while also delivering world-class entertainment and creating meaningful connections between traditional sport, esports and technology. What is important is that we do not define ourselves solely by comparison with existing models,” he said.

His long-term ambition is for the Games of the Future to become one of the world’s leading international sporting events while developing an identity that does not depend on resembling the Olympics, esports tournaments or any other existing model.

“Achieving that will require disciplined choices. We must protect sporting integrity, maintain high competitive standards and continue building trusted relationships with athletes, publishers, sports organizations, governments and commercial partners,” Merkley said.

“If we can balance those priorities, I believe phygital sport can become one of the defining sporting movements of the next generation,” he added.

World.title: Campaign Week in Review: Education Debate Leads Kazakhstan’s Election Race
World.content:
ASTANA – A nationally televised debate on education dominated Kazakhstan’s election campaign during the week of Aug. 3-9. Representatives of the country’s seven political parties outlined their visions for reforming the education system during the two-and-a-half-hour broadcast.

The debate consisted of four segments. Party representatives first presented their election platforms and questioned one another in an open discussion. The second segment focused on education reform, with candidates responding to questions submitted through social media. During the third round, audience members in the studio posed questions before candidates concluded the event with final appeals to voters.

Viewers also voted online for the most convincing performance. The Adilet party received 45.48% of the vote, followed by Auyl with 15.58% and Respublica with 12.01%. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) placed fourth with 9.71%, followed by the Aq Jol Democratic Party (7.98%), the People’s Party of Kazakhstan (6.96%) and Baytaq Green Party (1.58%). Another 0.7% of viewers said none of the participants had been convincing. A total of 73,628 people took part in the online poll.

Meanwhile, parties continued campaigning across the country, promoting proposals on rural development, healthcare, business support and social inclusion.

Adilet Party

The Adilet campaigned in the West Kazakhstan, Zhambyl, Kyzylorda and Kostanai regions, meeting residents in district centers as well as remote villages. The public raised concerns about road conditions, water supply, public utilities and social infrastructure. Poor mobile phone coverage and limited internet access in rural communities were recurring issues.

Party representatives said their election platform aims to provide high-quality internet access to at least 97% of Kazakhstan’s more than 6,000 rural settlements through a combination of mobile and fixed-line technologies.

Auyl Party

The Auyl party continued meetings with rural residents and agricultural workers, focusing on job creation, infrastructure development, modern farming technologies and measures to encourage young professionals to remain in rural areas.

The party representatives said all proposals and concerns raised during the meetings had been documented for follow-up.

Food security was another key topic. According to the party, ensuring national food security depends not only on agricultural production but also on efficient storage, processing, market access and affordable distribution. The representatives said strengthening every stage of the supply chain is essential for improving the country’s food security.

Aq Jol Democratic Party

The party met with manufacturing companies and logistics businesses in Almaty and the Almaty Region.

Discussions focused on creating a more favorable environment for domestic manufacturing and reducing administrative burdens on businesses. The party emphasized the need to encourage investment in the real economy and expand procurement opportunities for Kazakh producers.

The party also highlighted support for small and medium-sized businesses, job creation, investment attraction and the protection of workers’ rights.

Baytaq Green Party

In addition to its daily meetings with voters, the party organized an environmental cleanup campaign in Oskemen.

Volunteers collected household, construction and bulky waste in the Berezovaya Roshcha area along the Irtysh River and near the protected water zone in the Kulenovka neighborhood. Organizers said 140 bags of waste were removed.

Nationwide Social Democratic Party

The NSDP organized an Inclusive Forum in Astana, bringing together families, experts and advocates to discuss systemic challenges related to inclusion and the protection of the rights of people with disabilities.

The forum featured panel discussions, expert sessions and interactive workshops designed for children and adults with physical and intellectual disabilities. Participants also received free legal and social consultations from specialists and party representatives.

The event placed particular emphasis on early diagnosis, rehabilitation and social adaptation for children with autism spectrum disorder and other developmental disabilities. The NSDP also presented legislative proposals aimed at improving inclusion and quality of life.

People’s Party of Kazakhstan

Candidates from the party met with healthcare professionals in Semei to present its healthcare proposals.

The party pledged stronger labor protections for medical workers, including the creation of a national AI-powered medical quality control system designed to reduce bureaucracy and improve healthcare oversight. It also proposed higher salaries, particularly for rural doctors.

Other initiatives include targeted training programs based on regional workforce needs and expanded support for medical graduates through relocation grants, employer-provided housing and preferential mortgage programs.

For patients, the party proposed creating a unified digital health portal that would provide secure access to medical records, test results, prescriptions and treatment history. According to the party, the system would protect personal data, improve transparency and prevent unauthorized changes to medical records. It also called for greater transparency in the Social Health Insurance Fund and the expansion of palliative care services, particularly for children with severe illnesses.

Respublica Party

The Respublica held two major public forums in Shymkent on Aug. 7 and Almaty on Aug. 8, where party leaders reviewed the results of the party’s three and a half years of activity.

The party also focused its campaign on visits to manufacturing enterprises, arguing that industrial development is essential for creating jobs, increasing household incomes and strengthening the national economy.

According to the party, meetings at production facilities provide direct insight into workers’ concerns and help translate practical challenges into policy solutions.

Voting to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral parliament, is due on Aug. 23.

World.title: Kazakhstan Household Deposits Near $54 Billion as Savings Rise 20.9%
World.content:
ALMATY – Household deposits in Kazakhstan’s banks approached nearly 25 trillion tenge (US$53.5 billion) by the end of June 2026, increasing by 20.9% over the year, reported the Finprom financial and analytical agency. While the overall volume of savings continues to grow, deposits remain concentrated in several major cities and regions, revealing significant differences in household savings across the country.

Of the total, 84% or 21 trillion tenge (US$44.9 billion) was held in deposits denominated in the national currency, while foreign-currency deposits accounted for 16%. The predominance of tenge deposits is partly linked to the difference in returns. Interest rates on foreign-currency deposits cannot exceed 1%, while tenge deposits have offered comparatively high returns amid the elevated base rate.

Term deposits dominate

Term deposits accounted for 90% of all household deposits, making them by far the most common form of savings. Savings deposits represented 9.7%, while demand deposits accounted for only 0.05%. The concentration of deposits is particularly pronounced geographically.

The city of Almaty remained the country’s largest center for household savings, with 9.6 trillion tenge (US$20.5 billion) deposited in banks as of the end of June. This represented almost 40% of all household deposits in Kazakhstan. Astana followed with 3.2 trillion tenge (US$6.8 billion), while the Karagandy Region held 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3 billion). West Kazakhstan and Shymkent ranked fourth and fifth, with 1.2 trillion (US$2.6 billion) and 1.1 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion) respectively.

The smallest overall volumes of household deposits were recorded in the Ulytau, Almaty and Zhetisu Regions.

Savings gap exceeds 25 times

The regional differences become even more pronounced when deposits are calculated per resident. As of July 1, Kazakhstan had an average of 1.2 million tenge (US$2,570) in household deposits per person. However, only five regions exceeded the national average.

Almaty ranked first, with more than 4 million tenge (US$8,570) per resident, followed by Astana at 1.9 million tenge (US$4,070). West Kazakhstan recorded 1.7 million tenge (US$3,640) per resident, while the Karagandy and Kostanai Regions each recorded nearly 1.3 million tenge (US$2,780).

In contrast, average deposits per resident amounted to just 144,000 tenge (US$310) in the Almaty Region and 161,000 tenge (US$345) in the Turkistan Region.

Overall, 12 of Kazakhstan’s 20 regions had less than 1 million tenge (US$2,139) in deposits per resident. The difference between the highest and lowest regional figures therefore exceeded 25 times.

The figures point to a banking sector in which household savings are expanding, but where the ability to accumulate financial assets remains closely linked to regional economic conditions. The concentration of almost two-fifths of all household deposits in Almaty, alongside substantially lower savings in several regions, underscores the continuing gap between Kazakhstan’s major economic centers and less affluent areas.

World.title: Comic Con Astana 2026: How Kazakhstan Turns Pop Culture into Creative Industries
World.content:
ASTANA — Comic Con Astana 2026 drew more than 76,000 visitors from 40 countries over four days, underscoring the growing popularity of pop culture in Kazakhstan and the festival’s expanding international profile.

Held from Aug. 6 to 9, the festival brought together fans of films, TV series, comics, gaming and cosplay across two venues: Barys Arena and Alau Ice Palace. The program included meetings with international stars, Q&A sessions, an international cosplay competition with a 20 million tenge ($42,930) prize pool, gaming tournaments, workshops and other activities.

This year’s international headliners included “Game of Thrones” star Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, “Peaky Blinders” actor Paul Anderson, and “One Piece” stars Iñaki Godoy and Taz Skylar.

International stars discover Kazakhstan

For several international guests, Comic Con Astana marked their first visit to Kazakhstan.

Mexican actor Iñaki Godoy, known for playing Monkey D. Luffy in Netflix’s “One Piece” adaptation, shared his first impressions of Astana.

Godoy said he was particularly impressed by Astana’s distinctive architecture, mentioning the Nur Alem pavilion at EXPO and Khan Shatyr.

“I haven’t seen much of Astana yet. But when I went into one of the shopping malls, I saw this huge sphere right next to it. I also got to see the giant tent. It’s really impressive. I’d love to see even more interesting places,” the actor said.

During his Q&A session, Godoy also spoke about working on One Piece and said he would like to see Kazakhstan become one of the filming locations for the series. He noted that some storylines in One Piece feature nomadic themes, which could make Kazakhstan an interesting location for future productions.

“I would really love to come back here, and I would really love to film here,” Godoy said.

British actor Paul Anderson, known for his role as Arthur Shelby in “Peaky Blinders”, also visited Kazakhstan for the first time.

“I was really impressed when we drove in from the airport to the hotel. What I saw outside the window… I honestly thought I’d landed in Los Angeles,” Anderson said.

One of the festival’s main headliners was Danish actor Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, internationally known for playing Jaime Lannister in “Game of Thrones”.

His visit to Kazakhstan was also his first.

“This is my first visit to Kazakhstan, to Astana. I have to say, it’s a very big country. Wonderful food, especially the meat. Today I ate more of it than I have in the last three years,” Coster-Waldau said.

When asked where Kazakhstan might fit into the world of “Game of Thrones”, Coster-Waldau drew a parallel with the two powerful sides of the fictional universe.

“If we’re thinking in “Game of Thrones” categories, Kazakhstan would probably be kind of in the middle between two very powerful neighbours. So it would kinda be somewhere between the Lannisters and the Dothraki lands, like very diplomatic. And making each side believe that they are their best friends,” he said.

Coster-Waldau also expressed interest in discovering Kazakh cinema and praised the landscapes of the Mangystau region. His conversation with fans also touched on artificial intelligence, a technology that is increasingly becoming part of Kazakhstan’s creative landscape.

When asked about the use of AI in filmmaking, Coster-Waldau said he sees it primarily as a tool rather than a replacement for human creativity.

“I think AI can be used as a tool, and it should be used as a tool,” the actor said.

At the same time, he stressed that key creative decisions should remain in the hands of artists.

“When we talk about filmmaking, the entire creative process should remain in the hands of the creators, in the hands of artists,” Coster-Waldau said.

That discussion found a practical continuation at Comic Con Astana 2026 with the presentation of “Tengrida: Cyber Steppe”, a Kazakh art film created with AI as one of its production tools.

Tengrida: from a cosplay character to a new universe

The festival hosted the first public screening of a three-minute AI-animated episode titled “Arena,” which introduces a new original fictional universe.

The story follows Tengrida, a young woman who enters a techno-clan arena to fight for justice. In a future where technology has replaced much of human memory and brutal fights have become mass entertainment, she faces a warrior named Kanjar while trying to help people see the truth again.

The character was created by Almaty-based cosplayer Aruzhan Zhunusova, known as Aruvibez. Tengrida’s story began in 2025, when Zhunusova presented the original cosplay character at Comic Con Astana, combining elements of Kazakh national style with a futuristic aesthetic.

According to Zhunusova, the audience’s reaction was the moment she realized the cosplay character could become something much bigger.

“So many people came up to me, took photos and wrote to me. And I realised that I had found some kind of response in people’s hearts. I didn’t want to limit it to just one festival. I wanted to create something much bigger, ” Zhunusova told The Astana Times.

This led to the idea of developing an entire universe around the character.

“In the end, we decided to start with an animated video using AI, as we want to take part in the AI film festival, and then gradually reveal the character and her universe. It could be comics, games, feature films. So I think this is only the beginning,” she said.

Zhunusova describes Tengrida as a “Kazakh warrior from the future” who fights for justice and truth.

The production of “Tengrida: Cyber Steppe” took around four to five months. For the directors, the project was also their first major experience working with AI animation and a fantasy aesthetic. According to Zhunusova, the first two months were spent developing the project’s visual language and experimenting with the technology.

Despite the use of AI, the film was not created with a single automated process. Individual scenes were generated in short fragments, after which the team manually reviewed and approved the material.

“We didn’t generate it all at once. We worked in five-second fragments. Then we approved everything, put it together, edited it and worked on the sound design,” Zhunusova explained.

Zhunusova believes AI does not replace the creative team in the project, but expands its possibilities.

“I believe that if AI is in the hands of a professional, it can be used as a great tool,” she said.

From fan festival to creative industry platform

The festival has steadily expanded its international profile, welcoming stars such as Mads Mikkelsen, Andy Serkis, Pilou Asbæk, Scott Adkins, Esai Morales, Michael Rooker, Sean Gunn, Percy Hynes White and Alexander Kuznetsov over the years.

Its international cosplay competition has also become a major part of the program, attracting participants from more than 20 countries. This year, 64 finalists competed across 20 categories for a total prize pool of 20 million tenge ($42,930).

According to the festival’s General Producer Natalia Abrashkina, Comic Con Astana is increasingly becoming a platform for the development of the creative industries.

“Comic Con Astana is much more than a festival. It is an international platform that brings the industry together, creates new opportunities for talented people and contributes to the development of Kazakhstan’s creative economy,” Abrashkina said.

She stressed that the festival aims not only to attract international stars, but also to promote Kazakh authors, artists, cosplayers and content creators internationally.

The story of Tengrida offers one example of this shift. A character created for a cosplay competition has, within a year, evolved into a screen project using AI and the foundation for a potential universe that could eventually extend beyond animation into comics, games and film.

For Comic Con Astana, that trajectory points to a broader evolution: from bringing global pop culture to Kazakhstan to giving local creators a platform to build stories and intellectual properties of their own.

World.title: Abai’s Legacy Endures as Nearly 19,000 Kazakh Citizens Carry His Name
World.content:
ALMATY – Nearly 19,000 people in Kazakhstan bear the name Abai, according to the Bureau of National Statistics, as the country marks Abai Day on Aug. 10, commemorating the 181st anniversary of the birth of Abai Kunanbayev, who was born in 1845. The figures highlight how the name of the country’s renowned poet, philosopher and thinker continues to resonate across generations.

A total of 18,961 people in Kazakhstan are named Abai. The largest number live in Astana, with 2,186 people, followed by the Turkistan Region with 2,008 and Almaty with 1,740.

The name remains in use among younger generations. During the first half of 2026 alone, 91 newborns were given the name Abai. Although traditionally regarded as a male name, national statistics also record nine women named Abai.

The oldest Kazakhstan resident with the name was born in 1932, while the largest age group is people aged 30–34, numbering 3,267. The name is also reflected in Kazakhstan’s geography. One region, one city, three districts and 26 villages are named after Abai.

Abai’s legacy in national identity

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, in his message marking Abai Day, described the poet’s intellectual and creative heritage as an important part of Kazakhstan’s cultural legacy. He also linked Abai’s ideas about knowledge, diligence, responsibility and unity to contemporary efforts to strengthen social values and national identity.

Abai’s influence has also extended beyond the country’s borders. Monuments dedicated to the poet have been erected in more than 20 cities, including Beijing, Budapest, Istanbul, Moscow, Tashkent, Baku, Tehran and Vitebsk.

In 2016, monuments were unveiled in Cairo and Rennes, France, further expanding the international presence of the Kazakh thinker. In 2021, President Tokayev took part in the opening of a 2.2-metre monument to Abai in Seoul during his official visit to South Korea.

Abai’s international recognition also has a longer history. UNESCO declared 1995 the Year of Abai to mark the 150th anniversary of his birth, placing his literary and philosophical legacy within a broader international cultural context.

For Kazakhstan, the continued spread of the name Abai, from newborn children to towns and cities and monuments abroad, reflects how a historical figure has become part of both the country’s cultural memory and its contemporary identity.

World.title: Kazakhstan Emerges as Firebird AI Market With Data Center Valley Project in Ekibastuz
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has emerged as the second market for US-based AI infrastructure company Firebird, which is developing a 125-megawatt computing facility in Ekibastuz as part of the country’s broader effort to build domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure and attract a larger share of the global AI economy.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev announced the development during the official opening of the first phase of Firebird’s AI campus in Hrazdan, Armenia, on Aug. 8. The event brought together Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang, NVIDIA Vice President Rev Lebaredian, US government representatives, technology companies, investors and industry experts.

Firebird’s Armenian facility is described as the region’s largest operational AI factory based on NVIDIA’s DSX architecture. The company plans to expand its Armenian infrastructure to more than 70,000 NVIDIA Rubin and Blackwell GPUs and 300 MW of computing capacity by the end of 2027.

Kazakhstan is becoming the company’s second major market. In Ekibastuz, Firebird, together with Kazakhtelecom as project operator, is developing the Data Center Valley, with an initial capacity of 125 MW.

The project has received the necessary approvals from the Kazakh government as well as an export authorization from the US Bureau of Industry and Security for the supply of relevant technologies.

Kazakhstan targets global AI infrastructure market

Huang highlighted Kazakhstan alongside Armenia as part of Firebird’s expanding infrastructure network.

“Together with Firebird, we are building AI infrastructure in Armenia and Kazakhstan that will provide researchers, startups and industry with the computing foundation to develop artificial intelligence within their countries, attract international innovators and participate in the global AI economy,” Huang said.

According to Madiyev, the project forms part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop domestic computing capacity rather than rely exclusively on external infrastructure.

“Kazakhstan has the necessary energy base, territory and developed digital ecosystem to host large computing capacities. Our task is not only to attract global technology partners, but also to create a complete environment within the country for the development of artificial intelligence, research, startups and new digital services,” he said.

The Data Center Valley builds on plans announced earlier this year to develop a large-scale computing hub in Ekibastuz. Kazakhstan has been discussing the project with major international technology and investment companies, including Microsoft, OpenAI, G42 and Mubadala. The project has been envisioned as capable of eventually scaling to up to one gigawatt of computing capacity and attracting around $30 billion in investment.

Why Ekibastuz matters

Kazakhstan’s energy resources therefore provide one of the main potential advantages for developing large computing facilities. At the same time, the government is seeking to upgrade the digital infrastructure needed to connect these facilities to international markets.

One such project is the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable, which is being built between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. The new submarine connection is expected to establish an additional high-speed data route toward Europe, strengthening the infrastructure supporting international cloud and AI services.

Together, the projects point to a broader approach in which Kazakhstan is attempting to develop several layers of an AI ecosystem simultaneously: electricity and data centers on one side, international connectivity and computing capacity on the other, and regulation, talent and startups to build applications on top of that infrastructure.

Firebird plans to continue expanding internationally and aims to bring its total global AI infrastructure capacity to 2 gigawatts across Armenia, Kazakhstan and other markets by the end of 2028.

The company has also announced plans for NVIDIA to invest in Firebird, while CoreWeave has previously invested in the company. The new funding is expected to support the accelerated development of Firebird’s global AI infrastructure.

World.title: AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov on How AIFC is Preparing for Next Era of Finance
World.content:
ASTANA — When Renat Bekturov first joined what would become the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), the institution existed only as an idea.
