World.title: Armenian Catholicos Garegin II attends first hearing in criminal trial
World.content:
Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

A court in Armenia‘s Armavir region has begun hearing the criminal case against the Catholicos of All Armenians and six bishops who serve on the Supreme Spiritual Council. Garegin II attended the hearing in person.

Clergy members and politicians gathered outside the courthouse. Lawmakers from the opposition Armenia Alliance and I Have Honour Alliance left parliament during the afternoon and travelled to Etchmiadzin to show their support for the Catholicos. Dozens of worshippers also gathered outside, periodically chanting “Your Holiness” and singing traditional Armenian church hymns (sharakans).

Prosecutors accuse the Catholicos and the senior clergy of obstructing the enforcement of a court ruling.

Garegin II removed Bishop Gevorg Saroyan, head of the Masyatsotn Diocese, from his post. Saroyan is one of the senior clerics who joined Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s campaign to “reform the Church”. The bishop challenged his dismissal in court. The court ordered his temporary reinstatement as head of the diocese until it reaches a final decision in the case. However, before the court could rule on the merits, the Supreme Spiritual Council, led by the Catholicos, also defrocked him. The council argued that the courts have no jurisdiction over the Church’s internal affairs.

Lawyer Ara Zohrabyan says the Catholicos faces criminal prosecution for carrying out his “ecclesiastical and canonical duties”.

He argues that state interference in the Catholicos’s decisions violates the principle of Church autonomy, the constitutional relationship between the state and the Church, and freedom of religion.

“In this criminal case, the court will examine not only the charges against specific individuals, but also another fundamental question: whether the secular authorities can interfere in the internal life of the Church and criminalise the exercise of the canonical authority of the Catholicos of All Armenians,” the lawyer said.

The trial comes after tensions between the government and the Church steadily escalated.

About a year ago, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He first argued that Garegin II could not lead the Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and had a daughter. He later accused the Catholicos of having links to foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party has also included the removal of the “de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Members of the ruling party accuse the Church of interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy. The parliamentary opposition rejects that claim. Opposition lawmakers argue that it is the government that is unlawfully interfering in the Church’s affairs.

First hearing ends after 30 minutes as judge recuses himself

Shortly after the hearing began, Judge Hakob Manukyan announced that part of the proceedings would take place behind closed doors because they would involve “personal information”. He said the information concerned both himself and the Catholicos’s lawyer.

“A few minutes later, lawyer Ara Zohrabyan told journalists: “The judge has recused himself. He has withdrawn from hearing this case.”

According to Zohrabyan, the judge said he had once granted him his licence to practise law, which could “raise doubts about his impartiality”. Zohrabyan said he did not believe this constituted valid grounds for recusal.

“However, he refused to take part in this disgraceful trial. The very fact that the Catholicos is standing trial is deeply troubling. The case will now go to another judge.”

After the hearing, the Catholicos of All Armenians and his supporters headed to the cathedral to attend a church service and pray together.

Garegin II: “The authorities are trying to bring the Church under their control”

After the service, the Catholicos addressed those gathered outside the cathedral. He said the authorities were taking steps to undermine the Church’s authority, restrict its autonomy and bring it under their control.

“The authorities are persecuting the Church and the clergy. They have arrested and restricted the freedom of a number of clergymen, benefactors and other patriotic individuals through unlawful and fabricated criminal cases,” he said.

The Catholicos dismissed the charges against himself and the six clergymen as groundless.

“We remain steadfast in our faith and determination to defend our rights, which are guaranteed both by our country’s Constitution and by the fundamental principles of international law.”

Opposition declares a “day of shame”

Marianna Gakhramanyan, an MP from the opposition I Have Honour Alliance, said:

“Today is a day of shame. The Catholicos of All Armenians, our spiritual father and the head of our Church, is standing trial in Etchmiadzin. It is shameful and unprecedented. This is an attack not only on the independence of the Armenian Apostolic Church but also on Armenia’s Constitution, which clearly states that the political authorities have no right to interfere in the affairs of the Church and that the Church is separate from the state.”

“Who is defending the Church – us or you?” asks ruling party MP

Commenting on opposition lawmakers who came to support the Catholicos, Civil Contract MP Artur Hovhannisyan said:

“The Church has begun interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy.”

He also referred to the allegations that the Catholicos had violated his vow of celibacy:

“We are the ones standing with the Church. We are the ones defending the Church. You are defending clergymen who broke their vow of celibacy, who engage in politics and use religion and the Church to protect themselves from the consequences of breaking that vow and taking part in politics. Anyone who has broken the vow of celibacy should leave the Church.”

The ruling Civil Contract party’s election manifesto also outlines plans to reform the Church. Under the proposal, the “de facto head of the Church”, as Pashinyan’s team refers to the Catholicos, should leave office. The plan calls for the election of a locum tenens, the adoption of a new Church charter containing “mechanisms to preserve centuries-old traditions”, and, ultimately, the election of a new Catholicos.

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan told Reuters:

“Pashinyan has come to see the Church as a political threat and as an institution capable of supporting the opposition and various political parties in their efforts to gain power.

“The case against the clergy fits into a broader pattern of selective justice pursued by Pashinyan’s government, under which leading opposition figures have been arrested and some of their property has been confiscated by the state.”

Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

World.title: Azerbaijan FM in Kyiv: gas for Ukraine, visit to Irpin, Ukrainian drones
World.content:
Azerbaijani FM visits Ukraine

Azerbaijan‘s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov paid an official visit to Ukraine on 6 August.

It was the first visit by an Azerbaijani foreign minister to Kyiv since the start of Russia‘s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Bayramov began his visit with a trip to Irpin, where he viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones and laid a wreath at a memorial to fallen defenders at Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.

He also held meetings with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, President Volodymyr Zelensky, Head of the Presidential Office Andriy Yermak, Defence Intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov and National Security and Defence Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

One of the most notable announcements was Azerbaijan’s stated willingness to supply Ukraine with natural gas if needed.

The two sides also discussed the possible use of Ukraine’s underground gas storage facilities to strengthen regional energy security.

These developments are significant both regionally and internationally, particularly in the context of Azerbaijan’s relations with Russia.

In mid-July, Bayramov met Sergei Lavrov in Moscow and said the “difficult period” in bilateral relations was over and that ties had been fully normalised. A few weeks later, in Kyiv, he reaffirmed Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, while also signalling Baku’s interest in expanding energy cooperation.

The visit illustrates Baku’s multi-vector foreign policy. While maintaining dialogue with Russia, Azerbaijan has continued to provide humanitarian assistance to Ukraine and has expressed its readiness to support the country in the energy sector if required.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

Symbolic and practical significance of the Irpin visit

Irpin was one of the towns where the Russian advance on Kyiv was halted in 2022. Hundreds of civilians were killed during the fighting, and more than 70% of the town’s housing stock was destroyed.

Azerbaijan has contributed to Irpin’s reconstruction.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

The minister laid flowers at the bust of academician Zarifa Aliyeva in the park named after her, and visited the Zarifa Aliyeva Linguistic Lyceum and Irpin Central City Polyclinic, both rebuilt with Azerbaijan’s support. He was also briefed on future reconstruction projects, including plans to restore the town’s House of Culture.

In his statement, Zelensky said Bayramov had visited a school, a hospital and a rehabilitation centre supported by Azerbaijan. The visit to Irpin was seen as a demonstration of humanitarian solidarity with Ukraine, as well as Azerbaijan’s willingness to share its experience in rebuilding territories recovered from occupation.

I received Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, @Bayramov_Jeyhun. This is the Minister’s first visit to Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. He began his visit in Irpin, where he visited a school, a hospital, and a rehabilitation center supported by… pic.twitter.com/7HTLIaz3EF — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) August 6, 2026

The visit to a town devastated by Russian forces, together with Bayramov’s review of reconstruction efforts and Azerbaijan’s continued support, was seen as underscoring Baku’s intention to reaffirm its longstanding position despite the “normalisation” of relations with Moscow, particularly its commitment to the principle of territorial integrity.

Following the official welcoming ceremony at the Foreign Ministry, Bayramov and Sybiha viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones. They then laid a wreath at the Memorial to the Fallen Defenders of Ukraine and observed a moment of silence in their honour.

Meetings and gas supply pledge

During expanded talks with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, the two sides discussed their strategic partnership, trade, energy, transport, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Bayramov reiterated the need for an early end to the fighting and a diplomatic settlement based on international law, while reaffirming Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

He said Azerbaijan’s total humanitarian assistance to Ukraine had exceeded 50 million US dollars. Bayramov also highlighted reconstruction projects in Irpin and rehabilitation programmes for children.

During his meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the discussions focused on Russian attacks, the situation in the Black Sea, the disruption of grain export routes, defence cooperation, and cooperation in the energy, oil and gas, and agricultural sectors.

Zelensky thanked Azerbaijan for its energy and humanitarian assistance, as well as for maintaining constructive dialogue. Bayramov, in turn, spoke about the post-conflict situation in the South Caucasus and reconstruction efforts in the territories regained by Azerbaijan.

As part of his official visit to Ukraine 🇺🇦, FM of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 @Bayramov_Jeyhun visited the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Kyiv.



The Minister met with the Embassy staff and received a comprehensive briefing on the Mission’s activities. pic.twitter.com/UPqN5Hn9rx — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

At a joint press conference, particular attention was drawn to Bayramov’s remarks on possible gas supplies: “If the need arises, we will be ready to supply gas to our friendly Ukraine.”

He highlighted SOCAR’s long-standing presence on the Ukrainian market, as well as the importance of Ukraine’s underground gas storage system – the largest in Europe – for regional energy security.

The statement can be seen as signalling Azerbaijan’s willingness to contribute to the diversification of Ukraine’s energy supplies, while also supporting alternative routes for Caspian gas exports to Europe. Against the backdrop of Russia’s strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Ukraine, Baku’s offer also underscores the importance of competition and diversification in the energy sector.

During meetings with Kyrylo Budanov and Ihor Klymenko, the sides also discussed regional and international security, as well as prospects for energy cooperation. They reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of state sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognised borders.

Expert: “Azerbaijan will continue to provide Ukraine with political, economic and humanitarian support”

lkhan Shahinoglu, head of the Atlas Research Centre and a political commentator considered close to the Azerbaijani authorities, wrote that the visit is being closely watched by Russia:

The Kremlin will closely monitor Jeyhun Bayramov’s meetings in Kyiv. Azerbaijan’s partnership with any country is an exclusive sovereign right, and no other state has the right to interfere in that process.

At the same time, Russia, which is waging a war of conquest against Ukraine, closely watches those who cooperate with Kyiv. President Ilham Aliyev‘s response to the same question from Ukrainian journalist Gordon, asked at the Shusha Global Media Forum two years in a row – that ‘Ukraine should not reconcile itself to occupation’ – angered chauvinistic circles in Russia. They believe Azerbaijan should accept the annexation of Crimea and the occupation of Ukrainian territories.

Just as Jeyhun Bayramov visited Moscow some time ago, he has now travelled to Kyiv. Ukraine is Azerbaijan’s partner, and Baku will continue to provide it with political, economic and humanitarian support.”

World.title: Giga Avaliani case: Two more arrested 10 months after Georgian teacher’s murder
World.content:
Two more arrested in Giga Avaliani murder case

Two more suspects have been identified in the high-profile murder case of a 28-year-old teacher in Georgia. On 5 August 2026, two teenage girls – Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili – were arrested.

Giga Avaliani, a mathematics teacher, was killed in October 2025. Five people have already been convicted over his murder, while the trial of a sixth defendant is still under way. With the arrest of the two girls, the total number of suspects in the case has risen to eight – all of them minors.

The arrests of Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili, after several convictions had already been secured, mark an unexpected and significant development in the Giga Avaliani case.

Nia Imnadze was one of Giga Avaliani’s former students and the girlfriend of the principal defendant, Aleksandre Gabashvili. Prosecutors accuse her of incitement to commit the crime.

According to local media, Anastasia Beruashvili is a friend of both Nia Imnadze and another convicted defendant, Giorgi Rikadze. She has been charged with failing to report the crime.

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics tutor, was returning home late on 1 October 2025 when he was attacked outside his apartment building. He fell into a coma following the assault and died on 24 October without regaining consciousness. Investigators say the attack was motivated by jealousy and what they describe as “unwanted communication with a girl”. The defendants have given a similar account. According to their version of events, Avaliani sent sexually explicit messages to his student Nia Imnadze, who told her boyfriend, prompting him to confront the teacher. Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, rejects that account. She says Nia had been skipping lessons and that Avaliani informed the girl’s mother, angering the student. According to Kupatadze, the attack was planned afterwards.

The Giga Avaliani case has become one of Georgia’s most high-profile criminal cases in recent years. Much of the public attention surrounding it has been driven by Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, who campaigned for what she said should be a thorough and impartial investigation. Her efforts also helped generate significant public pressure over the handling of the case.

From the outset, Kupatadze maintained that Nia Imnadze bore primary responsibility for what had happened and repeatedly called for her arrest. The recent detention of the two girls has therefore raised new questions.

But the key question remains: if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, why were the two girls not arrested earlier? Was their detention the result of new evidence, or did it come only after sustained public pressure and Eka Kupatadze’s campaign?

Detention of two girls

Both girls were arrested late on the night of 5 August, in what appeared to be coordinated operations. News of the arrests first emerged through a video of Nia Imnadze’s detention, which was released by her lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili.

The footage is deeply distressing. It shows a large number of police officers arriving at Nia’s home. Her mother, visibly distressed, pounds on the front door, shouting: “Come in, all of you!”, “Maniacs!”, “Murderers!”, “Do you know that Niako is innocent?!”

The girl’s father, meanwhile, tells the police: “You are going to make me do something the whole of Georgia will be talking about. If you treat my child so unjustly, I will do it.”

Police officers try to calm the distraught parents.

“Why are you taking my child? On what grounds? What does the court order say?!” the mother asks.

“The lawyer has reviewed the court order,” one of the officers replies.

“Giorgi, on what grounds are they arresting her?” the mother asks the lawyer.

“On the basis of a court order containing only formal wording, nothing specific,” the lawyer replies.

Nia sits in the hallway on a sofa, curled up with her face buried in her hands. The video is being filmed by her lawyer, who occasionally strokes her hair.

Shortly after the video was released, reports began circulating on social media that the second girl, Anastasia Beruashvili, had also been detained. No footage of her arrest was made public, but the Ministry of Internal Affairs later confirmed that she had been taken into custody.

During her arrest, Nia Imnadze became unwell and was taken to hospital, where she spent the night. On 6 August, she was transferred to a pre-trial detention centre. Anastasia Beruashvili was also taken there.

Minors charged in Giga Avaliani's murder case in Georgia – read more Five people have already been convicted in connection with Giga Avaliani’s murder: Aleksandre Gabashvili – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. He was the principal defendant in the case and was found guilty of organising a group assault and intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm as part of a group, resulting in the victim’s death. Giorgi Rikadze – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. A friend of Aleksandre Gabashvili, he was convicted on the same charges. Demetere Chikovani – sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was convicted of attempted intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm in the Avaliani case, as well as organising group violence in connection with the case and four other incidents. Ani Naskidashvili – sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. She was found guilty of failing to report a particularly serious crime. Another minor – sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He was convicted of giving false testimony. The nature of the false statements has not been disclosed. His case was heard behind closed doors, lawyers involved in the proceedings are bound by a non-disclosure order, and the teenager’s parents have declined to speak to the media. According to TV Pirveli, the boy is named Luka Klatkin. Giorgi Malania – arrested in July 2026 and charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. Malania is the son of a former senior Interior Ministry official, who served as deputy interior minister between 2016 and 2019. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered.

Eka Kupatadze’s reaction

“Georgia has won another battle against the killers of a healthy, innocent and talented young man – Giga Avaliani!” Eka Kupatadze said in response to the girls’ arrests.

Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Dying woman urges PM to overturn 'cruel' law to save others suffering
World.content:
As she prepares to die tomorrow using voluntary assisted dying (VAD), Sandra Sarantou has one final request for the prime minister.

She is urging the nation's leaders to change a law that is limiting some Australians' access to VAD.

Sue died before she could access assisted dying Despite voluntary assisted dying being legal in Victoria, many regional patients are not getting the same end-of-life care.

Nine weeks ago, the 58-year-old Adelaide woman was diagnosed with the same aggressive lung cancer her father died from.

Medication is no longer effective for her nerve pain, nausea and dizziness. Having watched her father endure a long and painful death, before VAD was legal around the country, Ms Sarantou is "grateful" to be ending her life on her terms.

But she said she was shocked to learn a provision in the Commonwealth Criminal Code means some Australians are effectively denied access because of where they live.

"It's even a struggle just to move from one end from the house to another … for those people to travel hours to possibly see a doctor and not get the chance for VAD is just horrific," she told ABC News.

VAD is legal in every Australian jurisdiction except the Northern Territory, which is expected to pass legislation allowing it this month.

Other state laws do allow the use of telehealth for some discussions about VAD, particularly where patients are too ill to travel or live remotely.

But a provision in the Commonwealth Criminal Code, intended to outlaw the use of "carriage services" to "incite suicide", has been interpreted to apply to doctors advising patients about VAD and has overridden those state provisions.

That means doctors cannot use phone, email, internet or video to advise patients about accessing VAD medication.

Workforce shortages in rural and remote areas have meant some dying people have been forced to travel long distances to make those appointments. For some that has not been possible and they have missed out.

Families of people who wanted to access VAD but died before completing the process say telehealth consultations could have spared them unnecessary suffering.

Pressure on the prime minister

Federal Independent Kate Chaney will today attempt to bring on debate of her private members bill, which would see the Commonwealth Criminal Code amended.

Greens Senator Sarah Hanson Young will introduce a similar bill to the Upper House this month. Without government support, both bills may languish.

WA MP Kate Chaney has a private member's bill to allow the use of telehealth for VAD consultations. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

There is also a push within Labor's rank and file for change. Last month, delegates to Labor's National Conference voted to amend the party's platform, supporting the use of telehealth for end-of-life care.

Delegates also enshrined a commitment to give Labor MPs and senators a conscience vote on all VAD issues.

Albanese under pressure over telehealth for VAD At the recent Labor conference, only one issue was contested on the floor: support for the use of telehealth in voluntary assisted dying care.

Labor sources have said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese remains personally opposed to allowing telehealth for VAD, and his opposition may prove crucial to the fate of any legislative change.

He supports voluntary assisted dying but has argued face-to-face consultations are an important way to ensure vulnerable patients are not taken advantage of.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has also expressed reservations and raised concerns about the risk of elder abuse if telehealth was allowed.

Several Labor MPs have told the ABC they are confident the law will eventually change but that it will require more time and conversations to convince the prime minister.

Sandra Sarantou had a career as a paramedic, often working in rural areas of South Australia. (Supplied: Sandra Sarantou)

Ms Sarantou, who worked as a paramedic for 13 years and treated patients in rural areas, felt "guilty" she could access VAD while others could not.

"Their time is ticking and they have to suffer. It's cruel, it's not fair," she said.

She is pleading with the Albanese government to amend the criminal code.

"Please change these laws, make it fair and available for everyone despite where they are living."

Doctor: 'It's absolutely an equity issue'

Advocacy group, Go Gentle's latest "State of VAD report" suggested there was strong demand for the care outside cities, with 39 per cent of applicants in 2024-25 living in rural, regional and remote areas.

General practitioner Scott Lewis has travelled 3,000 kilometres across South Australia in the past fortnight alone to see people seeking voluntary assisted dying.

South Australian GP Dr Scott Lewis flies to regional areas of the state to see patients, including those who want to access voluntary assisted dying. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Dr Lewis, who flies his own plane to reach rural patients, said he saw about two new VAD patients a week.

He said workforce shortages and the lack of Medicare funding were preventing more rural doctors from offering VAD care.

"[Rural and remote] doctors are so busy as it is, that they simply haven't had the time or thought to extend their practice into voluntary assisted dying," he said.

"I don't make much money from it, to be blunt."

He told ABC News he had experienced "a sense of failure" knowing patients have missed out on VAD due to their isolation.

"To see the hurt in family members who've had to see their loved ones suffer and … come so close to being approved for voluntary assisted dying but not quite get there … it's hard at times."

A tricky issue

Sydney University Law Health expert Dr Christopher Rudge said he believed telehealth could be allowed without weakening overall protections.

"Across the country the states have very rigorous and documented process for permitting someone to undergo a VAD procedure, and all of those would apply whether it's by telehealth or any other circumstance," he said.

Dr Christopher Rudge, of the University of Sydney Law School. (Supplied)

"My understanding is that the telehealth communications would occur at an early stage of the process but that at some stage, the witnessing and some other processes, would presumably need to occur in an environment where doctors are present."

Generally, under state laws, people applying for VAD must have been diagnosed with a terminal illness and facing death within a year.

They must attend face-to-face medical appointments so that two independent, trained practitioners can assess whether they are eligible, acting voluntarily and capable of making their own decisions.

The patient must provide a written request for VAD, which has to be witnessed by independent adults — not family members.

A co-ordinating practitioner makes a final declaration and a state board — or oversight body — provides final approval.

Dr Rudge said he was "sympathetic" with concerns that telehealth could replace face-to-face consults, but did not think that would be a consequence of changes to the Commonwealth Criminal Code.

"In circumstances where informed consent is not clear, the in-person consultation is the best place for those questions to be answered. And so, I can understand why people could be concerned," he said.

Laughter and legacy

For Sandra Sarantou, the hardest part of preparing for VAD is knowing that she has to say goodbye to her son.

But, she said they had been "completely open" about the VAD process and had found comfort in black humour.

"We had the idea to put my ashes into a big party cracker … and then everybody has got a bit of my ashes," Ms Sarantou laughed.

World.title: Good Things festival returns in 2026 with big headliner
World.content:
Having cemented its status as an annual summer festival staple, Good Things has announced its return this December, boasting a line-up packed with metal, punk, emo, rock and more.

The event's seventh edition once again spans a range of genres and eras, bringing together both local and international acts across multiple stages. Let's dive in, shall we?

Who's topping the bill?

Arguably the defining band of nu-metal, Limp Bizkit are back in the country for the first time since headlining Good Things and sideshows back in 2023.

Emerging in the late '90s with a riotous fusion of rock, metal and rap, Limp Bizkit's angsty anthems were a polarising force but became a blockbuster success with teenage millennials.

Fronted by Fred Durst, songs like Nookie, Break Stuff, Rollin, and Mission: Impossible 2 theme Take A Look Around, were inescapable in the 2000s.

Limp Bizkit were also never far from headlines; most famously, their 2001 performance at the Sydney Big Day where 16-year-old Jessica Michalik died.

'I had her hand, then I let it go': the Big Day Out loses its innocence A confluence of factors during Limp Bizkit's 2001 Sydney performance led to the death of 16-year-old Jessica Michalik. Eighteen years later, the anger and the hurt remain.

At 2012's Soundwave festival, the band's first Australian dates in 11 years, Durst dedicated their performance to Jessica and was joined by her father, George Michalik.

Heavy fans will be thrilled to experience Spiritbox. Fronted by Courtney LaPlante, a vocalist capable of ethereal melodies and visceral screams, the Canadian metal group boldly mixed genre on their breakout 2020 debut album Eternal Blue.

Between that record and last year's acclaimed follow-up, Tsunami Sea, Spiritbox have been feted in just about every way that still matters: magazine covers, festival billings, a ferociously dedicated fanbase and multiple nominations at Canada's Juno music awards.

This marks Spiritbox's second time touring Australia, following their 2023 debut as part of Knotfest. (Supplied: Alexander Bemis)

Simple Plan, Montreal's premiere pop-punk exports and a staple of 2000s, are also at the top of the bill. Nearly 30 years after forming, the band still largely consists of the same high school friends, who've released six albums much loved by anyone who went through an emo phase in the 2000s.

Alexisonfire, yet another celebrated Canadian act, will mark the 20th anniversary of Crisis, their influential third album of bracing post-hardcore, by performing the record in full.

Similarly, Swedish punk group Millencolin will perform their 2000 album Pennybridge Pioneers — an international hit evidenced by its songs featuring in the blockbuster Tony Hawk's Pro Skater video games, as well as Penguins & Polarbears cracking triple j's Hottest 100.

What about Aussie acts?

The biggest homegrown heavy name is resilient metalcore crew Polaris, who are beginning work on new material to follow their first three ARIA-nominated albums.

Grinspoon, who've been touring rock favourites since the late '90s, are sure to draw big sing-alongs. Their addition follows frontman Phil Jamieson cancelling his current tour after a serious back injury sustained mid-show.

You've also got Speed, the J Award-winning crew who put Western Sydney's hardcore scene on international radars with their community-driven live shows.

Loading Instagram content

Plus, Slowly Slowly, who've hopped from emo-rock to pop-punk and even glossy electro-pop, Brisbane four-piece Headwreck and the Choirboys.

Best known for their 1987 pub rock hit Run To Paradise, the Choirboys fill a legacy slot that has become Good Things tradition, occupied in previous years by James Reyne and Dragon.

Who else is playing?

Bad Religion, pioneers of a melodic take on hardcore that helped draft the blueprint that '90s acts like Green Day and The Offspring drafted from, are billed to celebrate their "45 + 1 year anniversary."

The All-American Rejects will bring their alt-rock and pop--punk songbook to Australia for the first time in over 17 years, after having to pull out of last year's Good Things festival.

There's also The Devil Wears Prada, the Ohio metal group who, like the popular 2006 movie, take their name from the 2003 bestselling novel.

Industrial metal trailblazers Ministry will make Good Things the Australian stop of their global farewell tour, ending a 45-year career.

Ringleader Al Jourgensen has stated he's "f***ing done" after Ministry's final live shows and upcoming 17th album Hate To Go (Take Out or Delivery). (Supplied: Derick Smith)

Other Good Things acts include Christian nu-metal group P.O.D, Mudvanye and Hellyah vocalist Chad Gray; Bilmuri, aka US singer-songwriter John Franck; punk rock mainstays MxPx and Welsh pop-punk band Neck Deep.

Plus, there's German trio Future Palace; young internet sensation ivri; dynamic singer-drummer Kami Kehoe; and Voice of Baceprot, an all-female Muslim Indonesian heavy metal trio.

Here's the full Good Things line-up so far:

Limp Bizkit, Simple Plan, Spiritbox, Polaris, The All-American Rejects, Bad Religion, Alexisonfire, Grinspoon, Millencolin, Ministry, Bilmuri, Chad Gray, MxPx, Neck Deep, Speed, Slowly Slowly, P.O.D., The Devil Wears Prada, Choirboys, All Them Witches, The Black Queen, Future Palace, Headwreck, The Home Team, House of Protection, ivri, Kami Kehoe, Locked Shut, LØLØ, Vianova, Voice Of Baceprot

Here are the dates, and the festival is once again welcoming younger moshers:

Fri 4 December — Flemington Racecourse: Melbourne, Wurundjeri Woi Worrong Land, VIC (15+)

Sat 5 December — Sydney Showgrounds: Sydney, Gadigal Land, NSW (16+)

Sun 6 December — Brisbane Showgrounds: Brisbane, Turrbal Jagera Land, QLD (16+)

Tickets are on sale from 10am AEST, Thursday August 20. You'll find more info at the Good Things website.

World.title: Potholes force cars off Calder Freeway as Victorian road anger rises
World.content:
More drivers have been left stranded after their vehicles were damaged by a pothole on a major Victorian freeway this morning.

Macedon Ranges resident John told ABC Central Victoria, at least seven cars with damaged tyres were lined up on the side of the Calder Freeway between Gisborne and Sunbury about 6.30am.

He said another three were pulled over on the off-ramp.

"There were people changing tyres on the side of the road; one young lady was in tears because she didn't know what to do," he said.

" The same pothole was fixed one week ago. Clearly they're not fixing them adequately. "

He lanes have been closed due to road damage on the freeway between Kyneton and Sunbury for two weeks.

"They're just filling gaps, they're not actually going to the cause of the problem," he said.

"We just keep blaming the weather without proper remediation."

A spokesperson from the Department of Transport couldn't confirm how many vehicles had been affected.

The right lane of the freeway remains closed city-bound near Mundy Road, with patching works under way.

Elsewhere in central Victoria, Johnny Ravet from Seymour Tyre and Mechanical told ABC Statewide Mornings there were six cars in his workshop all with pothole damage.

"Just last week we had one, an Audi, travelling to Nagambie, hit a pothole and no spare tyre so it was towed in," he said.

"That rim [cost] $4000 before we even put a tyre on it."

This morning's traffic hazard on the Calder Freeway follows a similar problem on the Princes Freeway at Bunyip, east of Melbourne yesterday where about 30 cars suffered tyre damage by hitting a pothole that was hard to see in the rain.

World.title: Calvary considers new Launceston hospital at aged care site
World.content:
A Catholic health care provider has confirmed it is considering building a new private hospital in Tasmania's north, two years after it cancelled plans for a $130 million development.

Calvary Health Care said it was investigating redeveloping its Sandhill Residential Aged Care site in South Launceston to include a new hospital.

A spokesperson said the organisation had submitted a land use strategy for the site and was exploring a rezoning application to be considered by the Launceston City Council.

It is understood the existing aged care facilities would be retained.

The news has been welcomed by some healthcare advocates, who have become increasingly concerned by the aging state of Calvary's two Launceston hospitals, St Luke's and St Vincent's.

Micro tears found in hospital floor The shutdown of Calvary St Luke's Hospital will affect 40 planned surgeries this week, with 22 of those reallocated to nearby St Vincent's Hospital.

Last year, Calvary was forced to close three surgical operating theatres at St Luke's hospital after rips were found in the flooring.

While modular theatres were set up and patients diverted to St Vincent's hospital, some have warned it is also aging.

"So the real risk here then is that that infrastructure fails," Australian Medical Association Tasmania spokesperson Dr Michael Lumsden-Steel said.

" And that would effectively mean that there'd be no major elective surgery happening in Launceston in a private hospital. "

Dr Michael Lumsden-Steel says a new private hospital in Launceston is needed. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The Launceston Health Hub's Jerome Muir Wilson said he discussed the idea of a new hospital at the Sandhill site with Calvary Health Care chief executive Damien Bruce when the two met in Launceston yesterday.

"They [Calvary] mentioned they're exploring Sandhill … as an option."

Dr Muir Wilson said while the model may work for some medical or palliative care patients, he said he did not make sense to put a surgical hospital next to an aged care home.

Dr Jerome Muir Wilson says there's room for more than one private hospital in Launceston. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He said having a new private hospital next to the public Launceston General Hospital, which Calvary had been planning in 2024, would be ideal.

"That way, there's no wrong front door if someone goes into an emergency department," he said.

"They can be a public patient one way or a private patient the other way."

A Calvary spokesperson said Launceston-based visiting medical officers had been asked to give feedback on its idea for the Sandhill site, and the organisation's wider clinical services plan, by September 7.

Calvary Health Care is asking Launceston-based visiting medical officers for feedback on the idea. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Budget questioned

When Calvary withdrew from plans for a new private hospital beside the Launceston General Hospital in 2024 just months before work was set to start, it cited "insurmountable budget pressures".

Financial documents show those pressures have continued; Calvary has reported losses since 2019, with deficits of $138 million in 2025, $144 million in 2024, and $377 million in 2023.

But private health insurer St Lukes chief executive Paul Lupo, who also met with Mr Bruce yesterday, said investing in its infrastructure in Launceston would improve Calvary's position in the long run.

"There is no doubt that the assets in the north would be a drain on their financial position," Mr Lupo said.

"So I think if we can get over the hurdle of attracting some capital for them to renew the asset, that will actually make Calvary more sustainable going forward."

Paul Lupo says investment in its infrastructure will improve Calvary's financial position in the long run. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Mr Lupo said he hoped a decision on further Calvary investment in Tasmania's north would be made quickly.

"If I had my way it would have been about five years ago," he said.

"[Their current hospitals have] aging infrastructure and the implication of that is high maintenance, high disruption, a higher cost to maintain.

"Which means that the price that they require for services is greater than it could be if it was in a more modern and well-appointed hospital.

"And what that means is that it's more costly for Tasmanians."

St Luke's is one of two aging private hospitals operated by Calvary in Launceston. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

More clarity on healthcare future

Dr Lumsden-Steel said he hoped the state government was speaking with Calvary about how any future planned investment could also benefit the overwhelmed Launceston General Hospital.

While there are two other private hospital plans in the works for Launceston — with the state government wanting to partner with the private sector on a 250-bed facility and Dr Muir Wilson's Launceston Health Hub pushing for a two-stage development — there has been little progress on these in the past year.

Dr Muir Wilson said there was room for more than one private hospital in the city.

"We need to be able to attract and retain the best doctors. And currently the infrastructure in town is getting old," he said.

" So whether that's our private hospital or Calvary's plan, Launceston just desperately needs a new hospital. "

Along with the two Launceston private hospitals, Calvary Health Care also operates two hospitals in Hobart — Calvary Lenah Valley and St John's in South Hobart.

Its proposal to take over the Hobart Private Hospital following the collapse of Healthscope is being considered by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

World.title: 'Evidence is clear': Players association says brutal schedule behind injuries
World.content:
The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals from the Canadian Open underscore concerns that professional tennis's lengthy calendar and expanded top-level events are increasing injury risks.

The players' advocacy group said it was saddened but not surprised by the absences from the tournament, arguing that reduced recovery time between tournaments was contributing to injuries occurring earlier in the season and becoming more serious.

The Canadian Open men's event in Montreal was hit by the withdrawals of world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, while Carlos Alcaraz was also sidelined with a wrist injury. Hometown favourite Felix Auger-Aliassime also pulled out due to a back injury before his opening match.

On the women's side, defending champion Victoria Mboko, Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova, Emma Raducanu and Jasmine Paolini are also missing the tournament with injuries.

The first quarterfinal matches of the tournament begin later on Tuesday AEST.

Tournament organisers said last month that recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events had become a wider issue for the sport.

PTPA says 'evidence is clear'

The PTPA said it had collected and analysed injury data from more than 30,000 professional matches across all levels of the game over the past eight years in a project launched three years ago with its medical director, Dr Robby Sikka.

'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner pulls out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

"The evidence is clear: the season is too long, recovery time is shrinking, and injuries are occurring earlier and becoming more severe," the PTPA said in a statement posted on social media.

The group said upper-body injuries were up 42 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to its analysis. Arm injuries were up 112 per cent this year compared with the 2025 average, it added.

The ATP expanded seven of its nine Masters 1000 tournaments to 12-day events under its OneVision strategic plan, with 2025 the first season in which the longer format was used across those events.

The PTPA said the change had cut into the time players have to rest, train and travel between tournaments, despite players having voiced concerns about the demands of the schedule for years.

"Short-term commercial interests cannot come at the expense of player health," the association said. "Protecting players isn't just about today's competitors, it is about protecting the future of tennis."

Schedule the players' choice

The ATP has previously said players retain choices over their schedules and that it is working to create incentives for an appropriate number of matches to be played during the season.

Spokespeople for the ATP and WTA Tours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The PTPA called for the sport to take a player-health and data-driven approach to restructuring the calendar.

It said players should have a meaningful role in shaping the schedule, while mandatory tournament commitments should be reduced to allow adequate recovery.

It also urged the ATP to consider reversing the 12-day Masters 1000 format.

Reuters

World.title: Why Trump selling early access to his posts is causing controversy
World.content:
US President Donald Trump knows the world hangs on his every word.

A single social media post about tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or oil production can send stocks, commodities and currencies surging or plunging within seconds.

Now, Trump's media company wants to sell some investors a head start.

Investors have reacted sharply to Donald Trump's announcements on tariffs, sanctions, military action and energy policy. (AP Photo: Ahn Young-joon)

Earlier this month, the Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG), which owns the Truth Social platform, launched a premium data service known as the Truth Social API.

The company says subscribers can receive posts from selected high-profile accounts, including Trump's, within "milliseconds".

According to Reuters, subscriptions cost between $US60,000 ($AU84,930) and $US100,000 ($AU141,550) per month, with several trading firms already signing up.

The move has sparked legal and ethical questions, including whether it is appropriate for a company majority-owned by the sitting US president to profit from selling faster access to his market-moving statements.

But some researchers say there may be an even bigger concern, with data they describe as "extremely suspicious" suggesting some traders could already be receiving information well before Trump's posts appear publicly.

Who is the service for?

To most people, a few milliseconds of early access sounds meaningless.

But modern financial markets increasingly move at computer speed rather than human speed, QUT Digital Media Research Centre associate professor Stephen Harrington says.

Many of the world's biggest trading firms use high-frequency trading, with algorithms buying and selling shares in fractions of a second.

Donald Trump appears on a trader's screen on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. (AP Photo: Richard Drew)

"The only groups that are going to afford to subscribe to that service, and get a genuine advantage out of it, are high-frequency traders," Dr Harrington says.

At least five trading firms have signed up so far, according to The Wall Street Journal.

For companies trading billions of dollars every day, Dr Harrington says a $US100,000 monthly subscription is simply another business expense.

"Getting even the slightest advantage, even when it comes down to just fractions of a second, can be useful."

Does Trump stand to profit?

Trump's family remains the controlling shareholder in Trump Media through a trust, meaning he could benefit financially if the company generates more revenue.

According to the Associated Press, shares in the Truth Social parent company have fallen by 75 per cent since Trump returned to office last year.

The Truth Social platform is owned by Trump Media and Technology Group (TMTG).

Despite Trump's continued use of the platform to announce major policy decisions, Trump Media has continued reporting hundreds of millions of dollars in losses.

"Truth Social is essentially a scam," Dr Harrington says.

"The whole thing was set up not as a legitimate business, but potentially as a way to funnel money to Donald Trump rather than any serious money-making venture in the first place."

Is it illegal?

Finance researcher Dewan Rahman, from the University of Queensland's Business School, says whether the arrangement is unlawful depends on exactly what subscribers are receiving.

If the service simply delivers Trump's posts to paying customers a few milliseconds faster after they have already been published, then it is not illegal.

"If you're paying for speed rather than information, then that's fine," Dr Rahman says.

"The insider trading concern comes when you have an information advantage."

He says premium market data feeds that deliver public information in machine-readable formats within milliseconds are already common across financial markets.

The critical question, Dr Rahman says, is whether subscribers are also obtaining advance knowledge that a market-moving announcement is coming.

"If someone has private information beforehand, or even an indication that an announcement is coming, that's where the concern begins," he says.

"So we need to know those things and it's a question for investigation later on."

Dr Rahman says any evidence that politically connected firms received advance warning of presidential announcements would raise significant insider trading concerns.

Trump is not shy of collecting spoils The US president's most-recent filings indicate he pocketed more than $US2.2 billion last year through ventures ostensibly run by his family.

The service also raises ethical questions, Dr Harrington says.

"When we see a post on Truth Social, how do we know if that's informing the American people and everyone else in the world, or acting in his own financial interests?" he says.

"Public pronouncements by a sitting president should go out to everyone equally at the same time. There shouldn't be a sellable tier where people get that information first."

The White House did not respond to media requests for comment, but Trump has previously rejected criticism of his financial dealings.

Last month, he defended making about $US1.2 billion from cryptocurrency ventures in 2025, saying "everybody is profiting" from the stock market's gains since he returned to the White House.

A CNN/SSRS poll released in late July found 64 per cent of respondents believed Trump had gone too far in pursuing personal financial interests while in office.

Do Trump's posts really move markets?

Like any US president, Trump's public statements can move markets because they often signal changes to government policy or major geopolitical events.

Investors have reacted sharply to his announcements on tariffs, sanctions, military action and energy policy, while oil prices are particularly sensitive to developments in the Middle East.

But Dr Harrington says his team's latest research, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, points to something more unusual.

In one instance, QUT researchers found there was a sudden flurry of movement in the oil market about 20 minutes before Trump's post. (Supplied: QUT)

After analysing market activity surrounding Trump's Truth Social posts over a 73-day window, the researchers found 15 instances in which oil markets appeared to move before he posted on the topic.

In some cases, trading activity increased several minutes before the posts became public.

The researchers cannot say for certain why this happened or who was responsible, but Dr Harrington says the statistical pattern is difficult to dismiss as coincidence.

"It looks extremely suspicious," he says.

"What it seems like is that there are trades being placed by someone with inside information about what the president is about to say in the hour or two leading up to him posting on Truth Social."

Dr Harrington cautions the findings alone cannot prove insider trading is taking place, but says the repeated pattern suggests there may be a more sophisticated strategy at play.

"In reality, the milliseconds [advantage] aren't really the secret sauce," he says.

"If someone is getting information many minutes beforehand, that's where the real money is being made."

World.title: The absurdity of Aussie rules football inspires new comedy video game
World.content:
Even the filmmaker behind a 1960s-style cult Australian TV show, where World War II spies fight giant robots and resurrect dinosaurs, is well aware that Australian rules football is a ridiculous sport.

Danger 5 creator David Ashby, who also wrote the 2007 short-film parody Italian Spiderman, says trying to explain footy to someone new to the sport makes you "sound mad".

"If you describe the code to somebody who's unfamiliar with it, it sounds like you're making it up on the spot," he says.

"There's two teams, 18 players a side, chasing a footy, like two classrooms on a cricket oval, trying to do whatever they can to get the ball and kick it between sticks."

Ashby has swapped film cameras for joysticks as the developer of Pro Jank Footy, an Aussie rules-inspired arcade video game in which absurd new rules are constantly added as you play.

Teams in Pro Jank Footy are named after SA suburbs. (Supplied: Powerbomb Games)

Drawing on the aesthetic 1990s video games, Pro Jank Footy is also deeply South Australian and features teams such as the Salisbury Park Snags, Port Noarlunga Chips and the Ceduna Doonas.

"The comedy of the game lies in making fun or embracing, rather, Australian culture and sports culture," Ashby says.

"I think with our game we're really showcasing our exoticness, but also our weirdness, which we take for granted here in Australia."

Footy and comedy as a way to connect

Broden Kelly, one third of comedy group Aunty Donna, recorded thousands of lines of commentary for the project.

David Ashby and Tyler Roach (left and right in matching jackets) with Broden Kelly (wearing a scarf) exhibiting Pro Jank Footy at SXSW Sydney in 2025. (Supplied: Henrique Fanti/Powerbomb Games)

Kelly, who hosted a football podcast with ABC Sport journalist Marnie Vinall, says the game combined his love of comedy and football, even though video games aren't really his thing.

"I started doing a football podcast that was a bit silly and a bit cheeky and a bit dorky, called The Footy with Broden Kelly. I had these two worlds — one is comedy and one is footy — that built alongside each other," Kelly says.

"David Ashby got in touch and he said, 'I want to make a video game that is old-school NBA Jam but about Aussie rules', and I thought, 'That sounds like a lot of fun.'

"Nothing happened for 12 months and now I'm the superstar of a footy video game."

Loading Instagram content

Kelly, who recorded his lines in the Adelaide Hills ahead of a comedy show, said the tedium of the task led to some improvisation.

"I would hate to overdo it, but recording the voices for this game was the worst day of my life because it was four to five straight hours of saying it genuinely like two, three thousand lines, three times," he said.

"So John gets the ball. John gets the ball. John gets the ball.

"One of the improvs that went a little viral was me saying, 'These are all just pixels and one day we will all die'. And that really just came from me feeling like I would never stop recording this video game."

Kelly says it's rare that something captures what it's really like to be a football fan and how supporting a team can immediately bridge gaps between people, just like a good joke can.

"I can talk to 60-year-old blokes who I have nothing in common with and if they say I go for the Dees, we can chat for hours, and I just think that's so special.

"What I love about comedy is it's completely disarming. As soon as you make someone laugh, you feel like you know them deeply.

"There are jokes that David and his team have written that are relentlessly layered throughout this game that are very, very funny."

The arcade cabinets built by Louis Roots evoke the textures and materials of pubs and classic machines. (Supplied: Powerbomb Games)

Bringing 'tactility' to gameplay

Ashby and the team at Powerbomb Games commissioned Melbourne-based video game designer Louis Roots to construct two custom cabinets for the game, which can be played for free in the two Melbourne pubs where they are installed.

"I aim to bring a bit of joy into people's lives, bring some tactility to digital play. That's what I try to make," Roots says.

"Why is it that we can only access [games] with a keyboard, with the same things that we use for eight hours a day doing our office work?

"Also, it's … so satisfying to build this stuff, it's hard to overstate."

Pro Jank Footy cabinets have been installed in the Great Northern Hotel in Carlton North and the Victoria Hotel in Brunswick. (Supplied: Louis Roots)

Roots wanted the design to evoke the wood-panelled aesthetic of old pubs and arcades, as well as the green grass of the footy field.

"I wanted the visual landscape to [feature] a lot of different textures that mirrored what it was like to be at a footy ground," he says.

"I love having something that people will walk over just because they want to touch it."

Roots's design also incorporates the experience of hearing radio commentary at a game.

"My dad was a big Subi supporter in the WAFL and we'd sit up the back watching the game and you'd be hearing the commentary on some old bloke's AM radio," he says.

"I had this idea — what if it broadcast a radio signal with the commentary so people could hear it from across the pub?"

Both of the machines have an embedded FM transmitter that can be used to hear Kelly's commentary as other people play the game.

Pro Jank Footy features a range of quirky power-ups. (Supplied: Powerbomb Games)

Ashby is now working on a comedy series for Netflix but says he would "absolutely" make another game.

"Now that I've climbed the mountain and I know what it's like. It's fun," he says.

" This morning, I checked on PlayStation and the game is on the store. That's sick, dude. My 10-year-old self would be very happy with that. "

Pro Jank Footy is out on August 13.

World.title: First look at designs for new Town Hall Square 'in the heart' of Sydney
World.content:
New renders of what Sydney's new Town Hall Square will look like have been released, promising "the grandeur of a European square".

The new public square will be opposite Town Hall in the heart of Sydney's CBD and the design shows a plaza surrounded by a curved grove of 30 native Australian trees.

Fixed and movable chairs and tables are set to be included in the more than 4,500 square metres of accessible open space.

The City of Sydney has allocated $150 million to the project. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

A European nod

Speaking to 702 ABC Sydney on Tuesday, Lord Mayor of Sydney Clover Moore said the design had "the gravitas and grandeur of a European square" while maintaining Australian charm.

"It's going to be intrinsically Australian and Sydney because instead of [European] columns, it's going to be beautiful gum trees," she said.

" It should be a great gift for Sydney. "

Clover Moore says Town Hall Square will have a European feel to it. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

A key part of the design drawing the ire of some Sydneysiders is the plan to demolish the Woolworths block and six other buildings opposite Town Hall to create the space to build the new square.

City of Sydney Council said most business tenancies in the seven buildings were expected to relocate to alternative premises.

The Woolworths building at Town Hall will be demolished to make way for the new square. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

In response, Cr Moore said none of the buildings that were being removed were of heritage value.

"I think one of the good things about it also is that when those buildings are removed, people are then going to be able to have a really good view of the very beautiful heritage buildings; the Town Hall, Queen Victoria Building, St Andrew's Catheral and Pitt Street Church.

"So it will create an opportunity to have a lovely precinct, sandstone precinct, for those great buildings there."

Cr Moore said the ultimate aim of the square was for it to be a gathering point for the community, and a space for markets, festivals, cultural, music and live sports watching events.

Decades in the making

Sydney's Town Hall in the 1980s. (Supplied: City of Sydney Archives)

The square has been part of Sydney CBD's urban vision since the early 19th century, with successive lord mayors acquiring land on George and Park streets for the project since the 1980s.

There was extensive community consultation in 2007 as part of the council's long-term strategic plan, with the concept of public squares garnering strong support.

The council then resolved to move ahead with the design and construction of Town Hall Square in February, with an unanimous decision made to fast-track demolition work.

$150 million was budgeted in City of Sydney's long-term financial plan, with demolition set for 2028 and the project expected to be completed by 2031.

An artist's impression of what the new square at Town Hall would look like. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

Margy Osmond, chief executive officer of the Tourism and Transport Forum, said the square would attract visitation.

"This is fantastic for Sydney's visitor economy and a once-in-a-generation opportunity to create a new landmark in the heart of the city," she said.

"It has the potential to change the way people experience this part of the city, drawing more visitors and encouraging them to stay longer and spend more, which in turn will attract more investment into the surrounding precinct."

City of Sydney Council said they would give the square a First Nations name.

A development application for Town Hall Square will be lodged in the coming months, to allow Sydneysiders to provide feedback on the design.

World.title: From $1000 to half a million: How to build a valuable art collection
World.content:
MoneyInvestingCollectables From $1000 to half a million: How to build a valuable art collection Dan F Stapleton August 11, 2026 — 11:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In May, a painting by the abstract expressionist Mark Rothko fetched a staggering $US85.8 million ($120.8 million) at a Sotheby’s auction in New York. The result – the second-highest price ever paid for a Rothko at auction – made headlines. But what is arguably more remarkable is the painting’s ownership history, or provenance. The Emily Kam Kngwarray exhibition from the National Gallery of Australia. NGA The last time the Rothko changed hands, in 2003, Goldman Sachs banker Robert Mnuchin paid $US6.7 million for it. He held on to the work until his death late last year. For Mnuchin’s estate, the recent sale represents a gross return of more than 1100 per cent. It’s not the only example of artwork appreciating dramatically in a relatively short period of time. Here in Australia, works by the late, great Emily Kam Kngwarray regularly fetch $500,000 or more through dealers or at auction.



When they were painted, in the 1990s, they generally sold for a few thousand dollars each. Of course, not every artist’s reputation – and, correspondingly, the value of their work – grows over time. But if you have the opportunity to buy a painting by an artist on the ascent, should you? Of the thousands of artists who sell artworks each year, only a handful see their work appreciate in value. Art as an asset class It’s important to bear in mind that, to make money selling art, the resale price needs to be significantly higher than the price you paid. Dealers and auction houses generally charge commissions of between 25 and 35 per cent to sell work on a collector’s behalf, dwarfing the commissions charged by brokers of other asset types.



They can do this because art is a niche asset with a relatively small buyer pool. Often, sellers must rely on their brokers’ pre-existing relationships with buyers to secure sales. In Australia, those selling art on the secondary market must also pay the resale royalty: a 5 per cent fee collected by the government-run Copyright Agency and remitted to the artist or their estate. Finally, sellers must pay tax. The ATO classes art as a ‘collectable’, making it subject to the same capital gains tax (CGT) rules as most other assets. That means those reselling art after July 1, 2027 will receive an inflation-based discount, rather than the current 50 per cent CGT discount, and will be taxed at a minimum rate of 30 per cent. Reading the market Of the thousands of artists who sell artworks through galleries or online platforms each year, only a handful see their work appreciate in value.



Predicting which artists will rise is not an exact science, but certain conditions make price growth more likely, says D’Lan Davidson, whose D’Lan Galleries has outposts in Melbourne, Sydney and New York. Editor's pick Collectables Forget nostalgia: Why edgy Australian photography is suddenly worth a fortune “Signs to watch for are major exhibitions, museum acquisitions, strong curatorial interest, inclusion in important private collections and secondary-market demand.” Davidson gives the example of Kngwarray’s 2025 retrospective at Tate Modern in London. “That show ignited Emily’s market globally,” he says. Another way to identify artists with strong prospects is to familiarise yourself with the rosters of major commercial galleries.



“If an artist is strongly supported by a well-respected gallerist, there is a much better chance the work will have a broader market appreciation also,” Davidson says. Aspiring art collectors should proceed slowly and prioritise quality over quantity, he adds. “Even if it means buying fewer works, you should always buy the finest artwork that you can afford, from artists with a strong and consistent practice, impeccable provenance and real demand from serious collectors and institutions.” Works by Mark Rothko included in the Taubman Collection sale at Sotheby’s in New York. Reuters For love or money Many art collectors buy impulsively, motivated by dopamine and a fear of missing out, but circumspect buyers tend to build better collections, Davidson says.



Learning more about the artists and art movements that interest you is important, too, as it can help you accurately identify gems within a particular artist’s oeuvre. “The strongest collections are usually built with conviction, patience and knowledge,” Davidson says. Of course, the best reason to buy a piece of art is because you love it – and following your heart might be as good a money-making tactic as any. “In all my experience, and in a very strange way, artworks that have been adored generally resell for much better prices than artworks that have been stored away and never treasured,” Davidson says. Advice given in this article is general in nature and not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.
