His writing has appeared in The New York Times, the Financial Times and others. He is based in Sydney.

World.title: Australia to roll out bird flu vaccines for wildlife most at risk
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

The first vaccines against H5N1 bird flu will be administered to Australian wildlife over the coming days and weeks, the Albanese government has confirmed.

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said $2 million worth of vaccines – about 1500 vials – had been acquired for the initial vaccination program, which would target native animals in captivity most at risk of the disease.

Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins speaking at Parliament House, Canberra, on Tuesday morning. Alex Ellinghausen

“This approach will mean that the states and territories are able to commence vaccination activities, initially focusing on priority species in captivity,” Collins told reporters in Canberra on Tuesday.

“We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the [H5N1] … spreading amongst wild birds. But we can take action to protect the species most at risk, and the vaccination is now part of that response.”

World.title: How a director’s love of the speccy turned into a film about a Chinese football team
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How a director’s love of the speccy turned into a film about a Chinese football team Andrew Wu August 11, 2026 — 11:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In David Gung’s first season of senior football in 1968, the speedy rover arrived at games well into the first quarter due to his work at a Chinese church on Sundays. When he won the best and fairest award that year, the club president presented him with an electric clock. “I got that to remind me to play on time,” Gung said. David Gung, Peter Louey and Harold Chin Quan were members of the Chinese footy team depicted in a new film, Carn the Chinese! Joe Armao Harold Chin Quan was the centreman in that team. At 52kg, he was built to be a jockey rather than negotiating the chaos after a centre bounce. “I played scared for the first two years,” joked Chin Quan, a third-generation Australian whose grandfather came to the country in 1897.



Peter Louey was the ruckman. Standing 5′10 (178cm), he was undersized. The trio formed the heart of the midfield of a team called the Young Chinese League, a social football side consisting of Chinese Australians whose story of resilience and love of the game during the White Australian policy era has been turned into a short film by director Angela How. The Young Chinese League football team in 1966. Premiering on Wednesday at the Melbourne International Film Festival, Carn the Chinese! explores how sections of Melbourne’s Chinese community embraced the game long before names such as Barassi, Jesaulenko and Silvagni became synonymous with the code. How, a Singapore-born Australian, first saw the game after her family moved to this country in the 1990s. She was captivated by the speccy.



“What intrigued me was you climbed on someone else to get to the ball,” How told this masthead. “I’d never seen anyone jump so high. It was quite a sight.” Because of the lack of Chinese or Asian involvement in the sport, “I didn’t feel like the game belonged to me culturally”, How said. So she set about finding stories of Chinese Australians playing the sport. Though Chinese immigrants have been in Australia since the days of the gold rush, very few have reached the top level. Wally Koochew played for Carlton in 1908. George Tansing played five games for Geelong that year, Ernie Foo represented St Kilda four times in 1913. More recently, Fremantle’s Bailey Banfield is the most prominent men’s footballer with Chinese heritage, while Darcy Vescio is the torchbearer in the AFLW. They are also an executive producer of the film.



Though the YCL played for about 50 years from the 1930s to 1986, not much is known about the team beyond a chapter in author Patrick Skene’s book Celestial Footy, which chronicles the participation of Chinese immigrants in the game. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret Formed in the 1930s after a merger between the Chinese Progress Association and the Chinese Athletics Association, the YCL was not part of an official league. They quickly made an impression. “By 1938, weekly Young Chinese League matches in Albert Park were a much-anticipated fixture on the calendar of the Melbourne Chinese community; a meeting point to build friendships and keep community strong,” Skene wrote. The YCL played all around Melbourne and in the bush, arranging games against companies such as Ford, Holden and Kraft.



How cannot remember how she came across the YCL, but the more she learned, the keener she was to tell its story. Filming started in 2022, but other projects took up How’s time until last year. “I wanted it to be done and them to be celebrated while they’re here,” How said. “That was really important to me and I felt a responsibility to do the work and finish it. David Gung, now 78, was a talented footballer for the Young Chinese League, the team featured in the short film Carn the Chinese! “Because they played through the White Australia Policy era, the thing that struck me was they were quintessentially Aussie with their larrikinism and attitude to life. “Peter warmed to the game so naturally and played really well. By embracing the game, he became accepted. Just the fact he was good at sport, it broke a lot of barriers for him.”



Louey, 88, came to Australia on a boat at the age of 12. He lived in West Melbourne, became a North Melbourne supporter, and was a good enough footballer and cricketer to captain Brunswick Tech’s school team in both sports. He also led the YCL. In 2016, he was awarded an OAM as part of the Queen’s Birthday Honours for service to the Chinese community in Victoria. “In Australia, if you’re a good sport, they admire you,” he said in the film. High-flying marks were what first drew director Angela How to Australian rules football. Chin Quan is a third-generation Australian whose grandfather arrived in the country in 1897 and settled in Darwin. The national counter-terrorism coordinator has warned that online extremist material is “nearly always” driving radicalisation in Australia, telling the Antisemitism Royal Commission that the proliferation of such content has worked to legitimise ideological grievances and justify violent attacks among isolated members of society.

Brendan Dowling, who was named counter-terrorism coordinator at the Department of Home Affairs in May, issued the warning as he discussed the role online content plays in intensifying grievances towards an external group, party or person.

“In nearly all cases, there is an online dimension where access to violent extremist material online, access to a community of like-minded people, who foment that sense of grievance and anger,” Dowling told the commission.

“We see that the online environment is nearly always involved in accelerating some of those grievances and giving people access to material that supports their ideological interpretation of those grievances, their explanation, justification as to why their grievance is supposedly legitimate. In the cases that we’re most worried about, why mobilisation to violence is seen as a legitimate activity.”

World.title: Property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent, major bank warns
World.content:
Property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, economists with the ANZ bank have warned, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes.

In a report released on Tuesday morning, the ANZ, which had been the most bearish about the property market of all the major banks, said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year.

House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao

Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough.

The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘J’ to continue evidence in former 2GB broadcaster’s alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day six of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

Our live coverage was paused on Wednesday after Local Court Judge Glenn Walsh temporarily imposed a non-publication order on the cross-examination of the complainant, known as “J”, by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. That order was lifted on Thursday afternoon.

“J”, now in his early 40s, denied under questioning by Bashir that he had a financial motive for making the allegations against Jones, and denied that they were a fabrication.

He has given evidence that Jones groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. “J” has also told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box for a sixth day. He will be re-examined by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, after his cross-examination concluded on Friday.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

Bashir asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

World.title: Ten days ago, this theatre was on death row. Then something marvellous happened
World.content:
Breaking CultureTheatreArts Ten days ago, this theatre was on death row. Then something marvellous happened Linda Morris Updated August 11, 2026 — 10:40am ,first published June 27, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ten days ago, supporters of a beloved northside theatre dressed in red to convince Ku-ring-gai Council to revive a plan to convert the home of the Marian Street Theatre into a $30 million arts centre. Lead organiser Jessica Blaxland Ashby initially intended the rally as a simple demonstration of deep public support for a project the council had effectively shelved for the next decade. By the end of that day, she had received $30,000 in community pledges towards the $100,000 needed to fund minor works, keep the architectural plans alive, and bring council back to the table. Just seven days later, Blaxland Ashby had raised the full $100,000 from 312 donors, with contributions ranging from $10 to $10,000. Jessica Blaxland Ashby with daughter Ida, 3, and mother, Wendy. Sitthixay Ditthavong “Six weeks ago there was absolutely no hope. It was really grim and depressing, and there were a lot of tears at that point,” Blaxland Ashby said. “It was a very low point in the campaign, without a doubt. We’ve managed a complete 180-degree turn, and it was the community that made it happen.”



Built in 1906 as a community hall, Marian St became a professional theatre in 1966, hosting its first all-youth performance in 1969. Over the decades, many of Australia’s most notable actors graced its stage, including Helen Morse, Belinda Giblin and Ruth Cracknell. The venue was shut down in 2013 due to safety concerns, forcing drama classes and children’s performances to relocate. Council initially approved new plans in 2020, then estimated it would cost $15 million. Those approved designs by architects Tonkin Zulaikha Greer aimed to transform the building into a state-of-the-art, multipurpose arts centre featuring two theatres, a music space, community meeting rooms, a cafe, an exhibition foyer and an outdoor amphitheatre. Belinda Giblin, Paula Duncan and Maggie Kirkpatrick appearing in Social Climbers at yhe Marian St Theatre. Branco Gaica However, a majority of councillors last month voted to allow the development application to expire, noting that the project’s projected cost had doubled to $30.3 million as of October 2024.



The theatre holds a personal legacy for Blaxland Ashby. Her grandmother, Audrey Blaxland, founded it and her mother Wendy has long campaigned for its revival for her own granddaughter Ida. Playwright David Williamson, patron of the Save Marian St Theatre Action group, rallied to the cause, describing the setback as deeply disappointing and chipping in with a personal donation. “I had many very good and well-attended productions of my plays there in the past and think it would be a great community asset,” Williamson said. “The design of the renovation is first-class, but the council keeps deferring a decision while approving expensive sports oval developments, demonstrating yet again where the arts rate in our national psyche. I do hope it leads to this lovely venue becoming a reality.” Plans for the revamped Marian St Theatre. Los Angeles-based actor Barry Creyton had also urged the council to consider “giving new life to this once-thriving theatre” adding, “It’s of immense sadness to me to know that the theatre has been dark for so long.”



They were backed by actors Hugo Weaving, Jacki Weaver, Tony Sheldon, John Bell and rising names Ava Madon and Jordan Hare. Community advocate Bronwyn Hanna contrasted council’s refusal to spend the budgeted $100,000 required to preserve Marian St’s approved plans with its willingness to pursue the unbudgeted Norman Griffiths Oval development. Ku-ring-gai Council has invested heavily in sporting infrastructure over the past 13 years, supporting 44 sports fields, 67 tennis courts, two golf courses and spending $26.6 million on two indoor basketball courts at St Ives High School. Council unanimously voted on Monday to reverse its decision this week when a cheque for $100,000 was deposited two days ahead of the deadline it had set for the community to crowdfund minor works needed to extend the development application. While it doesn’t guarantee the theatre will be rebuilt or redeveloped, it does keep the consent alive. Meanwhile, the historic building has begun to rapidly degrade with most of the front windows smashed and boarded up and graffitied, and its exterior growing moss and mould.



“It was such an extraordinary relief when I transferred the funding, and I shed more tears,” Blaxland Ashby said. “There is still a big mountain to climb, the next step is we need to get funding for the full renovation. There is a Thriving Suburbs grant what we need to get and for that, we need state government support. We have a petition that needs 20,000 signatures for the matter to be debated in parliament.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: From $1000 to half a million: How to build a valuable art collection
World.content:
MoneyInvestingCollectables From $1000 to half a million: How to build a valuable art collection Dan F Stapleton August 11, 2026 — 11:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In May, a painting by the abstract expressionist Mark Rothko fetched a staggering $US85.8 million ($120.8 million) at a Sotheby’s auction in New York. The result – the second-highest price ever paid for a Rothko at auction – made headlines. But what is arguably more remarkable is the painting’s ownership history, or provenance. The Emily Kam Kngwarray exhibition from the National Gallery of Australia. NGA The last time the Rothko changed hands, in 2003, Goldman Sachs banker Robert Mnuchin paid $US6.7 million for it. He held on to the work until his death late last year. For Mnuchin’s estate, the recent sale represents a gross return of more than 1100 per cent. It’s not the only example of artwork appreciating dramatically in a relatively short period of time. Here in Australia, works by the late, great Emily Kam Kngwarray regularly fetch $500,000 or more through dealers or at auction.



When they were painted, in the 1990s, they generally sold for a few thousand dollars each. Of course, not every artist’s reputation – and, correspondingly, the value of their work – grows over time. But if you have the opportunity to buy a painting by an artist on the ascent, should you? Of the thousands of artists who sell artworks each year, only a handful see their work appreciate in value. Art as an asset class It’s important to bear in mind that, to make money selling art, the resale price needs to be significantly higher than the price you paid. Dealers and auction houses generally charge commissions of between 25 and 35 per cent to sell work on a collector’s behalf, dwarfing the commissions charged by brokers of other asset types.



They can do this because art is a niche asset with a relatively small buyer pool. Often, sellers must rely on their brokers’ pre-existing relationships with buyers to secure sales. In Australia, those selling art on the secondary market must also pay the resale royalty: a 5 per cent fee collected by the government-run Copyright Agency and remitted to the artist or their estate. Finally, sellers must pay tax. The ATO classes art as a ‘collectable’, making it subject to the same capital gains tax (CGT) rules as most other assets. That means those reselling art after July 1, 2027 will receive an inflation-based discount, rather than the current 50 per cent CGT discount, and will be taxed at a minimum rate of 30 per cent. Reading the market Of the thousands of artists who sell artworks through galleries or online platforms each year, only a handful see their work appreciate in value.



Predicting which artists will rise is not an exact science, but certain conditions make price growth more likely, says D’Lan Davidson, whose D’Lan Galleries has outposts in Melbourne, Sydney and New York. Editor's pick Collectables Forget nostalgia: Why edgy Australian photography is suddenly worth a fortune “Signs to watch for are major exhibitions, museum acquisitions, strong curatorial interest, inclusion in important private collections and secondary-market demand.” Davidson gives the example of Kngwarray’s 2025 retrospective at Tate Modern in London. “That show ignited Emily’s market globally,” he says. Another way to identify artists with strong prospects is to familiarise yourself with the rosters of major commercial galleries.



“If an artist is strongly supported by a well-respected gallerist, there is a much better chance the work will have a broader market appreciation also,” Davidson says. Aspiring art collectors should proceed slowly and prioritise quality over quantity, he adds. “Even if it means buying fewer works, you should always buy the finest artwork that you can afford, from artists with a strong and consistent practice, impeccable provenance and real demand from serious collectors and institutions.” Works by Mark Rothko included in the Taubman Collection sale at Sotheby’s in New York. Reuters For love or money Many art collectors buy impulsively, motivated by dopamine and a fear of missing out, but circumspect buyers tend to build better collections, Davidson says.



Learning more about the artists and art movements that interest you is important, too, as it can help you accurately identify gems within a particular artist’s oeuvre. “The strongest collections are usually built with conviction, patience and knowledge,” Davidson says. Of course, the best reason to buy a piece of art is because you love it – and following your heart might be as good a money-making tactic as any. “In all my experience, and in a very strange way, artworks that have been adored generally resell for much better prices than artworks that have been stored away and never treasured,” Davidson says. Advice given in this article is general in nature and not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. The first vaccines against H5N1 bird flu will be administered to Australian wildlife over the coming days and weeks, the Albanese government has confirmed.

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said $2 million worth of vaccines – about 1500 vials – had been acquired for the initial vaccination program, which would target native animals in captivity most at risk of the disease.

Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins speaking at Parliament House, Canberra, on Tuesday morning. Alex Ellinghausen

“This approach will mean that the states and territories are able to commence vaccination activities, initially focusing on priority species in captivity,” Collins told reporters in Canberra on Tuesday.

“We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the [H5N1] … spreading amongst wild birds. But we can take action to protect the species most at risk, and the vaccination is now part of that response.”

When he won the best and fairest award that year, the club president presented him with an electric clock. “I got that to remind me to play on time,” Gung said. David Gung, Peter Louey and Harold Chin Quan were members of the Chinese footy team depicted in a new film, Carn the Chinese! Joe Armao Harold Chin Quan was the centreman in that team. At 52kg, he was built to be a jockey rather than negotiating the chaos after a centre bounce. “I played scared for the first two years,” joked Chin Quan, a third-generation Australian whose grandfather came to the country in 1897.



Peter Louey was the ruckman. Standing 5′10 (178cm), he was undersized. The trio formed the heart of the midfield of a team called the Young Chinese League, a social football side consisting of Chinese Australians whose story of resilience and love of the game during the White Australian policy era has been turned into a short film by director Angela How. The Young Chinese League football team in 1966. Premiering on Wednesday at the Melbourne International Film Festival, Carn the Chinese! explores how sections of Melbourne’s Chinese community embraced the game long before names such as Barassi, Jesaulenko and Silvagni became synonymous with the code. How, a Singapore-born Australian, first saw the game after her family moved to this country in the 1990s. She was captivated by the speccy.

It was quite a sight.” Because of the lack of Chinese or Asian involvement in the sport, “I didn’t feel like the game belonged to me culturally”, How said. So she set about finding stories of Chinese Australians playing the sport. Though Chinese immigrants have been in Australia since the days of the gold rush, very few have reached the top level. Wally Koochew played for Carlton in 1908. George Tansing played five games for Geelong that year, Ernie Foo represented St Kilda four times in 1913. World.title: Sarah Pound’s slow-cooker lemongrass beef curry
World.content:
This slow-cooker lemongrass beef curry is a tried and tested favourite. Sarah Pound

This is one of those magical slow-cooker recipes that delivers unbelievable flavour with barely any effort. Everything simply gets thrown straight into the slow cooker – no frying off, no extra pans and absolutely no complicated prep. It’s just 10 minutes of hands-on work, and then you let the machine do the rest.

I’ve been making this recipe for more than 20 years, and it is still one of my all-time favourites. By the end of the day, the beef becomes melt-in-your-mouth tender, the sauce turns rich and deeply fragrant, and the whole house smells incredible.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Albanese tells Labor caucus he expects gambling bill to pass with Coalition support; At least 110 killed in Colombia after 7.4 magnitude earthquake
World.content:
The national counter-terrorism coordinator has warned that online extremist material is “nearly always” driving radicalisation in Australia, telling the Antisemitism Royal Commission that the proliferation of such content has worked to legitimise ideological grievances and justify violent attacks among isolated members of society.

Brendan Dowling, who was named counter-terrorism coordinator at the Department of Home Affairs in May, issued the warning as he discussed the role online content plays in intensifying grievances towards an external group, party or person.

“In nearly all cases, there is an online dimension where access to violent extremist material online, access to a community of like-minded people, who foment that sense of grievance and anger,” Dowling told the commission.

“We see that the online environment is nearly always involved in accelerating some of those grievances and giving people access to material that supports their ideological interpretation of those grievances, their explanation, justification as to why their grievance is supposedly legitimate. In the cases that we’re most worried about, why mobilisation to violence is seen as a legitimate activity.”

World.title: Property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent, major bank warns
World.content:
Property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, economists with the ANZ bank have warned, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes.

In a report released on Tuesday morning, the ANZ, which had been the most bearish about the property market of all the major banks, said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year.

House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao

Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough.

The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak.

World.title: Ten days ago, this theatre was on death row. Then something marvellous happened
World.content:
Breaking CultureTheatreArts Ten days ago, this theatre was on death row. Then something marvellous happened Linda Morris Updated August 11, 2026 — 10:40am ,first published June 27, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ten days ago, supporters of a beloved northside theatre dressed in red to convince Ku-ring-gai Council to revive a plan to convert the home of the Marian Street Theatre into a $30 million arts centre. Lead organiser Jessica Blaxland Ashby initially intended the rally as a simple demonstration of deep public support for a project the council had effectively shelved for the next decade. By the end of that day, she had received $30,000 in community pledges towards the $100,000 needed to fund minor works, keep the architectural plans alive, and bring council back to the table. Just seven days later, Blaxland Ashby had raised the full $100,000 from 312 donors, with contributions ranging from $10 to $10,000. Jessica Blaxland Ashby with daughter Ida, 3, and mother, Wendy. Sitthixay Ditthavong “Six weeks ago there was absolutely no hope. It was really grim and depressing, and there were a lot of tears at that point,” Blaxland Ashby said. “It was a very low point in the campaign, without a doubt. We’ve managed a complete 180-degree turn, and it was the community that made it happen.”



Built in 1906 as a community hall, Marian St became a professional theatre in 1966, hosting its first all-youth performance in 1969. Over the decades, many of Australia’s most notable actors graced its stage, including Helen Morse, Belinda Giblin and Ruth Cracknell. The venue was shut down in 2013 due to safety concerns, forcing drama classes and children’s performances to relocate. Council initially approved new plans in 2020, then estimated it would cost $15 million. Those approved designs by architects Tonkin Zulaikha Greer aimed to transform the building into a state-of-the-art, multipurpose arts centre featuring two theatres, a music space, community meeting rooms, a cafe, an exhibition foyer and an outdoor amphitheatre. Belinda Giblin, Paula Duncan and Maggie Kirkpatrick appearing in Social Climbers at yhe Marian St Theatre. Branco Gaica However, a majority of councillors last month voted to allow the development application to expire, noting that the project’s projected cost had doubled to $30.3 million as of October 2024.



The theatre holds a personal legacy for Blaxland Ashby. Her grandmother, Audrey Blaxland, founded it and her mother Wendy has long campaigned for its revival for her own granddaughter Ida. Playwright David Williamson, patron of the Save Marian St Theatre Action group, rallied to the cause, describing the setback as deeply disappointing and chipping in with a personal donation. “I had many very good and well-attended productions of my plays there in the past and think it would be a great community asset,” Williamson said. “The design of the renovation is first-class, but the council keeps deferring a decision while approving expensive sports oval developments, demonstrating yet again where the arts rate in our national psyche.” Plans for the revamped Marian St Theatre. Los Angeles-based actor Barry Creyton had also urged the council to consider “giving new life to this once-thriving theatre” adding, “It’s of immense sadness to me to know that the theatre has been dark for so long.”



They were backed by actors Hugo Weaving, Jacki Weaver, Tony Sheldon, John Bell and rising names Ava Madon and Jordan Hare. Community advocate Bronwyn Hanna contrasted council’s refusal to spend the budgeted $100,000 required to preserve Marian St’s approved plans with its willingness to pursue the unbudgeted Norman Griffiths Oval development. Ku-ring-gai Council has invested heavily in sporting infrastructure over the past 13 years, supporting 44 sports fields, 67 tennis courts, two golf courses and spending $26.6 million on two indoor basketball courts at St Ives High School. Council unanimously voted on Monday to reverse its decision this week when a cheque for $100,000 was deposited two days ahead of the deadline it had set for the community to crowdfund minor works needed to extend the development application. While it doesn’t guarantee the theatre will be rebuilt or redeveloped, it does keep the consent alive. Meanwhile, the historic building has begun to rapidly degrade with most of the front windows smashed and boarded up and graffitied, and its exterior growing moss and mould.



“It was such an extraordinary relief when I transferred the funding, and I shed more tears,” Blaxland Ashby said. “There is still a big mountain to climb, the next step is we need to get funding for the full renovation. There is a Thriving Suburbs grant what we need to get and for that, we need state government support. We have a petition that needs 20,000 signatures for the matter to be debated in parliament.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: Philip Polkinghorne deleted sex worker photos when he realised he was a suspect in wife's death
World.content:
Philip Polkinghorne says he began to delete photos and data on his phone from sex worker Madison Ashton when he realised he was the "prime suspect" in his wife's death.

He told a coroner he felt "betrayed" by the police who had been interviewing him for several hours before a defence lawyer friend called him to tell he was likely a suspect.

He did not testify during the trial.

His lawyer, Ron Mansfield, asked him to explain why he had deleted pictures and data from his phone after Hanna's death.

"It was embarrassing. I wanted to keep it private."

There were also messages from other sex workers, he said.

"It had compromising material that I didn't want anyone to see," he said.

Polkinghorne said he had gone to the police station to be interviewed the same day he found his wife.

He got a call midway through from his friend, defence lawyer Tony Bouchier, who told him his house was a crime scene and he was likely a suspect.

Police had not told him that, he said.

"I felt I had been betrayed and that they had taken advantage of my vulnerability," he said.

Polkinghorne started his testimony today by reading written evidence, breaking down several times, before being questioned by his lawyer Ron Mansfield.

Some of the details he remembered from the morning, particulary physical evidence at the scene did not match what he was later told by police or saw in photos.

Much of that cannot be reported because of suppressions.

When he looked back, he was shocked and confused, Polkinghorne said.

Mansfield asked him about his state of mind the morning he found Hanna.

"I was absolutely devastated and I couldn't think straight. I couldn't get my phone to work. I mean how pathetic is that?" Polkinghorne said.

"I knew she was cold. I wanted to cover her up ... She was dead. She didn't need a blanket."

The next sequence of events was unclear to him but he remembered calling 111, and then calling his sister, Ruth, he said.

He answered questions from Mansfield about whether he had used methamphetamine the night before Hanna's death.

He raised his voice as he answered "no".

He also denied using the bathroom of the room where Hanna had slept and where traces of methamphetamine were found.

In 2024, he had been convicted for possession of methamphetamine.

Polkinghorne spent some of his evidence talking about the stress Hanna had been under in the lead up to her death.

She was part of the Covid-19 vaccine roll-out and had been working very hard, he said.

Emails on many days were sent over a 13-hour period.

His voice cracked when he said one day, they had spanned 20 hours.

The day before she died she had gone to the gym, then gone straight to work in her gym clothes, he said.

That was unusual.

"She was always pristine and well presented and would not normally be seen in gym gear or what she would wear at home," he said.

Counsel for police Alysha McClintock has begun cross examining Polkinghorne, asking him why he had previously given three descriptions of the scene where he found Pauline Hanna.

World.title: Man arrested after fire at Auckland supermarket at weekend
World.content:
A man has been arrested after a fire at a West Auckland supermarket at the weekend.

Emergency services were called at about 4.15pm on Sunday afternoon to reports of a fire at a Great North Road supermarket.

The fire was extinguished by firefighters and no one was injured.

Acting detective inspector Megan Goldie said the blaze was treated as suspicious.

Police arrested a 34-year-old man on Tuesday morning, charging him with arson, she said.

World.title: Cabinet reshuffle on the cards, Tonga PM confirms
World.content:
Tonga's Prime Minister Lord Fatafehi Fakafanua confirmed on Tuesday that a Cabinet reshuffle is likely to happen by the end of the week .

"Yes, we'll make an announcement once it's all ready," Lord Fakafanua told RNZ Pacific.

It comes after the resignations of two of the most senior government ministers who were "unseated" by the Tongan Legislative Assembly on 3 August.

The two - former Tourism and Infrastructure Minister Semisi Sika and former Finance Minister Lata Tangimana - were found guilty of bribery by the Nuku'alofa Magistrates' Court during the 2025 general election.

Lord Fakafanua has been acting as finance minister.

Tangimana, who held the Niua 17 seat, was found guilty of electoral bribery during the November 2025 election and his appeal was quashed by the Court of Appeal in Nuku'alofa last month.

Sika, the Member for Tongatapu 2, had his election declared void by the courts over breaches of electoral expense rules, including failure to properly declare his campaign expenditure, which exceeded the legal spending limit. While he challenged the ruling, the Court of Appeal upheld the earlier decision.

Section 24 on Permitted Election Expenses of the Tonga Electoral Act 1989 states: "No candidates may spend more than TOP$10,000 during, or six months before, or after, any election campaign."

Lord Fakafanua said they are currently following due process, according to Tonga's Constitution, on the appointing of ministers to replace the pair.

This includes advising King Tupou VI.

The prime minister has the choice to select replacements from both inside and outside parliament.

Meanwhile, the by-elections for the two vacant seats will be held on 8 October.

World.title: Christopher Luxon calls urgent meeting to resolve 'increased speculation' about leadership
World.content:
Political update with Craig McCulloch Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The Prime Minister has called for an "urgent-in person" caucus meeting in Wellington on Wednesday morning.

It comes amid renewed pressure on Christopher Luxon's leadership.

Luxon wrote on social media on Tuesday, after postponing various prior arrangements, that it was "clear from various media reports and conversations there is increased speculation about my leadership".

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

For those reasons, he wrote, the issue "needs to be resolved quickly".

"I am calling an urgent in-person Caucus meeting tomorrow at 9:30am in Wellington to resolve the issue."

Moments before the social media post was published, Luxon's team abruptly postponed an RNZ podcast interview which had been scheduled for this afternoon.

Earlier today, National's Chris Bishop and Rima Nakhle threw their full support behind Christopher Luxon as his leadership comes under renewed pressure.

The Prime Minister last week endured days of mishaps and missteps and started this week inadvertently talking about three taxes the National Party may introduce if back in government.

He and his deputy, Nicola Willis, had called a press conference on Sunday to put pressure on Labour to sign up to its Budget responsibility rules, yet by his Monday morning media round Luxon was instead explaining that a fuel excise tax, bed tax, and bank tax would be on the table under a future National-led government.

On Monday night the NZ Herald reported National MPs had spent the day on the phones with one confirming they had fielded "several" phone calls about a potential leadership change.

"There's going to be change in the top job. It's just a question of who is going to be it", the NZ Herald reported the MP to have said.

Bishop, who was opening a pedestrian bridge at a railway station in Auckland alongside local MP Rima Nakhle on Tuesday morning, confirmed the party caucus would hold a meeting on Zoom later in the day, as earlier reported by RNZ, but he denied Luxon's leadership would be on the agenda.

"I'm not talking to you about the internal machinations of what time the Zoom appointments are, but there is a meeting tonight."

He said it wasn't unusual to hold a meeting during a recess week.

"Last week the PM apologised for remarks about Rotorua, and obviously there's been a bit over the MMP call, but we back our leader, and you know he's made his position clear in relation to the MMP referendum that we'll be taking that to the election. It's not going to be the focus of the campaign, as he says in his own words."

RNZ spoke to about 10 MPs on Monday night and received a mixture of responses.

Some said they wouldn't comment, while another said they couldn't comment, and others denied there were any leadership murmurings or that they knew about them.

One MP said the direct quotes in the reporting suggested there must be some truth to it, and at least one MP said it was nonsense.

Chris Bishop dismissed the suggestion there were phone calls on Monday about the National party leadership. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Often tipped to be a leadership contender, Bishop has previously denied plotting a challenge, insisting late last year that Luxon remained the best person to be prime minister.

He dismissed the suggestion there were phone calls on Monday about the National party leadership, saying he talked to caucus members "all the time about a whole range of different things".

"Yesterday was a cabinet day, so you know clearly there were conversations between ministers and between MPs."

Bishop said it was "unhelpful" MPs were speaking to media and encouraged his colleagues not to.

"All I would say is you know people people shouldn't be talking to media like that."

Bishop said he was "getting on with the job", but then continued to answer questions from media about the leadership issue.

He said he hadn't spoken to Erica Stanford - also considered a contender - about the leadership, nor had he spoken to any of his colleagues.

Nakhle also backed Luxon saying he was "the man and the boss" and she backed him "150 percent".

Luxon says his caucus backs him

On Saturday it was put to Luxon whether the confidence vote he called on his leadership back in April had resulted in a caucus split of 27 votes to 22.

He responded, "I have the support of my caucus - I'm very confident in my leadership."

On Tuesday Bishop told RNZ it wasn't worth speculating on the leadership vote, as only "two or three" people in the country know the results for certain.

"I don't know where that reporting came from. The caucus vote is secret, and I don't know what the result was," he said.

It was speculation about whether Luxon was up to the job and had the backing of his caucus to stay on as leader that prompted him to test his support with a vote in April.

At the time Luxon said that had put the rumour to bed and he had his caucus behind him.

Just four months later MPs appear to be musing about the prospect of changing leaders again.

While some spoken to by RNZ on Monday night said they supported Luxon, it wasn't unanimous.

There has been agitating since late last year from some MPs concerned Luxon's lack of personal popularity was also dragging the party vote down, and some MPs would lose their seats in Parliament if he didn't improve.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll in July had National down 2.1 points to 28.7 percent, its fourth consecutive decline in the Reid Research series and its weakest result since Luxon became leader in November 2021.

While Luxon's confidence vote win looked to have given him some reprieve, his performance in recent weeks has done little to convince concerned MPs they'll be safe come November 7.

Chris Bishop said he hadn't spoken to Erica Stanford about the leadership, nor had he spoken to any of his colleagues. RNZ / Nick Monro

Last Monday Luxon apologised to leaders from the Rotorua Business Chamber after he criticised them for having a "parent-child mentality" and relying on government too much.

He also faced questions about his foreign minister Winston Peters, and why he wasn't doing anything to reprimand him after labelling his comments about another MP, "racist".

Luxon then had to justify his use of a New Zealand Defence Force plane flying him home from a National Party fundraising dinner, and on the same day unemployment hit a record 11-year high.

On Thursday he was using talkback radio to make a captain's call to hold a referendum on MMP, which blindsided his own caucus.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki under fire for telling police to wait six months for investigation information
World.content:
The chief victims advisor has "significant concern" about revelations Oranga Tamariki told police they would have to wait almost six months for information requested as part of a investigation.

She also wants to know how one of 40 child protection complaints that have been re-opened was closed without the victim's details.

It comes after RNZ received more than 100 pages of emails under the Official Information Act (OIA) in relation to Operation Hark.

Operation Hark began after concerns were raised in May about Detective Inspector Kevan Verry's handling of a historical sexual abuse case in Northland that had sat for a couple of years with no investigation.

That led to more than 50 child protection and sexual assault cases being re-opened.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Police are also reviewing their systems used to manage child protection and sexual assault cases and have established an External Advisory Group to provide external oversight and assurance.

The emails obtained under the OIA revealed that On 25 June, police sent an information request to Oranga Tamariki. Five days later they got a response from OT saying they would grant their request.

"As we are currently receiving more requests than anticipated, we are experiencing delays in processing these."

OT said it would supply the information by 7 December.

Internal police emails reveal the request was urgent because investigators needed information that would help identify the victim including the names and details of children placed in a person's care.

Police then emailed a staff member at OT saying they were taking another look at an older file "which we believe holds risk for both police and OT".

"It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can't elaborate on at this time.

"What I can say is that this IR relates to [redacted] so there is obvious risk and additional scrutiny attached to this."

Police asked for the request to be "escalated in the priority queue".

"The estimated response time of December 2026 by OT is going to create significant problems in addressing the risk."

The documents do not reveal what action, if any, OT took in response. It was not until 6 July, after media began asking questions, that the agency was formally told about what police had dubbed Operation Hark.

Chief victims advisor Ruth Money. NZME / Alex Burton

Chief victims advisor Ruth Money told RNZ on Tuesday she had "significant concern" that OT told police it would take almost six months to get the requested information.

"As the Chief Victims Advisor, I want to understand why this is the case.

"For example, was the initial Police request not clear, or is OT that under resourced that children at risk have to wait this long? I will be following this up because I am sure all the victims and whanau across New Zealand also wish to understand this."

She would also be seeking to understand how a file that had a victim attached to it could be closed "and then seemingly Police do not have the victims details."

"These types of issues are why the external reference group exists and these are the questions we seek to understand and more importantly ensure processes are changed so they are not repeated."

Nine reports of concern

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan earlier told RNZ OT had completed a review of all cases identified by police as potentially impacted and which involved children, all of whom were under 18 at the time of reporting to police.

"We did not identify any cases requiring urgent intervention to keep children safe.

"However, we continue to work with police locally to consider each case, share information, and determine any further actions required."

Asked how many of the Child Protection Protocol cases required further action by OT, Ronan said the agency had worked with police on most of the cases identified thus far to determine what further response was appropriate. This included engaging with children and families.

"Nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases," he said.

A report of concern is a notification to Oranga Tamariki about suspected abuse, neglect, harm, or wellbeing concerns for a child or young person.

RNZ also approached police for comment on the OIA including why the victim's name was not known and why Oranga Tamariki was not informed of the investigation before 6 July.

In response, Detective Superintendent Keith Borrell said police had made specific enquiries with OT "during an early and sensitive stage of our investigations".

"During the initial assessment phase of Operation Hark we were working to understand the scale of the situation. We have shared more fulsome information once it was appropriate to do so with OT."

World.title: CNMI's 2026 general election field takes shape
World.content:
The Northern Mariana Islands' 2026 general election is off to the races, with three tickets competing for governor and lieutenant governor and contested races for other key offices ahead of the 3 November vote.

Former governor Ralph DLG Torres is seeking a return to office under the Republican banner with educator Benjamin Jones Jr as his running mate, while two independent tickets - Blas Jonathan "BJ" Attao and House Speaker Edmund Villagomez, and former education commissioner Dr Lawrence Camacho and former Senate president Edith Deleon Guerrero - are also seeking the Commonwealth's top two posts.

The three lieutenant governor candidates have already faced each other at the Saipan Chamber of Commerce's 2026 CNMI Lt Governor Candidates Business Forum, where the economy, workforce shortages, immigration, tourism, government spending and disaster resilience dominated discussion.

Jones argued that rebuilding the private sector should precede major reductions in government employment.

"Right now, the government looks large because our economy is small," he said.

Edith Deleon Guerrero advocated gradually reducing payroll costs through attrition and using federal grants to offset some expenses now paid from local revenues, while Villagomez called for a detailed assessment of government staffing and greater cross-training of employees.

Workforce availability also emerged as a common concern, with all three supporting Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds' proposed federal legislation aimed at stabilising the CNMI's foreign labour force, including an extension of the Commonwealth-only Transitional Worker programme.

Deleon Guerrero also stressed the need to make the islands more resilient following repeated destructive typhoons.

"We need to harden our infrastructure," she said. "We cannot continue to be waiting for power and water for 30 days, 60 days, 90 days."

The gubernatorial campaign began taking formal shape last 30 July when Attao and Villagomez filed their petitions with the Commonwealth Election Commission.

Villagomez described the filing as the moment when the campaign became tangible.

"Today's an important day for us because this just brings reality closer to officially getting off to the races," he said.

Attao, meanwhile, urged residents to participate in November.

"Your vote is your voice. We're a voice for all, and together we will make the CNMI stronger and prouder," he said.

The Republican Party followed with a mass filing on 3 August led by Torres and King-Hinds, who is seeking a second term as the CNMI's non-voting delegate to the US House of Representatives.

Torres, who lost the 2022 gubernatorial runoff, has put economic recovery, pensions and government services at the centre of his comeback bid.

"We want to give you opportunity, give you, all the retirees, the protection of your pension, and our goal is to bring back our economy," Torres said.

King-Hinds said she has unfinished business in Washington after winning the delegate seat in 2024.

"There's a lot of work that still needs to happen, and we spend much of this term building foundations, building relationships, with the hopes that we open up more opportunities for our people," she said.

She faces independent and former Northern Marianas College president Dr Galvin Guerrero for the delegate seat, with Attao's independent group endorsing Deleon Guerrero's candidacy.

The third gubernatorial ticket became official on 4 August, when Camacho and Deleon Guerrero filed their petitions.

Camacho filed a day after the death of his father, saying his father had urged him to continue the campaign.

"My father passed away yesterday," Camacho said.

"But one thing he said before he passed, as he looked at me straight in the eye, and he said, 'No matter what happens, you must continue on because this is something important, not just for him, for our family, but it is important for our Commonwealth.'"

Deleon Guerrero said the filing formally marked the next stage of their campaign.

"We are very capable. We have the capacity. We have the network. We can definitely push forward and make it a better life," she said.

Away from the gubernatorial contest, voters will also choose a new attorney-general after incumbent Edward Manibusan decided not to seek reelection following three terms in office.

Michael Evangelista, Robert Glass Jr, and Joaquin DLG Torres are competing for the position.

Evangelista said his campaign is focused on protecting the integrity and independence of the Office of the Attorney-General.

"I'm running because I want to protect the integrity of the office and to preserve and hold the highest standard of integrity for this office," he said.

Glass has similarly emphasised independence and transparency, saying the attorney general's decisions should be based on the law rather than political considerations.

"We're not here to just advance a governor's agenda. We're here to make sure that the governor's agenda is done in accordance with law," he said.

Joaquin DLG Torres, meanwhile, said he wants the attorney general to take a more visible role.

"We need an attorney general who's active, who's in front, who faces the problem," he said.

CNMI voters will decide on 3 November who will lead a Commonwealth RNZ Pacific / Mark Rabago

The Republican Party is also fielding candidates across Senate, House, and mayoral races on Saipan, Tinian, Rota, and the Northern Islands.

Its slate includes Senate candidates Vinnie Sablan and Marco Peter on Saipan, Tito Hocog II on Rota, and incumbent senators Jude Hofschneider and Francisco Cruz on Tinian.

The Democratic Party has fielded a smaller legislative slate, including Labor secretary Leila Staffler for the House in Precinct 5, Gabriel Boki Babauta and incumbent Rep Denita Yangetmai in Precinct 3, and Peter Francis Muña in Precinct 5.

Staffler described the party's approach as "quality versus quantity".

"All of the Democrats that are running in this election are definitely quality Democrats. They are people who have integrity, people who believe in accountability and transparency," she said.

The Democratic slate also includes Ricardo Castro Cruz Jr for Precinct 1, Frances Marie "Kika" Guerrero Sablan for Precinct 3, and incumbent Sen Celina Roberto Babauta, who is seeking reelection to the Senate.

World.title: Chorus outages hit fibre internet across Auckland
World.content:
An overnight network update was to blame for as many as 30,000 internet connections cutting out in different parts of Auckland.

RNZ readers on the North Shore, Hibiscus Coast and Papatoetoe have all reported issues with internet.

A Chorus map showed several outages dotted across the Auckland region including the North Shore areas of Albany, Redvale, Long Bay and Rosedale. Browns Bay and Milford were also affected.
